why: Everyone is at risk in extreme heat, and working hardest in the hottest hours increases the danger.
Thirst lags behind dehydration, and salt tablets are not recommended as a control measure.
Sun cream does not prevent heat exhaustion or heatstroke, which depend on workload, hydration and cooling.
bank.ex: Heat and sun risks are controlled by acclimatisation, hydration, shade, rescheduling and skin cover together, because no single measure is enough.
bank.cm: Relying on sun cream and thirst alone while ignoring workload, shade and acclimatisation.

bank.stem: Look at the trench. The operator wants to continue digging along the same line with the machine. What is the most important concern?
o: The yellow pipe is likely a gas service, so machine digging should stop near it, the owner be contacted and further excavation done by hand
The depth is the only real concern because the trench is shallow enough to work in, so the pipes can be dealt with once digging is finished
The colours suggest low-pressure plastic services which are not hazardous, so digging can continue provided the operator slows down and watches closely
The blue pipe is the main concern because water mains cause flooding, so the gas pipe can stay unsupported provided the bucket avoids the blue line
why: Services must be dealt with before further digging, not afterwards, and depth does not make a gas pipe safe.
Plastic gas pipe can be damaged by a bucket, and a strike can lead to escaping gas or explosion.
Blue indicates water, and the unsupported yellow gas pipe next to the bucket is the greater danger.
bank.ex: Colour coding identifies likely services, and yellow marks gas, so a bucket working close to it risks a strike and needs hand digging with the pipe supported.
bank.cm: Carrying on with the machine once services appear because the colours suggest plastic pipes that are tough enough.
bank.alt: An excavator digs in a supported trench beside a street; a yellow pipe and a blue pipe run across the trench close to the bucket.

bank.stem: Tippers leave a wet site with muddy wheels and uncovered spoil loads. The manager has booked a road sweeper once a week and put up "Mud on road" signs, saying the highway is the council's responsibility. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Stop mud and dust leaving at source with wheel washing, a clean exit and sheeted loads, using sweeping only as a back-up as often as needed
Wheel washing is needed only when the site is on clay soil, so on other ground the sweeper and signs will control the problem
Sheeting loads matters only on motorways and fast roads, so on local roads warning signs and sweeping meet the site's duty
A weekly sweep and warning signs are enough, because once the mud is on the public highway the council has to deal with it
why: Any site that can carry soil or dust out on wheels needs controls at the exit, whatever the type of ground.
Uncovered loads can spill or blow dust on any public road, so sheeting is not limited to fast roads.
Whoever allows mud onto the road can be held to account, and signs and a weekly sweep do not stop the hazard arising.
bank.ex: Controlling the material at source stops hazards for road users and the site remains answerable for what its vehicles deposit, so sweeping is a support measure rather than the main control.
bank.cm: Treating mud on the road as a council problem once vehicles have left the gate, rather than something to stop at source.

bank.stem: A drill was held in week one of a frame build. Since then the hoarding has moved, the main stair is closed and a new groundworks subcontractor has started. The manager says the emergency plan was drilled and signed, so nothing more is needed. What is the correct position?
o: Leave the plan unchanged until its next scheduled annual review, since a drill already held proves the arrangements work and new starters can learn them from colleagues
Make the new subcontractor responsible for its own emergency arrangements, because each employer's plan covers its own staff and the principal contractor need not coordinate them
Update the plan for the changes, brief the new subcontractor on routes and alarm signals, and rehearse the revised arrangements, including how rescuers reach the structure
Update the paper plan only, because the emergency services have their own procedures and will find the quickest way in without any on-site briefing or rehearsal
why: A past drill says nothing about a layout that has since changed, and relying on colleagues leaves new arrivals without a proper briefing.
The principal contractor must manage site-wide emergency arrangements so that all trades share one plan, rather than leaving separate plans to conflict.
Responders depend on accurate access routes and site information, and an untested paper change gives workers no practice of the new arrangements.
bank.ex: Emergency procedures must reflect the site as it now is, so changed layouts and new arrivals require revised arrangements, briefing and rehearsal, including access for rescue and the emergency services.
bank.cm: Assuming that one successful drill and a signed emergency plan stay valid however much the site layout and workforce change afterwards.

bank.stem: In a damp basement, 110 V centre-tapped festoon lighting hangs at head height. Several lamps have no guards and one cable joint is wrapped in insulating tape. The electrician says the 110 V supply makes the system safe. Which statement is most accurate?
o: He is right, because a centre-tapped 110 V supply limits any shock to a harmless level, so only the transformer itself needs to be checked for damp
Lowering the lights to floor level fixes the problem, since lamps below head height are out of the way and damp has little effect on a 110 V supply
Taped joints are acceptable in damp conditions if a competent electrician makes them and the circuit is protected by an RCD, so the fault is minor
Reduced voltage cuts shock severity but not damage or moisture, so lamps need guards and the taped joint needs a suitably rated connector
why: Reduced voltage lowers but does not eliminate the risk, and damaged lamps and cable joints remain hazards.
Lamps and joints at floor level are more exposed to standing water and impact, which worsens the damp hazard.
Tape does not restore a joint's moisture protection or mechanical strength, and an RCD does not make a poor repair suitable.
bank.ex: A 110 V centre-tapped supply reduces the risk but does not remove it, and temporary installations in damp places still need robust, guarded and properly rated fittings and connections.
bank.cm: Treating a reduced-voltage supply as the whole answer to electrical risk in damp conditions and ignoring the condition of the fittings.

bank.stem: A telehandler operator starts a prescribed painkiller whose leaflet warns of drowsiness. He tells nobody, saying the drug is legal and he feels fine. His supervisor later learns of it. What should happen next?
o: Take him off safety-critical driving, assess his fitness with the prescriber or occupational health, and make clear such medicines are reported
Test him for illegal drugs only, because a company policy on drugs and alcohol applies to banned substances and not to medicines
Let him drive if he drinks coffee and takes more breaks, as self-monitoring is enough for a worker who says he feels alert and capable
Let him continue because a legal prescription makes the drug acceptable, and check his fitness only if there is an incident or visible impairment at work
why: Policies on fitness cover legal medicines that affect safe operation as well as illegal drugs and alcohol.
Drowsiness can be unnoticed by the person affected, so self-judgement and caffeine are not reliable controls.
Legality does not remove the impairment risk, so waiting for an incident is too late.
bank.ex: Prescribed drugs can impair alertness, so safety-critical workers must report them and the employer must manage fitness for the task.
bank.cm: Believing that a medicine from a doctor needs no mention to the employer, whatever the job.

bank.stem: A pan of cooking oil on the hob in the welfare cabin catches fire. One worker grabs a bucket of water to throw over it, while another suggests carrying the pan outside. Which action is correct?
o: Open the windows and doors to clear the smoke, then let the oil burn out under supervision while the cabin is ventilated
Carry the pan outside at arm's length, because removing the fire from the cabin protects the building and the people inside it
Raise the alarm and, if safe, switch off the heat and use a wet chemical extinguisher or fire blanket; otherwise leave and close the door
Throw the water from a safe distance, since a large volume will cool the pan quickly and put out the flames before the oil can spread to the cabin
why: More air feeds the fire, and leaving it to burn out ignores the danger of it spreading to the cabin.
Moving a burning pan risks spilling fat onto the carrier and spreading the fire along the route.
Water sinks below the burning oil and flashes to steam, throwing flaming fat across the room.
bank.ex: Fat fires need smothering or cooling with a suitable agent after the heat is removed, and anyone who cannot do that safely should evacuate and raise the alarm.
bank.cm: Reaching for water on any fire because it is the nearest and most familiar extinguishing agent.

bank.stem: A self-employed welder fixing a gate leaves an unfenced, unlit pit beside a public footpath overnight. He says health and safety law protects employees, and that the principal contractor is responsible for the whole site. Which statement is most accurate?
o: He owes a duty to the public only when a written contract with the principal contractor says so, because contracts define exactly who his work must protect.
The Act's duties cover employees, so a passer-by falls outside what he owes, and responsibility for the footpath rests with the principal contractor on site.
His duty ends when he leaves site for the day, because the principal contractor takes over control of his work area and its hazards overnight.
He has his own duty as a self-employed person to protect others affected by his work, such as passers-by, whatever the principal contractor also owes.
why: Statutory duties to non-employees exist by law and do not depend on any contract wording.
This wrongly limits the Act to employees, when section 3 protects other people affected by a self-employed person's work.
The hazard he created remains his responsibility, and leaving it unfenced and unlit is the failing.
bank.ex: The Health and Safety at Work Act extends duties to the self-employed for the safety of non-employees, so a pit left open beside a public footpath is his breach whatever the principal contractor also owes.
bank.cm: Assuming that health and safety duties belong only to employers and only to their own workers.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The groundworker says he is fully protected because he has everything the site rules ask for. Which item of protection is missing?
o: A full-face respirator, because cutting green timber releases fine dust that is as harmful as silica and is breathed in deeply by the sawyer.
Arm guards over the sleeves, because the forearm is the part of the body most often struck during a chainsaw cut on a fallen branch.
A fall-arrest harness with a lanyard, because a heavy branch could pull him off balance while he is cutting it up on the ground.
Cut-resistant chainsaw trousers, because a chain that kicks or slips strikes the thighs first and ordinary clothing gives no resistance.
why: Green timber cutting is not a respirable silica task, and the visible gap in the PPE is leg protection.
The thigh is the usual injury site, and arm guards are not the standard missing item here.
He is working at ground level beside a trestle, so a harness is not relevant to the hazard shown.
bank.ex: The picture shows head, face, hearing, hand and foot protection but plain denim jeans, and cut-resistant leg protection is the essential item for chainsaw use.
bank.cm: Checking that a worker has a full set of PPE without checking that it matches the part of the body the tool threatens.
bank.alt: A worker cuts a log on a trestle with a chainsaw; he wears a helmet with visor and ear defenders, a hi-vis jacket, gloves, jeans and boots.

bank.stem: A foreman who does the task daily and knows the site writes his gang's RAMS. The principal contractor rejects them because he holds no safety qualification. At the briefing, one operative signs but admits he did not follow the work sequence. What is the correct position?
o: Knowing the task and site makes the foreman competent to write them, but the operative must have the RAMS re-explained before starting
The foreman may write them, and the signature protects the firm, so work may start if the operative's comment is noted in the daily diary
The RAMS must be rewritten by a qualified safety professional, and the operative's signature is valid once he has been given a full copy to read first
The foreman may write them only if the client's adviser co-signs, and the briefing is complete once every operative has been handed a copy
why: A signature without understanding does not make the briefing effective, and noting a concern is no substitute for resolving it.
No formal safety qualification is required to write RAMS, and receiving a copy does not prove the operative understood the controls.
No co-signature is required for competent authorship, and handing out copies does not equal a briefing that people understand.
bank.ex: A competent person with real knowledge of the task and site can write RAMS, and an operative's signature only shows understanding if the briefing has genuinely been understood.
bank.cm: Treating a signature on a briefing sheet as proof that the operative understood the RAMS.

bank.stem: A crew will break out a thick concrete slab using pneumatic breakers all week. Daily exposure is assessed above the upper action value. The supervisor plans extra ear defenders. A hire firm offers a hydraulic crusher. What is the best approach?
o: Keep the breakers and issue higher-rated ear defenders, because protection that cuts noise sufficiently satisfies the regulations
Use the crusher but skip the noise assessment, since a quieter machine means the exposure limits cannot be reached in the work area
Use the quieter, lower-vibration crusher if it suits the job, with hearing protection kept for any remaining noise
Keep the breakers and shorten each operative's turn on the tool, since limiting time is the preferred way to control noise exposure
why: Hearing protection comes after reducing noise at source, and does nothing for the vibration the breakers also cause.
A quieter machine reduces exposure but the assessment still has to confirm the remaining levels and what controls are needed.
Limiting time is a weaker administrative control than removing the noise source through a quieter method.
bank.ex: Reducing noise and vibration at source by changing the method ranks above relying on hearing protection, which is only the last line of defence once other measures have been used.
bank.cm: Reaching for ear defenders first instead of asking whether a quieter method could remove the noise.

bank.stem: A contractor will strip the front of a corner shop on a busy road opposite a primary school. His assessor writes that only employees are at risk, as members of the public are not on his payroll. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The assessment must also cover pedestrians and schoolchildren, with controls such as hoarding, protected walkways and timed deliveries
Employee-only assessments are acceptable, as the local council is responsible for keeping the pavements and school routes safe near building work
A single warning sign at the site entrance removes the duty, since people choosing to walk past have accepted the risk themselves
The public only need covering if an incident occurs, so keeping a record of any near misses involving passers-by is enough for now
why: The contractor creating the risk holds the duty and cannot pass it to the council.
A sign alone is a weak control and passers-by, especially children, cannot accept risks they cannot see.
Risks to the public must be assessed beforehand, and waiting for harm to occur is not prevention.
bank.ex: Employers must assess risks to other people affected by their work, and vulnerable groups such as children near a site need specific controls.
bank.cm: Believing that duties to assess risk apply only to your own workforce and not to passers-by or neighbours.

bank.stem: A gang needs somewhere to keep six full and four empty LPG cylinders for roofing torches on a site with a basement car park and a surface-water drain beside the compound. Which storage arrangement best controls the fire and explosion risk?
o: Inside a locked, unventilated store room within the main building, because shelter from the weather and from theft is the main concern
A locked steel container at the lowest point of the car park, with cylinders laid flat so that they cannot fall over and rupture a valve
A secure, ventilated outdoor cage on level ground with cylinders upright, valves closed, clear of drains and the basement, and full and empty kept apart
Beside the drain under a tarpaulin, so that any leaking gas drains away from the working areas and out of the site altogether
why: Enclosed storage lets leaking gas build up to explosive concentrations, so ventilation matters more than shelter.
Low points collect heavy LPG vapour, and cylinders should be stored upright rather than lying flat.
Vapour entering a drain can travel and collect elsewhere, and a tarpaulin traps leaks rather than letting gas disperse.
bank.ex: LPG vapour is heavier than air and collects in low points and drains, so open-air, upright, secure storage away from ignition sources and below-ground spaces limits the risk.
bank.cm: Choosing a lockable low or enclosed store to prevent theft without thinking about where heavier-than-air gas would collect.

bank.stem: Roofers cleaning hot bitumen off their hands and forearms use rags soaked in white spirit, then eat sandwiches. The supervisor says skin checks are only needed if someone complains of a rash. What should the employer do?
o: Keep the white spirit but issue barrier cream, since cream applied before work lets rags be used safely and replaces checks
Provide skin cleansers with hot and cold water, stop solvent cleaning, and have trained staff check skin regularly
Change nothing until a worker reports a rash, because health surveillance is only triggered once a problem has been reported by a worker
Allow the rags but provide a clean eating area in the cabin, because separating eating from cleaning deals with skin exposure
why: Barrier cream does not make solvent cleaning safe and is not a substitute for proper washing facilities or checks.
Waiting for symptoms means damage is already done, and the point of checks is to find problems early.
Eating separately lowers the chance of swallowing contamination but does nothing about solvent damage to skin.
bank.ex: Solvents strip skin and carry contaminants in, so safe cleansers, proper washing facilities and regular skin checks help catch dermatitis or early skin damage before it becomes serious.
bank.cm: Waiting for a complaint before looking at workers' skin, instead of checking it regularly where substances are handled.

bank.stem: A lorry must reverse into a site gate across a busy public footway. The marshal stands directly behind it in the gateway and waves pedestrians through behind him whenever the footway looks clear. What is the main fault in this arrangement?
o: He stands in the lorry's path and blind spot, so he should stand clear, stay visible to the driver and keep pedestrians out of the reversing area
He should carry a radio headset and remain behind the lorry, because radio contact lets him warn pedestrians in good time if the driver starts to reverse
His position is acceptable if his clothing is high-visibility, because a reversing driver is required to stop for any person who is wearing it
Pedestrians must be stopped from using the footway altogether for every delivery, because a marshal has no practical means of controlling members of the public
why: A radio does not remove him from the swept path, and a person directly behind a reversing lorry is exposed to being struck.
Visibility helps but does not make a blind spot safe, and drivers cannot be relied on to see or stop in time.
Closing the footway is not the only control, as a marshal can hold pedestrians clear from a safe position, with barriers or planned routes where needed.
bank.ex: A signaller must stand in a safe position out of the vehicle's way, be visible to the driver at all times and keep the reversing area clear of pedestrians.
bank.cm: Thinking that a marshal standing behind a reversing vehicle can safely control pedestrians just by watching them and waving.

bank.stem: On a two-storey house extension with a 40-degree pitched roof, a scaffold with guardrails runs along the eaves only. Roofers must fix barge boards along the gable verge. The foreman says the eaves protection covers the whole roof. What is the correct view?
o: The verge is a separate fall edge needing its own edge protection, such as a gable scaffold lift, with harnesses only as a fallback
Harnesses clipped to the ridge are enough for the verge, as collective protection is needed only where roofers work alone on the slope
Keeping a metre back from the verge in dry weather is enough, since careful, experienced roofers reduce the need for any edge protection at all
The eaves guardrails count for every edge of the roof, because a person falling at the verge would be stopped by the same top rail
why: Collective protection should come before personal protection, which depends on correct use, a sound anchor and a rescue plan.
Reliance on behaviour and weather is not a control, and a fall of this height can seriously injure whoever slips.
A guardrail protects only the edge it runs along, and the gable verge lies beyond it.
bank.ex: Edge protection protects only where it is fitted, and collective measures take priority over personal fall protection at every edge from which a person could fall.
bank.cm: Assuming edge protection at the eaves covers every other edge of a roof, such as verges and gable ends.

bank.stem: A scraper strips a patch of textured ceiling coating in a school corridor, and a lab result later suggests it contained asbestos. A colleague proposes brushing the dust off the floor with the site dustpan and washing his overalls at home. What is the correct response?
o: Lightly spray the dust and sweep it up with the dustpan, then wash the overalls at home on a hot cycle to remove fibres
Carry on once the dust is out of sight, since one short disturbance of a thin coating is too small an exposure to matter
Use the site vacuum cleaner on the floor, because a few minutes of suction is safe for such a small patch of dust
Stop work, keep others away, tell the supervisor, leave cleaning to trained staff using damp methods, and bag the overalls as waste
why: Sweeping still raises fibres and domestic washing carries them into the home and the machine.
Any exposure matters and the area must be controlled, because no safe level of asbestos exposure is known.
An ordinary vacuum passes fine fibres through its filter back into the air and is not suitable for asbestos.
bank.ex: Dry brushing and taking clothing home spread fibres, so work stops and trained people clean up using damp or Class H methods while contaminated overalls are treated as asbestos waste.
bank.cm: Assuming that a small amount of dust can be tidied away with ordinary site cleaning tools before telling anyone.

bank.stem: A firm hires a scissor-lift MEWP to change light fittings in a warehouse. The trained operator will work alone in the platform, and nobody else has looked at the machine's controls. Besides the operator's pre-use checks, which arrangement must be in place before the lift starts?
o: A delivery check carried out by the hire company, which covers the machine for the hire and makes daily user checks unnecessary.
The fire service number displayed by the machine, as the brigade will carry out any rescue if the platform fails or the operator is taken ill.
A colleague standing at the base to hand up tools, who can pull the emergency lowering lever if the operator shouts for help.
A rescue plan naming someone trained to use the ground controls and emergency lowering, and a marked exclusion zone below the platform.
why: The hire company's inspection does not replace the operator's pre- use check, and it says nothing about rescue or the area underneath.
Relying on the emergency services leaves the operator stranded for too long, and a rescue plan must be workable by people on site.
A person who has not been trained on the controls may lower the machine wrongly, and standing under the platform puts him in the fall zone.
bank.ex: If the platform stops with the operator aloft, a trained person must be able to bring him down quickly, and the zone below keeps people clear of falling tools and moving parts.
bank.cm: Assuming a MEWP rescue can be worked out on the day if something goes wrong.

bank.stem: A contractor wants to crane a 4-tonne mini excavator onto a first-floor suspended slab to break out a screed. The slab is cured and looks sound. What must be established before the machine goes on it?
o: That the machine runs on rubber tracks, which spread its weight enough that no check of the slab structure is then needed at all
That the concrete is over 28 days old, because slabs reach full design capacity then, whatever the load placed on them
That the machine's weight is below the crane's rated capacity, since a satisfactory crane check also proves the slab can bear it afterwards
The slab's permitted loading, including track point loads, confirmed by a competent person such as the structural designer
why: Rubber tracks lower ground pressure but the total and point loads still need checking against the slab design.
Age shows strength gain but does not confirm the slab was designed for this machine's loading.
The crane's rating relates to the lift and says nothing about what the slab can carry afterwards.
bank.ex: A suspended slab has a limited design capacity, so a competent person must confirm it can carry the machine, its point loads and other loads on that floor.
bank.cm: Judging a floor by how solid it looks instead of checking what the structure was designed to carry.

bank.stem: On the fifth floor of a concrete frame, a plasterer will work beside an unprotected lift-shaft door opening. The planner proposes orange mesh fencing on freestanding feet plus a sign, saying only lift installers will need the gap. Which control is required before plastering starts?
o: Let the plasterer work if he wears a harness clipped to a mobile anchor, with the barrier deferred until the lift installers arrive
Post a colleague to watch the opening during plastering, because a lookout can warn the plasterer before he gets too close to the edge
Keep the freestanding mesh and add a taped line two metres back, since keeping distance from the opening is as good as a fixed guardrail does
Fit a rigid barrier fixed to the structure, with top rail, intermediate rail and toe board, able to take a falling person
why: Personal protection with a mobile anchor is lower in the hierarchy than a fixed barrier and leaves others exposed to the opening.
A lookout is an administrative control that fails when attention lapses and does not physically stop a fall.
Tape and distance only warn, and a person stumbling or pushing a trolley can still reach the opening.
bank.ex: Openings need robust, fixed collective protection that can resist a person's weight, which freestanding mesh and signs cannot do.
bank.cm: Believing a sign, tape or freestanding mesh counts as edge protection simply because it is visible.

bank.stem: Groundworks 20 m from a pond holding great crested newts are covered by a licence method statement requiring an exclusion fence. A dumper flattens 6 m of fence, and an open pipe trench is left overnight beside the gap. What is the best response?
o: Cover the trench each evening and continue working, because the licence applies only when a newt has actually been seen on site
Repair the fence at the start of next shift and continue, since newts are active at night and the gap was not open while work was under way
Carry on and ask the dumper driver to watch for newts as he works, because a sighting would then trigger a stop under the method statement
Stop work in the affected area, have the ecologist check and reinstate the fence, and fit ramps or covers to the trench first
why: The licence conditions apply to the whole works area, whether or not an animal has been seen.
Newts may already be inside the area, and continuing without a check risks killing or injuring them.
Spotting animals by chance is not a control, and the damaged fence must be dealt with first.
bank.ex: Newts may already be inside the working area or trapped in the trench, so work stops until the licensed ecologist checks and the barrier and trench are made safe for wildlife.
bank.cm: Treating wildlife protection measures as paperwork that only matters once an animal has actually been seen.

bank.stem: A kerb layer returns after seven months off with a lower-back injury. He says he feels fine and wants his old full duties from day one. The site manager must decide how to bring him back. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Keep him away until he is completely free of any restriction, because an employer cannot support any adjustments to a worker's duties
Give him light duties with no end date and no review, since a lighter workload removes the need for any further follow-up
Accept his own judgement and return him to full duties, because a competent adult knows his body better than his employer does
Hold a return conversation, agree phased lifting adjustments, review his manual handling assessment, and check progress regularly
why: Reasonable adjustments are encouraged, and waiting for full recovery with no support can prolong absence needlessly.
Open- ended light duties without review fail to support recovery and ignore changes in his condition or ability.
Employers still owe a duty of care, so the worker's confidence does not replace a planned return and review of the risks.
bank.ex: A planned, reviewed return with agreed adjustments protects against relapse, and the employer should review risk assessments for the individual rather than rely on the worker's own opinion.
bank.cm: Assuming a worker who says he is fine can go straight back to full duties without a planned, reviewed return.

bank.stem: A 14-employee groundworks firm has no recognised trade union. Staff elect a colleague as their representative of employee safety, but the owner says he need only consult union-appointed representatives, and any training would be in the colleague's own time. Which statement is correct?
o: He may consult only the foreman, who then passes decisions on, as long as the firm keeps a signed record that staff were told
He must consult, though elected representatives have no right to paid time for their role and the owner alone decides what is discussed
Consultation applies only where a union is recognised, but an elected colleague may attend training at his own expense if the firm gives approval first
Staff must still be consulted, directly or through elected representatives, who get paid time off and training at the employer's cost
why: Passing on decisions is information, not consultation, which means listening to employees' views before decisions are made.
Elected representatives are entitled to paid time off, and consultation must cover set matters such as new equipment, training and competent persons.
The duty to consult covers employees not represented by a union, and the employer must bear the cost of reasonable training.
bank.ex: Where there is no union safety representative the employer must consult employees directly or through elected representatives of employee safety, who get reasonable training and paid time off to carry out the role.
bank.cm: Thinking consultation on safety is a union matter that a non-union firm can skip or leave to one trusted supervisor.

bank.stem: A haul route for excavators and dumpers must cross beneath an 11 kV overhead line. The planner proposes leaving the route open, trusting operators to keep their booms low and a banksman to watch the gap. What is the better control?
o: Rely on the line being insulated, because covered conductors can be passed at any height by plant without any exclusion zone being set
Keep the banksman's watch and ask drivers to go slowly, because a trained person on the spot can stop a vehicle that gets too close to the wires
Mark the line with red and white bunting along the full route, since a visible warning lets experienced operators judge a safe gap for themselves
Consult the line owner, fence off the zone, and allow one goalposted crossing with a clearance-height notice, so plant passes with booms lowered
why: Insulation on overhead lines cannot be relied on to protect against contact, so exclusion zones still apply.
A banksman cannot reliably judge clearance to a high line, and people are not a physical barrier.
Warning flags alone do not physically restrain plant, and judging distances by eye risks arcing.
bank.ex: HSE guidance says to keep plant out of the zone with ground-level barriers, to create a minimum number of marked passageways with non-conducting goalposts, and to consult the line owner.
bank.cm: Relying on operator judgement or a spotter to keep plant clear of overhead lines instead of physical barriers and a controlled crossing.

bank.stem: A mobile crane on a quiet road will lift roof trusses over the site hoarding, and the slew path crosses the public footway. The crane supervisor proposes a banksman who stops pedestrians for each lift, with no barriers. Which approach is correct?
o: Plan the lifts so loads avoid the footway, or close and divert it with barriers while lifting, as part of the lift plan
Lift only when the footway looks empty, judged by the operator from the cab, since no one can be harmed if nobody is there
A banksman holding pedestrians back is enough, because each lift lasts only seconds and he can watch the load and the footway together
Wrap the trusses in netting and use slings of a higher rating, so a dropped load cannot reach anyone on the footway
why: A pedestrian can step into the danger zone at any moment and the operator cannot see the whole footway from the cab.
One person cannot reliably control passers-by while also directing a lift, and a short exposure still carries a serious consequence.
Stronger slings and netting reduce some risks but do not prevent a load swinging or falling onto people below.
bank.ex: The lift plan must remove people from the danger area, and physically closing or avoiding the footway is more reliable than relying on one person to stop pedestrians.
bank.cm: Depending on one person or a quiet period to keep the public safe instead of keeping the public out of the lifting area.

bank.stem: A supplier replaces the FFP3 disposable masks a clean-shaven gang passed fit tests on with a different make of the same class. They look similar, so the supervisor says the earlier fit tests still apply. Which statement is correct?
o: A fit test applies to a specific make, model and size, so each wearer needs a new test on the new mask, plus a fit check at each donning
The earlier tests remain valid because both masks are the same FFP3 class, and the class marking guarantees an equivalent seal on every face shape
A new test is needed only for workers who report a leak, as the others have shown they can achieve a seal and will notice any problem themselves
A new test is unnecessary if the wearers are clean-shaven, since the absence of facial hair removes the main cause of a mask failing to seal
why: The class describes filter efficiency, not how well the mask seals on a given face.
Wearers cannot reliably detect a poor seal by feel, so everyone using the new mask needs testing.
Being clean-shaven helps but does not guarantee fit, as mask shape and size also determine the seal.
bank.ex: Face shapes suit different masks differently, so a fit test only validates the make, model and size tested, and a user seal check is still needed each time the mask is put on.
bank.cm: Treating a passed fit test as a personal qualification rather than a check on one particular make, model and size of mask.

bank.stem: A housing site backs onto a play area. At finish, a telehandler is left beside the hoarding with its engine off and brake on, but the forks are raised and the key stays in the cab to save time at 7 am. What is wrong?
o: Nothing, because the brake being on and the engine being off make it safe, and leaving the key in lets the early crew move it quickly in an emergency
The forks need lowering, but the key may stay in the cab if the site gate is locked, since a locked gate keeps all unauthorised people out
The forks should be lowered and the key removed and secured, so that unauthorised people, including children, cannot start or climb on it
The key must be removed, but the forks may stay raised, since raised forks are harder for a trespasser or a child to climb onto from the ground
why: Leaving the key in and the forks raised allows unauthorised use and climbing, and an early start is not a reason to relax security.
Gates and hoardings can be climbed or breached, so the key still needs to be secured as a second barrier.
Raised forks can fall or be climbed, and attachments should be lowered to the ground to remove stored energy and access.
bank.ex: Unattended plant should be left with brakes on, engine off, equipment lowered and keys removed and secured, which stops unauthorised use and removes a fall and crush hazard.
bank.cm: Assuming that a locked gate, a brake and an off engine are enough to secure plant overnight.

bank.stem: A fitter cuts out a corroded pipe with an oxy-propane torch that throws molten globules and hot spatter near his face. He is given clear spectacles marked '3 F' and told they are rated for splashes. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Field-of-use numbers rank the protection, so a '9' lens resists everything and the '3' is a weaker version suitable only for lighter spatter
The '3' covers every liquid hazard including molten metal, and the 'F' shows the lenses are heat resistant, so the spectacles suit the task
The '3' covers liquid droplets and splashes, not molten metal, so he needs eye protection marked '9' for molten metals and hot solids
Any eyewear with an impact rating is adequate for hot work, provided the lenses are tinted dark enough to cut the glare from the torch flame
why: The numbers identify different fields of use and are not a scale, so a higher number is not a stronger version.
The F marks low-energy impact resistance only and says nothing about heat, and the 3 does not cover molten metal.
Impact resistance and tint do not give protection from molten metal, which needs the field-of-use symbol 9.
bank.ex: In EN 166 the field-of-use symbol 3 means liquid droplets or splashes, while 9 means molten metals and hot solids, and the F only shows resistance to low-energy impact.
bank.cm: Reading a lens marking as a general quality rating instead of checking that the symbol matches the actual hazard.

bank.stem: A firm's method statement for roof sheeting sets out sound controls, but nobody checks that the gangs follow them. After a near miss, the director says the paperwork proves the risk is managed. What is the best view?
o: The gang leaders should sign a statement each month that they followed the plan, and no supervision is then needed
The paperwork is enough because the law requires the plan to exist, and gangs are assumed to follow what is written
Checks are needed only after an injury, so the near miss changes nothing until somebody is actually harmed
Controls must be monitored on site by supervision and checks, then reviewed, because a written plan alone does not show it is working
why: A signed statement without observation does not check that controls are working.
Having a plan does not show it is followed, and the duty is to manage the risk in practice.
Monitoring should be continuing and a near miss is a prompt to review.
bank.ex: Risk assessment does not end with writing controls down: supervisors must check they are in place and effective, and findings should feed a review.
bank.cm: Treating a written method statement as proof that the risk is controlled without checking the work.

bank.stem: A rubble chute is fixed from a second-floor opening into a skip. It is loosely tied at the top, has a gap at one joint and the skip stands uncovered in a pedestrian route. A labourer says the chute is just a way to tip waste safely. What is needed?
o: Leave the arrangement as it is, since any chute is accepted as proof that debris is being safely lowered to the skip
Have someone watch the pedestrian route and shout when waste is tipped, instead of fixing the chute and fencing the skip
Secure and join the chute properly, enclose the skip area with a barrier and control the loading, so debris cannot fall on people
Put a sign beside the skip warning pedestrians, because a sign is enough to keep people out of a drop zone
why: A poorly fixed chute with gaps can still drop debris onto a route used by people.
A watcher cannot stop debris leaving through a gap and shouting is unreliable.
A sign does not physically prevent people being struck.
bank.ex: A chute reduces falling debris only if it is secure, free of gaps and discharges into a controlled area, so the zone beneath needs to be fenced and managed.
bank.cm: Assuming that fitting a chute is enough without checking its joints, fixings and the area where it discharges.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. Which feature creates the most serious risk of a fatal injury to the operator?
o: His body is trapped between the beam and the controls if he is pushed forward, and nobody at ground level is placed to lower the basket
The cordless drill is held above head height, which could cause an overreaching strain and a risk of the drill or its battery being dropped
The harness is clipped to the basket anchor point, which will drag the operator out of the basket if the boom suddenly moves
The boom is not set on outriggers, so the whole machine will overturn when the operator moves around inside the raised basket
why: Overhead drilling carries ergonomic and dropped-object risks, but these are minor compared with entrapment against the structure.
Clipping to the basket anchor is normal practice for a boom MEWP and is not the most serious hazard in the scene.
A boom MEWP of this type on firm level concrete does not need outriggers to be used safely, and the operator's movement within the basket is not the main danger.
bank.ex: Operators have been crushed between an overhead obstruction and the basket controls, and a trained person at the base controls can lower the platform quickly in an emergency.
bank.cm: Assuming that a harness and intact guardrails make a MEWP basket safe, when the structure overhead can crush the operator.
bank.alt: An operator in the basket of a boom-type mobile elevating work platform works directly under a steel roof beam in a warehouse; another worker walks away across the floor.

bank.stem: A sub-contractor is hired for a two-day job fitting glazed roof panels. Its owner, a fitter with thirty years' experience but no assessment training, writes the risk assessment alone without speaking to his two operatives, saying a short job needs little. What is the best view?
o: The principal contractor's generic site assessment can stand in for it, since the two operatives will be working under that company's control on site
A brief assessment is acceptable for jobs of under three days, provided the owner signs it and tells the operatives about the controls on the first morning
The assessor needs knowledge of the work plus an understanding of risk assessment, and should talk to the people doing the job, however short
Thirty years of practical experience makes him competent to assess it alone, because nobody understands the hazards of glazing better than the fitter himself
why: A generic site document cannot cover the specific hazards of the sub-contractor's own task, so the employer must still assess its own work.
The duty to assess does not depend on how long a job lasts, and a briefing after the event does not replace gathering their input beforehand.
Task experience does not by itself give the skill to identify hazards systematically, rank risks and record controls, and it ignores what the operatives can add.
bank.ex: Competence means enough training, knowledge and experience for the task in hand, and assessments must reflect how the work is really done, so involving the operatives matters on a short job as much as a long one.
bank.cm: Assuming that years of practical experience, or the shortness of a job, can stand in for assessment skills and input from the people doing the work.

bank.stem: An inspector finds a hired-in concrete pump being run with its boom hose clamp visibly worn, and fears a hose could whip loose. The site manager says no notice can be served because no regulation is named and only the employer can receive one. What is correct?
o: The inspector may only serve an Improvement Notice with a compliance period, since the pump is hired and the hire company holds the legal duty
A notice needs a proven breach of a named regulation and must go to the employer, so the inspector can only give verbal advice until one is found
A Prohibition Notice can be served only after an injury has happened, because the inspector must show the risk has already caused serious harm
A Prohibition Notice goes to whoever controls the activity if the inspector sees a risk of serious personal injury, with no breach needed
why: An Improvement Notice needs a contravention and gives time to comply, whereas a serious risk can be stopped at once whoever owns the equipment.
Both halves are wrong, because a breach is not a precondition and the notice goes to whoever controls the activity.
The power exists to stop a risk before harm occurs, so no injury is required.
bank.ex: The test for a Prohibition Notice is the inspector's opinion of a risk of serious personal injury, and it goes to the person in control of the activity, which may be an operator rather than the employer.
bank.cm: Assuming an inspector needs a named legal breach, or must deal only with the employer, before stopping a dangerous activity.

bank.stem: A loaded dumper is bogged to its axles in soft clay. The foreman wants to pull it out with a chain from an excavator, looped round the dumper's front axle, and tells two labourers to guide the chain from beside the dumper. What is the best approach?
o: Use designated recovery points with rated tackle, pull in line slowly without jerking, and keep everyone clear of the pulling line
Loop the chain round the axle but have the labourers stand behind a plant-mounted guard while the excavator takes up the slack with a sharp tug to free it
Let the labourers stay close to the dumper to watch the chain, since they can warn the driver sooner if the chain begins to slip or the tackle shifts
Empty the dumper first, then pull from any strong part of the frame using an old chain, since the lighter load removes the need for special care
why: A sharp tug increases shock loading, and axles and unrated chain are not designed as recovery points.
People near a loaded chain are in the recoil path, and signalling should come from a safe distance outside the line.
A lighter load does not make unrated tackle or an unsuitable fixing point safe.
bank.ex: Recovery loads can be high and a failed link or chain can recoil, so rated gear on designated points and an exclusion zone along the line protect people.
bank.cm: Treating recovery of stuck plant as a quick improvised job where any chain and any strong-looking part will do.

bank.stem: A permit to work for maintenance on a roof-mounted extract fan is valid from 07:00 to 15:00. At 14:30 the engineer says the job needs another two hours, and the isolation is still in place. What should happen?
o: The engineer can carry on to finish, since the isolation is unchanged, and then note the overrun on his own copy when he hands the permit back
The engineer can extend it himself by writing a later time on his copy, because as the holder he best knows how long the task will take
Work can continue until 17:00 because a permit stays valid until the task it describes is complete, whatever times are written on it
Work should stop at expiry unless the issuing authorised person re-checks the area and signs an extension with a new expiry time
why: An expired permit gives no authority to work, and noting the overrun afterwards does not replace the issuer's check.
Only the authorised person who issued the permit may extend it, not the person holding it.
A permit is a time-limited document, and the stated expiry time is part of the control.
bank.ex: A permit is time-limited, and it can only be extended by the person who issued it after confirming the area is still safe and that everyone working under it knows the details.
bank.cm: Treating the end time on a permit as a rough guide that the holder can stretch when a job runs late.

bank.stem: Debris has built up in the pit under a material hoist, whose platform is parked at third-floor level. A labourer plans to climb in and shovel it out, saying the hoist is switched off and the gate is shut. What should happen first?
o: Finish the clean-out quickly with the platform parked, because the pit is entered for only a few minutes and the brake is holding the load
Station a colleague at the control with a radio, so he can stop the platform at once if it starts to move while the pit is being cleared
Isolate and lock off the hoist, then mechanically support the raised platform so it cannot descend, before anyone enters the pit
Switch off at the hoist control and close the landing gate, because an unpowered platform stays where it was left and cannot fall on someone
why: A short exposure does not make it safe to stand beneath a platform held only by its brake.
A person at the controls cannot stop a mechanical failure, and a radio call is too slow to prevent a fall.
Isolation alone relies on the rope and brake holding, and a failure would drop the platform onto the labourer.
bank.ex: Entry beneath a raised platform needs power isolation and a positive mechanical support, because brakes, controls and switches can fail.
bank.cm: Trusting a switched-off control or a brake to hold a raised platform while someone is underneath it.

bank.stem: A contractor works nights beside a hedgerow and housing. Two tower floodlights are aimed horizontally to light the work, and light floods bedroom windows and the hedge where bats and birds feed. Residents complain. What is the best response?
o: Leave the lights as they are because night work needs strong lighting, and tell residents to close their curtains if they object
Aim lights downward, shield and lower them, use only the lighting needed and switch off when not working, keeping spill off the hedge
Keep the lights on all night so that the hedge and the work area stay lit, which is said to deter bats and birds from nesting
Raise the lights higher on the towers to reach more of the site, since a wider beam spreads the light thinner over homes
why: Spill light can be reduced without making the work unsafe.
Continuous light can disturb wildlife and increases the nuisance.
Higher lights usually spill more widely over neighbours and wildlife.
bank.ex: Light can be a nuisance to neighbours and harm wildlife, so lights should be directed to the work area, shielded, kept as low as practicable and switched off when not needed.
bank.cm: Aiming floodlights outward at the site boundary and treating the neighbours' complaints as unavoidable.

bank.stem: A floor layer scrapes old adhesive from a screed using a short- handled hand scraper, kneeling with the wrist cocked upward for hours, and now has forearm pain. The supervisor offers wrist supports. Which change best controls the cause?
o: Issue elasticated wrist supports to every floor layer, because limiting wrist movement removes the strain while the same short scraper is used
Provide a long-handled scraper used standing so the wrist stays straight and the body supplies the force, and mix the task with other work
Rotate a colleague onto the scraper each hour, so total exposure is shared between two people although the short tool and kneeling remain
Supply thick padded gloves, to cushion the handle and spread pressure over the palm, which relieves the strain on the wrist joint
why: Supports mask the symptoms and leave the awkward posture and sustained force that cause the injury unchanged.
Sharing the exposure reduces each person's dose but still puts two people in the same harmful posture.
Bulky gloves reduce grip and often increase the force needed, and they do nothing to correct wrist angle.
bank.ex: Tools should let the wrist stay straight and use a power grip, and removing the kneeling, bent-wrist posture tackles the cause rather than the symptom.
bank.cm: Fixing the worker's wrist with a support instead of fixing the tool and posture that bend it.

bank.stem: A safety representative inspects a loading bay and writes to the site manager about a missing edge barrier and a damaged floodlight cable. The manager replies that this is only opinion, that he will act if an inspector agrees, and that the representative will be liable if anyone is hurt meanwhile. Which statement is correct?
o: The manager keeps his own duty to assess the reported hazards and act in proportion to the risk, and the representative carries no personal liability for them
The manager may wait for an inspector to agree, because a representative's report has no legal weight until an enforcing authority has confirmed it in writing first
The representative is now responsible for the hazards he listed, because putting a problem in writing transfers the duty to deal with it to him
The manager need only act once the representative has served an improvement notice, because reports are not enforceable until formal notice is given
why: An employer's duty arises from the hazard itself and does not depend on an inspector confirming a representative's report.
Reporting a hazard never moves the employer's duty onto the representative, who has no duty under these regulations.
Safety representatives cannot serve notices, which only inspectors can issue, and the employer's duty exists without one.
bank.ex: The employer's general duties apply once he knows of a hazard, and the regulations state that a representative's functions do not impose any duty on him personally.
bank.cm: Assuming a hazard becomes someone else's problem, or can wait for an inspector, once a representative has reported it.

bank.stem: A decorator must move twelve 25-litre drums of masonry sealer, about 27 kg each, from a van up two flights of stairs to a flat. The back-belt-wearing carriers propose one drum per trip with rests. What is the best approach?
o: Hold a briefing on bending the knees and keeping a straight back, as technique training is the main control for repeated stair carrying
Keep the back belts for everyone carrying, as they take the compressive load off the spine and so permit the heavier drums to be carried
Allow one drum per trip with a rest between, since the carried weight is then within a capable adult's strength and no assessment is needed
Cut the handling at source by ordering smaller containers or floor delivery, then assess whatever carrying remains and reduce it further
why: Training supports but does not replace avoiding and reducing the load.
Back belts are not an accepted control for heavy handling and do not remove the risk.
Repeated carrying of heavy loads on stairs still needs avoidance and assessment, whatever one person can manage.
bank.ex: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations require avoiding hazardous handling where reasonably practicable, then assessing and reducing the risk of any that remains.
bank.cm: Relying on lifting technique, rests or support belts instead of first asking whether the load can be avoided or made smaller.

bank.stem: A civil contractor applies a head-office annual test rule to all portable electrical equipment, including 110 V grinders and drills used on a muddy site, where the last test found many failures. A manager says an annual interval is a legal requirement. Which view is most accurate?
o: Because 110 V tools carry little shock risk, they are exempt from formal inspection, so only the 230 V items need any scheduled checks on site
The legal minimum is an annual test for all work equipment, and a rising failure rate only makes a six-monthly test advisable as good practice
The interval is set by the tool maker and cannot be altered by the employer, so the annual rule applies only if the maker's manual states it
The law sets no fixed interval; equipment must be maintained to prevent danger, so frequency should follow risk and be cut where faults are found
why: Reduced voltage lowers the risk but the tools still need maintenance, particularly in harsh conditions.
No legal minimum interval exists, and a high failure rate is itself a reason to increase frequency.
The dutyholder sets the frequency based on risk and need not be limited to a maker's figure.
bank.ex: The Electricity at Work Regulations require maintenance to prevent danger without a set interval, so the frequency of checks and tests should reflect the equipment, environment, use and fault history.
bank.cm: Believing there is a single legal test interval for portable tools instead of setting frequency by risk and fault history.

bank.stem: After a burst pipe, a refurbishment crew must strip black- mould-covered plasterboard from a bedroom. They plan to scrape it off, dry-sweep the debris, then spray bleach over the studs. One labourer already has a chesty cough. Which plan best controls the respiratory risk?
o: Scrape and sweep as planned, then spray bleach on every surface, because bleach kills the spores and so removes the respiratory hazard
Let the crew work in basic dust masks with a window open, because mould is natural and the coughing worker will simply adapt
Stop the leak, remove wet board with dust suppressed and bag it, use fit-tested respiratory protection, and get health advice for the cough
Remove the boards but leave the leak until the end of the job, since the water source does not affect the mould exposure
why: Dry scraping and sweeping throw spores into the air, and dead spores can still trigger allergic and asthmatic reactions.
A basic mask may not suit the exposure, and sensitised or symptomatic workers should not be expected to just adapt.
An active leak keeps the area damp and allows mould to regrow, so the moisture source must be dealt with first.
bank.ex: Cutting off the moisture source, limiting disturbance of spores, using suitable RPE and checking on an already symptomatic worker together tackle both the cause and the exposure.
bank.cm: Believing that killing mould with bleach makes it safe to disturb, when the spores and dust are what people breathe in.

bank.stem: Look at the plasterer working on stilts in the picture. Which condition in the scene is most likely to cause him to fall?
o: The absence of a harness anchor, because anyone working on stilts must be fall-arrested whenever the stilts are raised above knee height
The height setting of the stilts, since adjustable stilts above ankle height are prohibited under the Work at Height Regulations
The wet plaster on the wall ahead of him, which will make him lean away from the surface and lose his footing on the stilts
A trailing cable and loose offcuts lying on the floor across his walking route, which can catch a stilt and throw him off balance
why: No rule requires a harness for stilts, and the real danger is losing balance on the floor because of obstructions.
The regulations do not ban stilts at any set height, and the key control is a clear, even floor for the user.
Wet plaster does not make him lean away, whereas obstructions on the floor are a direct cause of falls.
bank.ex: Stilts raise the user and make him far more sensitive to trip hazards, so the floor must be kept clear of cables, offcuts and debris before he moves around.
bank.cm: Assuming that stilts are safe because the user is not far off the ground, and ignoring trip hazards on the floor.
bank.alt: A plasterer on stilts works in an empty room; an extension cable and offcuts of board lie on the floor.

bank.stem: Roofers set up a bitumen boiler on a flat roof 3 m from a plant-room air intake serving the occupied offices below. Fumes are drifting into the building. The foreman proposes handing out disposable dust masks. What is the best response?
o: Move the boiler well away from and downwind of the intake, agree with building management to close or shut it down during heating, and keep the temperature as low as workable
Raise the boiler temperature so the bitumen is used quickly and the fumes pass sooner, which cuts the time that the office occupants are exposed to them
Fit a taller flue to the boiler alone, because dispersing the fumes higher removes the risk to the offices without needing to move equipment or contact the building's managers
Issue the masks to the roofers and ask the office staff to keep windows shut, since the fumes are a short-term nuisance and not a health hazard to the occupants
why: Higher temperatures increase fume emission and fire and burn risk, so they worsen exposure rather than reducing it.
Raising the discharge does not guarantee fumes stay clear of intakes, and the building's occupants and managers still need to be involved.
Fume from heated bitumen is an irritant hazard, and paper dust masks give poor protection while doing nothing for people in the building.
bank.ex: Fumes are best controlled at source by siting, downwind positioning and the lowest workable temperature, with building management protecting occupants, who masks for the roofers would not protect.
bank.cm: Reaching for respirators or masks for the workers first, instead of moving the source and protecting other people who share the building.

bank.stem: A groundworker who uses breakers and vibrating plates every day gives his employer a doctor's letter diagnosing hand-arm vibration syndrome. The manager says RIDDOR covers only accident injuries and files the letter. What is the correct position?
o: The worker must report it to the HSE himself, since a diagnosis letter is his own medical information and the employer has no part in reporting it
RIDDOR covers only sudden injuries, so a gradual condition belongs in the health record and becomes reportable only if he later loses more than seven days
The employer must report the disease to the HSE, because it is reportable where the work regularly involves vibrating tools and a doctor has diagnosed it
Reporting is required only if the doctor ties the condition in writing to one named incident, because years of general tool use cannot be linked to work
why: Once an employee gives a written diagnosis, the employer has the duty to make the report.
RIDDOR also lists specified work-related diseases, and reporting does not depend on lost working days.
The disease is reportable from regular use of vibrating tools and needs no single named incident.
bank.ex: RIDDOR lists hand-arm vibration syndrome as a reportable disease when a doctor diagnoses it in someone whose work regularly involves vibrating tools, whether or not any time is lost.
bank.cm: Thinking that RIDDOR reporting applies only to sudden accidents and not to diagnosed work-related diseases.

bank.stem: A scaffolder's competent person inspects a facade scaffold each week and hangs a fresh tag, but keeps the written reports at the scaffolder's yard. The principal contractor holds no copies. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Reports are needed only for a monthly check, since the weekly inspections need nothing more than a verbal confirmation to the principal contractor on the day concerned
For a platform with a possible fall of 2 m or more, the report must reach the person it was done for within 24 hours and stay on site until work ends
The tag is the legal record of the inspection, so a separate written report is optional provided the tag carries the date, the inspector's initials and the lift covered
The reports may stay at the scaffolder's yard indefinitely, because only the firm that carried out the inspection has any duty to hold the records of its own checks
why: Each required inspection must be recorded and reported, and a verbal confirmation does not meet that duty.
A tag is only evidence of a recent inspection, and the written report is still required.
The report goes to the person who obtained the inspection, who must keep it on site until the work ends.
bank.ex: The inspection report must be given to the person on whose behalf the inspection was carried out within 24 hours and kept at the site until the construction work is finished.
bank.cm: Treating a scaffold tag as a substitute for the written inspection report that has to be on site.

bank.stem: While trenching, an excavator bucket cuts into an unmarked buried cable, with a flash and bang. The operator is unhurt in the cab, and the cable may still be live. A banksman shouts for him to climb out. What is the best action?
o: Reverse the bucket out of the cable at once to free it, then lower the bucket and check the damage on foot
Stay in the cab, keep the machine still, warn others to keep clear and call the network operator at once
Climb down quickly and run to the banksman, so that he can check for burns while the machine stays where it stopped
Wait a few minutes to see if the flash dies away, then cover the cable with soil and carry on with the trench
why: Moving the machine could drag or tear the cable further and increase the danger to everyone close by.
Stepping from an energised machine to the ground can cause a fatal shock and the area is not safe.
A cable that has flashed is a continuing danger and burying it hides it from the supplier.
bank.ex: A damaged live cable can energise the machine and the ground nearby, so the operator stays inside, others are kept well away and the supplier is called to make the cable dead.
bank.cm: Assuming the danger is over once the bang and flash have stopped.

bank.stem: A worker in a dusty area wears contact lenses and is told standard safety glasses are unnecessary because 'the lenses already protect the eyes'. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Lens wearers must be moved off all dusty work permanently, because lenses cannot be worn safely in any dust and no PPE can address this
Contact lenses are not eye protection and can trap dust against the eye, so suitable protection is still needed, with goggles where dust makes glasses inadequate
Standard safety glasses are adequate for any level of dust, because gaps at the sides are covered by the contact lenses underneath
Contact lenses form a protective barrier over the eye, so additional eye protection becomes optional for lens wearers working in dusty areas
why: No blanket ban exists; the answer is suitable protection chosen through assessment.
Some dust conditions need sealed goggles because glasses leave gaps.
Lenses are a vision aid, not protective equipment.
bank.ex: Lenses give no barrier against debris or dust and can make dust exposure worse, so the worker still needs PPE matched to the hazard.
bank.cm: Assuming a vision aid contributes to eye protection.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The worker says he will only be on the roof for a minute and will walk carefully. Which statement best describes the hazard?
o: Walking carefully along the ridge or valley lines of the sheets, where the support is strongest, makes it safe to cross a short distance without boards
A short visit of under two minutes is classed as low risk because of the limited exposure, so crawl boards, edge protection and signs are not needed
Fragile sheets and rooflights can fail under body weight however carefully or briefly someone walks, so crawl boards, edge protection and signs are needed
The main hazard is the moss and dirt on the rooflights, which should be cleaned off before anyone steps onto the roof surface to start work
why: Weathered sheets and hidden rooflights can fail anywhere; there is no safe line to walk.
Duration does not reduce the chance of a fragile roof failing under weight.
The dirt masks the rooflights, but the hazard is the fragility of the roof itself.
bank.ex: There is no safe way to put weight directly on fragile roofing; care and speed do not change that, and the missing warning sign removes a barrier against unplanned access.
bank.cm: Thinking that care and a short duration make walking on a fragile roof acceptable.
bank.alt: A worker carrying a tool bag walks across an old corrugated sheet roof with clear rooflight panels; a ladder rises at the roof edge and a sign lies on the roof.

bank.stem: In May, a manager authorises stripping ivy from a wall that contains an active nest, saying it is a common bird such as a sparrow and so not protected. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Only nests of rare or specially listed species are protected by wildlife law, so removing a sparrow's nest from the wall is lawful
Every wild bird's active nest is protected, not only rare species, and clearance should avoid the nesting season of about March to August
Nests are protected only from October to February, which is outside the main works season, so ivy clearance in May is lawful
Active nests may be removed if a replacement nest box is installed beforehand, since the birds can then relocate without any harm to them
why: Protection covers all wild birds' active nests.
The nesting season is broadly spring and summer.
A nest box does not make destroying an active nest lawful.
bank.ex: Wildlife law makes it an offence to intentionally damage or destroy an active nest of any wild bird, so the common species argument fails and the timing should have been planned.
bank.cm: Assuming that only rare species have legal protection for their nests.

bank.stem: A site manager stocks the first-aid kit by copying a list he believes is set out in law, and adds paracetamol and antiseptic cream as 'standard'. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Contents depend on a needs assessment, but medicines may be included on larger sites where a qualified first-aider is always present to supervise their use
No list exists, so contents are left to the manager's judgement, and common painkillers are permitted if the first-aider records every dose that is given
No legally prescribed list exists; contents should follow a first-aid needs assessment, and tablets and medicines should not be kept in the kit
The list is fixed in the First-Aid Regulations, but labelled painkillers and creams are allowed when the first-aider is trained to give them to colleagues
why: Site size and first-aider presence do not change the guidance that medicines should not be kept in the kit.
Contents must be based on a needs assessment rather than personal judgement, and recording doses does not make medicines acceptable.
The Regulations do not prescribe a fixed list, and medicines should not be held in the kit even by trained first-aiders.
bank.ex: HSE guidance says kit contents should reflect the needs assessment for the site, and that tablets and medicines should not be kept in a first-aid container.
bank.cm: Assuming a first-aid kit has a legal checklist and that everyday medicines count as normal first-aid supplies.

bank.stem: A scaffold tie is in the way of a window opening. A labourer unhooks it, planning to refit it after the window is installed, saying ties only stop sway. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Removing a tie is acceptable if an extra board is laid across the lift to share the load, because that offsets the loss of restraint
Ties hold the scaffold to the building against falling away, so only a competent scaffolder should alter them, and the scaffold needs inspecting before use again
Ties only reduce sway, so a labourer may unhook one briefly if he refits it afterwards and mentions it at the next routine weekly scaffold inspection
Anyone may remove a tie once the lift above is clear of materials, because the load on the scaffold decides whether it can overturn
why: An extra board does nothing to restrain the scaffold against falling away from the building.
Ties do far more than reduce sway, and an altered scaffold must be inspected before use, not at the next routine check.
The risk comes from loss of restraint to the structure, whatever the loading, and alterations are for competent scaffolders.
bank.ex: Ties restrain the scaffold against overturning outwards, so changing them is scaffolder's work, and any alteration requires an inspection before the scaffold is used again.
bank.cm: Treating scaffold ties as optional fixings that any trade can unhook for convenience.

bank.stem: A trained driver on a ROPS-fitted forward-tip dumper skips his seat belt on a slope, saying he would jump clear if it tipped. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The belt keeps him inside the protective frame in a rollover, while jumping clear risks being crushed, and slopes should be taken straight on
The frame protects him whether or not he is belted, so the belt is only an extra comfort feature and is not needed on short site trips
Seat belts matter only on public roads, because site speeds are low and the main slope risk is instead from loads falling off the skip
Jumping clear is the safer option on slopes, because a dumper rolls slowly and a trained driver has time to get out of the way
why: A frame protects only a retained driver, and unbelted occupants can be thrown out and crushed.
Belt use is expected on site, where dumper rollover is a leading cause of serious injury.
Rollovers happen too fast to escape, and the machine often lands on the driver.
bank.ex: Rollover protection works only if the driver is retained within it, and drivers who try to jump out are often crushed by the machine.
bank.cm: Believing that you can jump clear from a tipping vehicle faster than it can fall on you.

bank.stem: A fabricator's yard store holds oxygen and acetylene cylinders standing together against a wall, unchained, with a 20-litre can of petrol-based thinner on the same shelf. Which statement best describes the failings?
o: Acetylene should be stored beside the oxygen so matching sets stay together for issue, but the thinner needs a lid and a drip tray to be acceptable there
Only the thinner is wrong, because oxygen is not flammable and can stand beside acetylene, and standing a cylinder upright against a wall is enough to secure it
Oxygen needs separating from fuel gas by distance or a fire-resisting partition, cylinders must be secured upright, and flammable liquid must be stored elsewhere
The gases are acceptable with valve caps fitted, and the thinner is safest on the top shelf, since flammable vapour rises and would collect above the cylinders
why: Keeping gas sets together is the opposite of required separation, and a drip tray does not make a shared flammables shelf acceptable.
Oxygen accelerates combustion so it must be separated from fuel gas, and leaning against a wall does not restrain a cylinder.
Valve caps do not provide separation, and many flammable vapours are heavier than air and gather low rather than rising.
bank.ex: Oxygen feeds fires so it must be separated from acetylene, cylinders must be restrained against falling, and flammable liquids should not share a store with compressed gases.
bank.cm: Thinking that because oxygen itself does not burn it can be stored next to fuel gases and flammable liquids.

bank.stem: A groundworker using a breaker most days notices tingling in his fingertips on cold mornings and dismisses it as poor circulation. He tells nobody because he fears being taken off the tool. What should he do?
o: Wear thicker gloves and keep working at the same rate, because staying warm removes the cause of tingling in the fingers
Wait until his fingertips turn white on most days, since blanching is the only sign that confirms the condition and earlier tingling is a normal cold reaction
Report the symptoms promptly to his employer or health provider, so surveillance and tool controls can be reviewed while damage may still be limited
Mention it only to his own GP, because a health problem is private and his employer has no duty to respond to it
why: Warmth helps comfort but does not remove the vibration, so exposure and damage continue.
Tingling and numbness are recognised early symptoms, and waiting for blanching allows permanent damage to develop.
The employer has duties to review exposure and provide health surveillance, which cannot happen if it is never told.
bank.ex: Early symptoms such as tingling and numbness can signal hand-arm vibration syndrome, and prompt reporting lets the employer act before the damage becomes permanent.
bank.cm: Keeping quiet about early tingling or numbness because it seems minor or might lead to being moved off the work.

bank.stem: A guardrail section at a first-floor loading bay is taken out so a telehandler can place pallets on the slab. The foreman plans to leave the gap open all day, with cones behind it and a banksman to warn people. What should happen instead?
o: Leave the gap open until the last delivery, since removing a rail for loading is permitted whenever the gang has been briefed about the edge
Accept the plan, since cones and a banksman are enough warning for everyone and remain adequate for as long as the deliveries are being made all day
Issue harnesses to everyone nearby in place of the rail, because personal fall protection is the preferred control once a rail must be removed
Remove it only as far and as long as needed, fit a barrier or gate across the gap, allow trained people only, and refit the rail promptly
why: Briefing does not replace physical protection, and removal must be limited to what the task needs rather than the whole day.
Cones and a signaller warn people but cannot physically stop a fall, so they are not effective compensatory protection.
Collective protection takes priority over personal protection, which also depends on anchor points, training and rescue arrangements.
bank.ex: Edge protection may be removed only for as long and as far as the task needs, with effective compensatory measures in place, and must be replaced as soon as practicable.
bank.cm: Assuming that once a rail has to come out for a delivery, warning signs, cones and a briefing are an acceptable substitute.

bank.stem: A lorry-mounted platform is set up on a pavement above old basement vaults. A parked car stops the outriggers extending fully on one side, so the driver proposes raising the boom with that outrigger part-extended and the operator in the cage. What is the correct decision?
o: Raise it with the short side kept away from the car, as the operator can keep the boom over the fully extended side to remain stable
