Raise it slowly with the operator wearing a harness attached to the cage, as the harness will stop a fall if the machine tips over
Raise it slowly, since a lorry chassis is stable on any paved surface and outriggers are only required at maximum reach
Do not raise it until the ground is checked and every outrigger is fully extended on suitable pads, or the machine is moved
why: Limiting the boom direction without the full set-up goes against the manufacturer's instructions and does not address the unchecked ground.
A harness does not prevent the machine overturning and may drag the operator out or injure him if the platform tips.
Outriggers are required to the manufacturer's set-up, and paving may hide weak ground such as vaults and cellars.
bank.ex: Stability depends on the manufacturer's outrigger set-up on ground that can bear the loads, and voids such as vaults must be considered, so partial extension is not acceptable.
bank.cm: Believing a harness or careful operation can make up for incomplete outrigger set-up and unchecked ground.

bank.stem: A trench box is to be lowered into a 2.5 m trench by the excavator. The banksman asks a groundworker to climb in and steady it by hand while it hangs. What is the correct way to install it?
o: Choose any chain from the cabin to lift it, because the box itself is steel and the lifting accessories cannot be the weak point in the lift
Keep everyone out of the excavation while the box is suspended, use its rated lifting points and inspected accessories, and enter once seated
Slide the box in empty and have him enter at once, because boxes need not be fully seated before people go in to check the excavation sides
Let him steady the box with a tag line from inside the trench, as long as he wears a hard hat and moves clear if it swings toward him
why: Accessories must be rated for the load, marked and in-date for thorough examination, and the weak link can be the sling.
Nobody should enter until the box is seated and stable, since the unsupported sides may collapse.
A suspended box can swing or drop, and a hard hat gives no protection against its mass.
bank.ex: People must never be in or beneath a suspended box, and a box must be lifted by its designed points with accessories of adequate rating.
bank.cm: Entering an excavation to help position the support while the load is still moving.

bank.stem: A facade scaffold was handed over last week with a valid inspection record. Bricklayers now want to fix debris sheeting along its full length to keep dust off the street. What should happen first?
o: The bricklayers can fit the sheeting themselves, because the existing record stays valid until the next seven-day inspection is due
The bricklayers can fit the sheeting if it is a fire-retardant grade, since flammability is the only extra risk it adds
The bricklayers can fit the sheeting if they leave a gap at the top to let wind through, so no further assessment is needed
The scaffold contractor should assess the extra wind loading and ties, make any changes, then re-inspect and record it before use
why: An alteration to the scaffold requires inspection before further use, so the earlier record no longer covers the changed structure.
Fire rating addresses ignition only and ignores the major increase in wind loading on the scaffold and its ties.
A gap does not remove the extra wind loading and the scaffold's ties and design were not made for sheeted conditions.
bank.ex: Sheeting increases wind load on the structure, so the alteration needs competent assessment and a fresh inspection before anyone relies on the scaffold.
bank.cm: Thinking a scaffold inspection tag stays valid after other trades alter or add to the structure.

bank.stem: A client appoints a principal contractor for a four-month refit involving several trades. The client says her architect will write the construction phase plan, and the contractor intends to start setting up the site while it drafts one. Who should produce the plan, and when?
o: The client should draw up the plan from her pre-construction information, and the principal contractor then adds site detail once the site has been set up
Each contractor should write a plan for its own package, and the principal designer then merges these into one document before handover to the client
The principal contractor must draw up the plan, with the principal designer's help, before the site is set up, then keep it under review as work changes
The principal contractor may draft the plan once work has started, provided it is finished before the first higher-risk activity begins on the site
why: The plan is the principal contractor's duty, and it is needed before the site is set up rather than added to afterwards.
This confuses contractors' method statements with the single plan the principal contractor must produce and own.
The duty requires the plan before setting up the site, not a draft completed later.
bank.ex: Regulation 12 of CDM 2015 makes the principal contractor responsible for the construction phase plan, to be in place before setting up the site and reviewed as the work develops.
bank.cm: Assuming the construction phase plan is a client or designer document that can be finished after work has started.

bank.stem: Before using a 110 V angle grinder, a labourer sees the cable sheath is cut near the plug, showing a coloured core. The PAT label on the grinder is in date. A colleague wraps the cut in insulating tape. Which action is correct?
o: Do not use it; label it defective and withdraw it for a competent person to repair, since an in-date label does not cover new damage
Use it for the rest of the shift and report the cut at the end, because the in-date PAT label shows the grinder passed its last inspection
Use it with the taped repair, since the 110 V supply limits the shock risk to a level that insulating tape can hold safely for a day
Cut off the damaged section and refit the plug himself, since shortening the cable removes the fault and any labourer can do this safely
why: A label records a past test and cannot show the condition of the cable today, so a known defect means stopping use immediately.
Tape is not a proper repair for a cut cable, and a reduced voltage lowers the risk without removing it.
Re-terminating a cable is work for a competent person, and a wrongly wired plug creates a fresh hazard.
bank.ex: Damage found at a pre-use check means the tool is unsafe whatever the label says, so it must be withdrawn and repaired properly by a competent person, not patched with tape.
bank.cm: Trusting a valid test label over what is plainly visible on the cable at the pre-use check.

bank.stem: A new-build site backs onto a footpath used by schoolchildren. During deliveries the gate is left open, and the hoarding has a gap behind the skips. The contractor says his duties end at the site boundary and children are not his responsibility. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Duties to the public arise only after an actual incident, so the contractor may rely on his public liability insurance until a child enters the site
His duties extend to others affected by the work, so access must be controlled with secure hoarding, managed gates and end-of-day checks
A warning sign at the gate stating that unauthorised entry is prohibited is enough, since anyone who ignores it accepts responsibility for their own safety
Securing the site is the council's concern because the footpath is public, and the contractor needs only to protect people who work inside the fence
why: Duties are preventive and apply before any incident; insurance does not discharge the legal duty to control foreseeable risks.
Signs alone do not prevent foreseeable trespass by children, who cannot be assumed to read or heed them.
The contractor's duty is to those affected by his work, including pedestrians outside the fence, regardless of who owns the path.
bank.ex: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act covers non-workers affected by the work, and CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to prevent unauthorised access to the site.
bank.cm: Assuming that health and safety duties stop at the site fence and cover only the people who are paid to be inside it.

bank.stem: At dusk, a labourer crosses a haul road used by reversing dumpers, wearing an old faded vest left open over a dark jacket. His supervisor says that hi-vis makes him safe to cross. What is the correct view?
o: Fluorescent colour alone is enough at dusk, so reflective bands matter only on night shifts when street lighting is the only light
Hi-vis removes the need for crossing points and barriers, since a driver who sees the vest is certain to stop in time
Clean, fastened hi-vis with reflective bands helps drivers see him in poor light, but it supplements crossing controls
Any hi-vis vest worn over the jacket is adequate, because the colour is what matters and the condition of the garment is secondary
why: At dusk the background light is low and retroreflective bands are needed for headlights to illuminate the wearer.
Being seen does not guarantee a reversing driver can stop, so separating people and vehicles remains the primary control.
Faded, dirty or unfastened garments lose their effect, and the dark jacket then hides the high-visibility area.
bank.ex: Hi-vis improves conspicuousness only when it is clean, in good condition, fastened and has retroreflective material for low light, and it never replaces traffic management.
bank.cm: Thinking that wearing hi-vis, whatever its condition, lets people share routes with moving vehicles.

bank.stem: A new floor resin arrives with a label showing a pictogram of a human silhouette with a star burst on the chest. A flooring operative says only the skull and crossbones means serious harm. How should the supervisor respond?
o: It matters little because the label is for transport rules only, and site controls can rely on the operative's own long experience
It signals serious long-term effects such as sensitisation, so the safety data sheet should feed into the COSHH assessment
It marks a flammable product, so the main step is to keep ignition sources away and a separate COSHH assessment can be skipped entirely
It only warns of short-lived skin irritation, so basic gloves are enough and the safety data sheet is only needed after any exposure occurs
why: Labels and data sheets are to inform users about workplace risks, and experience alone cannot detect a long-term effect.
Flammability has a different pictogram, and COSHH still applies to this product's health risks.
The symbol relates to serious chronic effects, and the data sheet is needed beforehand to plan controls.
bank.ex: The health hazard pictogram can indicate carcinogenic, sensitising or organ-damaging effects, and the safety data sheet gives the information needed to assess and control exposure.
bank.cm: Assuming that only the skull and crossbones means a product is seriously harmful to health.

bank.stem: On Friday afternoon the client orders extra partition work to start on Monday. The supervisor reuses the RAMS from a similar job last month, adds the new room numbers and tells the gang to 'work the same way'. What is the main weakness?
o: There is none, because RAMS from a comparable job remain valid for like-for-like tasks done by the same trade with the same tools
The missing client signature, because a written variation order becomes the method statement once the client has authorised the extra work
The RAMS was not reviewed for this job's conditions or briefed to the operatives, so it needs revising and communicating before work begins
Short notice waives the need for a written RAMS on a variation, and a toolbox talk on Monday morning is enough to cover the added scope
why: Site conditions, access, services and neighbouring trades differ between jobs, so a generic copy ignores the real hazards.
A variation instruction is a change to scope, not a safe system of work, so it cannot replace a reviewed RAMS.
There is no exemption for short notice, and a verbal talk does not replace a suitable and sufficient assessment.
bank.ex: Changed work needs its risks reassessed and the method statement updated, and the people doing it must understand the revised controls before they start.
bank.cm: Treating a client's variation or a short deadline as a reason to recycle old paperwork instead of reassessing the new task.

bank.stem: A store holds unissued helmets stamped with a manufacture date four years ago. The maker's guidance gives a five-year service life. The foreman says the clock starts when a helmet is issued, and wants crews to write their names on shells with solvent marker. What is correct?
o: The helmets are already out of life, because any helmet over three years old must be binned whatever the maker's guidance says on it
Life runs from the manufacture date, leaving about a year, and no solvents or adhesives should touch shells unless the maker approves
The clock starts at issue, so the helmets are good for five years from then, and a solvent marker is fine on a thick plastic shell
The helmets can be used until cracked, because the date stamp is advisory and visible damage is the only reason to replace them
why: There is no universal three-year limit, and the maker's stated service life for the model in use is the guide.
Ageing begins at manufacture, and solvents can soften or craze plastic shells without any sign that shows.
The stated service life is a limit even without visible cracks, as age and unseen damage can reduce protection.
bank.ex: Helmet life is counted from the date stamped on the shell, as plastics age in storage, and unapproved solvents or adhesives can weaken the shell and hide damage.
bank.cm: Counting a helmet's life from the day it was handed out instead of the date it was made.

bank.stem: A roadworker has signed an opt-out from the 48-hour weekly working limit. His supervisor rosters him for six 11-hour night shifts every week for the next two months, saying the opt-out covers it. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The opt-out covers only the weekly limit, and night workers cannot opt out of the 8-hour average in 24 hours, so this roster breaches the night rule
The opt-out also removes the night limit, provided the employer pays a night premium and confirms the roster in writing at the start of every single week
The 8-hour night figure is a guideline for workers with special hazards, so an ordinary road crew can be rostered well beyond it by agreement with the employer
Eleven-hour shifts are lawful as long as each is followed by at least 11 hours of rest, because daily rest is the one limit that really matters for night work
why: The night work limit cannot be opted out of, and extra pay or written confirmation does not change that.
The average limit applies to all night workers, and the special-hazards rule makes the cap stricter, not looser.
Daily rest and the average night-hours limit are separate rules, and meeting one does not satisfy the other.
bank.ex: A night worker's hours must average no more than 8 in each 24-hour period over the reference period, and unlike the weekly limit this cannot be waived by signing an opt-out.
bank.cm: Believing that a signed opt-out from the 48-hour week lifts every working time limit, including those protecting night workers.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative is properly protected because he has a hard hat, glasses, a mask, ear defenders and gloves. What is the most significant problem?
o: A half mask and glasses cannot cope with rebounding grit and fine dust, so he needs a supplied-air blasting helmet.
Cotton overalls are the weak point, because leather aprons would offer better protection from the rebounding grit and the heat.
Ear defenders should be replaced with earplugs, because defenders cannot seal properly against the hard hat brim in this noise.
Leather gauntlets should be fitted with grip-assist coatings so the nozzle hose cannot be dropped during the blasting task.
why: Clothing matters, but the breathing and face protection is a far greater risk from the dust cloud.
Defenders suit this noise level, and the picture does not show a sealing problem that plugs would fix.
Grip is a minor point compared with the breathing and eye risk, and gauntlets are a normal choice for this task.
bank.ex: Abrasive blasting creates a heavy cloud of grit and dust which rebounds, so the face, eyes and airways need a purpose- made blasting helmet with a clean air supply rather than a half mask under glasses.
bank.cm: Counting the number of PPE items worn instead of asking whether each one suits the actual hazard.
bank.alt: A worker abrasive-blasts a steel beam in a cloud of dust, wearing a hard hat, glasses, a half-mask, ear defenders and gauntlets; a compressor stands behind him.

bank.stem: A method statement for lifting a chiller onto a plant-room roof lists the hazards and PPE, then says only "lift into place" and "call 999 if needed". Which addition would improve it most?
o: The company safety policy and general site rules attached in full, so every operative can see the standards that apply across the whole project and its trades
A step-by-step sequence naming the crane and accessories, plus task-specific emergency arrangements such as who raises the alarm
Copies of each operative's CSCS card and the crane brochure, since evidence of competence and capacity makes a stated sequence unnecessary
A line saying the foreman will decide the order of work and the equipment on the day, as he knows the roof and the crew best
why: General policy does not describe how this specific lift will be carried out or how an emergency on the roof would be handled.
Evidence of competence and capacity supports the plan but does not replace a clear sequence of work and emergency arrangements.
The sequence and plant must be planned in advance so that risks are controlled, and cannot be left to be improvised during the lift.
bank.ex: A method statement should set out how the task is done in order, with the plant needed and the emergency arrangements that apply to this particular job.
bank.cm: Treating a method statement as a list of hazards and PPE rather than a practical description of the order of work, the plant used and the emergency plan.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. Which combination of faults makes a serious injury most likely during this delivery?
o: The lorry has been parked on a steep slope, and the platform edge has a barrier that has been tied back out of the way
The operator is walking backwards towards an unprotected drop, and the lorry sits off the platform without its wheels chocked
The pallet is stacked too high and unwrapped, and a second worker is standing in the path of the pallet truck
The operator has no hard hat or gloves, and the platform surface is wet and poorly lit for the pallet truck
why: No slope or tied-back barrier is shown, since the picture shows an edge with no protection at all.
The pallet is low, stable and shrink- wrapped, and the second worker is well away from the pallet truck.
The operator is wearing a hard hat, gloves and boots, and the platform is dry and well lit.
bank.ex: Walking backwards towards an open edge with no barrier risks a fall, and an unchocked vehicle with a gap beside the platform can move or leave a gap to fall into.
bank.cm: Looking only at the load or the clothing and missing the unprotected edge and the unsecured vehicle beside it.
bank.alt: At a loading bay, a worker pulls a pallet truck backwards along a raised concrete platform beside a parked curtain-sided lorry.

bank.stem: A site has six empty 205-litre steel drums that held solvent- based sealant. They still smell of solvent and contain residue. The foreman books a registered carrier to take them away as scrap metal on a standard transfer note. What is the right approach?
o: Send them as scrap metal, since steel is recyclable and a registered carrier with a transfer note meets the duty of care
Check the carrier's registration number only, because the destination site's permit is the carrier's concern rather than the producer's
Rinse them in the yard and run the washings to the gully, which then lets the drums be classed as non-hazardous waste
Treat them as hazardous waste: classify them correctly, use a consignment note, and check the carrier's registration and the destination's permit
why: The residue makes the drums hazardous, so a standard transfer note and a recyclable material label are not enough.
The producer's duty of care extends to confirming that the waste goes to a site holding the proper permit.
Washing solvent into a drain is a pollution offence and the resulting washings are themselves waste.
bank.ex: Drums holding hazardous residue count as hazardous waste, which in England needs a consignment note and checks that the carrier is registered and the receiving site is permitted.
bank.cm: Calling a container empty because it is no longer usable, when residue inside can still make it hazardous waste.

bank.stem: A joiner who wears prescription glasses is about to use an angle grinder on masonry. He says his own glasses, with a pair of stick-on side shields, are enough, and the site goggles feel too loose to fit over them. Which action is correct?
o: Allow his own glasses, because the lenses already give a barrier and the stick-on side shields stop particles reaching the eyes from the side
Provide eye protection suited to the grinding hazard that fits him properly, either over-glasses goggles or prescription safety eyewear
Let him use the loose goggles anyway with the strap tightened up, since any goggles are better than none for a short task like this
Let him do the task without eye protection by keeping his head turned away from the sparks and debris, since the cut is a short one
why: Ordinary lenses and add-on shields are not impact-rated for grinding, so they can break or let fragments through.
Eye protection that does not fit properly cannot protect reliably, and tightening a poor fit does not fix the problem.
Positioning is not a substitute for protection, and grinding throws fragments in unpredictable directions.
bank.ex: Everyday spectacles are not designed to resist impact, so he needs protection chosen for the hazard and fitted to him, either worn over his glasses or made to his prescription.
bank.cm: Thinking that everyday prescription glasses count as eye protection for grinding.

bank.stem: A joiner restoring old doors in an occupied school uses a strong solvent-based paint stripper, with a half-mask respirator and one open window. The assessment simply lists the mask. What should the assessor consider next under COSHH?
o: Strip only in the school holidays, as removing other people from the building is a sufficient control for the joiner who is applying it
Whether the stripper can be eliminated or substituted, by a safer product or another removal method, before relying on ventilation or masks
Open three more windows and limit each person to two hours of stripping, since cutting exposure time makes substitution unnecessary
Upgrade to a full-face respirator and keep the stripper, because protective equipment gives the best protection when substitution might alter the finish of the doors
why: Clearing the building protects others but leaves the person applying the stripper exposed.
Reducing duration and diluting vapour are lower in the hierarchy and do not replace consideration of a safer product.
PPE is the last line of defence, and a change of finish does not justify skipping substitution.
bank.ex: COSHH requires elimination or substitution to be considered first, with ventilation and then respiratory protection used only for the risk that remains.
bank.cm: Starting the control search at the mask or the window instead of asking whether the hazardous product is needed at all.

bank.stem: A two-day fencing job in open farmland is a 25-minute drive from the nearest public toilet. The contractor plans to ask the farmer if the crew can use the farmhouse bathroom, and to bring bottled water for hands. The farmer is often out. Which approach best meets the welfare duty?
o: Supply hand gel and a spade for the two days, since the full welfare duty applies to sites that last longer than a week
Rely on the farmer's verbal permission, because an agreement to use the house counts as provision even when nobody is home to open it up
Provide welfare before starting, such as a mobile unit, with a toilet, soap, clean water and towels that the crew can reach quickly
Let workers drive to the town toilets when needed, because travel time to a public facility is accepted as reasonable access on remote jobs
why: Welfare duties apply to any construction site regardless of how short the job is, and gel does not replace washing facilities.
Facilities that may be locked or unavailable are not reliably accessible when the crew needs them.
A 25-minute drive each way is not reasonable access and wastes working time.
bank.ex: Workers in remote locations still need toilets and washing facilities within easy reach, and a short job or a hoped- for favour does not remove that duty.
bank.cm: Assuming a very short or remote job does not need proper toilets and washing provided for the crew.

bank.stem: A decorator who strips old paintwork in powdered latex gloves develops itchy red hands. Days later he wheezes and his eyes stream when a colleague opens a new box of the same gloves nearby. Which response best fits the risk?
o: Issue cotton liners under the latex gloves and a barrier cream, because the rash comes from sweat and the wheeze is probably just hay fever
Give him powder-free latex gloves only, as the allergy is to the powder rather than the latex, and let colleagues keep using powdered ones
Have him wash his hands after each glove change and carry on, since symptoms that ease overnight show irritation rather than a true allergy
Remove him from latex exposure, switch the team to powder-free nitrile gloves, and refer him to occupational health, as airborne glove powder can trigger asthma
why: Liners and cream leave latex exposure in place and wrongly dismiss two linked symptoms that point to an allergy.
The allergen is the latex protein itself, and colleagues' powdered gloves would still spread it through the air.
Symptoms that ease away from work often indicate a work-related allergy, so continued exposure risks lasting sensitisation.
bank.ex: Latex allergy can affect skin and breathing, and powder carries the allergen into the air, so the source must be substituted and the worker medically assessed.
bank.cm: Treating a work-related rash or wheeze as a minor irritation instead of reporting it and removing the cause.

bank.stem: Pedestrians cross a haul road used by loaded dumpers where it bends past a stockpile that hides each party from the other. The planner proposes mirrors and a signaller there. What is the better control for the crossing?
o: Keep the crossing at the bend as it is the shortest route to the cabins, and add a speed hump and a warning sign facing approaching drivers
Cut the stockpile height to knee level and keep the crossing in place, relying on drivers sounding their horns as they round the bend
Move the crossing to a straight length giving clear view both ways within stopping distance, and mark, light and fence the approach
Leave the crossing where it is, paint it clearly across the road, and brief all drivers that pedestrians always have priority on it
why: A speed hump and sign do not restore the missing sight lines, and a short walking route does not justify a blind crossing.
A horn only warns people who are already in view, and relying on drivers rather than layout leaves the cause of the blind spot unmanaged.
Paint and a priority rule cannot help a driver who cannot see the pedestrian until it is too late to stop.
bank.ex: Siting crossings where drivers and pedestrians can see each other in time, with a clearly marked and lit crossing, removes the hazard at source instead of compensating for it.
bank.cm: Adding warning devices to a bad crossing position instead of moving the crossing to where people can see each other.

bank.stem: A telehandler driver must move a 1.8-tonne pack of blocks 50 m across a gently sloping, rutted yard to a scaffold. He plans to travel with the boom raised for visibility, saying the load moment indicator will warn him of instability. Which approach is correct?
o: Carry the pack just clear of the ground with the boom retracted and tilted back, go straight up or down slopes, and extend only to place it
Carry the pack low but cross the slope diagonally, because that spreads the weight over all four wheels and gives better stability
Travel with the boom raised as planned, because a working load moment indicator warns before instability and so removes the need to carry the load low
Carry it low with the boom partly extended so the pack sits well ahead of the tyres and gives the driver a clearer view
why: Crossing a slope puts the load's weight toward the downhill wheels and increases the risk of side overturn.
An indicator is a last-line warning and cannot stop a raised load tipping the machine when it hits a rut or turns.
Extending the boom moves the load further from the front axle and reduces stability and the rated capacity.
bank.ex: A low, retracted, tilted-back load keeps the combined centre of gravity inside the wheelbase, and the load chart applies only when raising and extending to place it.
bank.cm: Relying on an alarm or indicator to protect against instability instead of travelling with the load low and close.

bank.stem: A flashback burns out a hose in a fabrication bay, and an acetylene cylinder was engulfed in flames for several minutes. The fire is out and the cylinder now feels only warm. The supervisor wants it moved outside. What is the correct action?
o: Open the valve slowly to vent the pressure outside the bay, which removes the stored gas and stops the cylinder from becoming dangerous again
Leave it where it is, keep people clear, tell the fire service it was heated, and have it cooled and monitored until they declare it safe
Spray it with the nearest water extinguisher until cool to touch, then return it to the store because no flames remain and the cylinder feels cool
Close the valve, wheel it carefully into open air away from the building, and leave it standing there until the supplier collects it on the next delivery
why: Venting acetylene creates a flammable atmosphere and does not address possible decomposition inside the cylinder.
Feeling cool does not show the contents are stable, and returning it to the store puts a potentially unstable cylinder among other gases.
Moving a heated cylinder risks triggering internal decomposition, and the fire service must be told before anyone handles it.
bank.ex: A heated acetylene cylinder can decompose internally and may heat up again or burst, so it must be left to the emergency services, who will cool it and monitor it.
bank.cm: Judging a cylinder safe because the flames are out and it is no longer hot to touch.

bank.stem: A building firm has six employees, two of them part-time, plus three self-employed bricklayers. The owner keeps his safety arrangements in his head and says risks are covered in verbal morning chats. Which statement best describes his legal position?
o: He must write the policy down, tell employees about it and record significant risk assessment findings, because he has five or more employees
He must write the policy down, but need only show it to an HSE inspector on request, as the daily talks already inform his employees
He may rely on verbal chats until he employs twenty or more people, since smaller firms are expected to write policies only when an inspector asks
He must record the risk assessments, but the policy is optional because the morning chats already set out who does what and when
why: The policy, and any changes to it, must be brought to the attention of employees and not just held for inspectors.
The written-policy threshold is five or more employees, so verbal chats alone do not satisfy the law for this firm.
A written policy is itself a legal requirement at this size, and chats are not a substitute for a recorded statement.
bank.ex: Employers with five or more employees must have a written health and safety policy that employees are told about, and must record the significant findings of their risk assessments.
bank.cm: Assuming that a small firm with good daily communication does not need written arrangements.

bank.stem: For several weeks an electrician has soldered with rosin-cored solder in a small plant room. He now wheezes and coughs at night, but thinks it is a cold. He borrows a colleague's inhaler and keeps working as before. What should happen?
o: He should tell his employer and see a doctor, mentioning the soldering, so the fume exposure is reviewed and the controls are improved
He should wait a few weeks to see whether the cough clears, as reporting is only worthwhile once a doctor has confirmed a diagnosis
He should keep using the inhaler and monitor the cough himself, since symptoms that begin at night cannot be caused by the work done by day
He should change to a stronger disposable mask and carry on, because a better mask removes the need to report symptoms to anyone else
why: Early reporting is what allows exposure to be reduced, and waiting for a confirmed diagnosis risks him becoming permanently sensitised.
Asthma symptoms from a workplace sensitiser can appear several hours after exposure, including at night, and masking them delays action.
A mask is not a substitute for assessing exposure, and once sensitised he may react to very low levels that a mask does not stop.
bank.ex: Rosin flux fume can cause occupational asthma, which may show hours after exposure, so early reporting lets the employer reassess controls under COSHH before permanent lung damage develops.
bank.cm: Writing off a work-related cough or wheeze as a cold because it appears at night instead of during the shift.

bank.stem: An electrician has isolated and locked off a circuit and must replace a socket. He holds a non-contact voltage stick near the cable, hears no beep and starts work. Which statement is correct?
o: A stick is acceptable when its battery light is on, and a plug-in socket tester used afterwards on the same circuit is enough to confirm that it is dead
Absence of voltage must be proved with an approved voltage indicator, itself checked on a known live source or proving unit before and after
A multimeter on its bare probes is better than any voltage indicator, because a numeric reading proves the conductors are dead without further checks
Locking off the isolator proves the circuit dead, so testing is needed only where the isolation was not locked or was done by someone else
why: A lit battery indicator does not show the stick can detect voltage, and a socket tester is not a means of proving a circuit dead.
An unproved multimeter with unshrouded probes can fail or give a false zero and is itself a shock and short-circuit hazard.
Isolation and proving dead are separate steps, and the test is still needed after a lock is applied.
bank.ex: A tester can fail without warning, so it must be shown to work immediately before and after use, and non-contact sticks are not suitable for proving a circuit dead.
bank.cm: Trusting a silent tester or a lock-off without proving the tester itself works.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The scaffolder says it is ready for handover because the platforms, rails, ties and ladder all look complete. Which problem must be corrected before anyone uses it?
o: The outer face has no debris netting, which must be fitted before the next shift because falling material cannot otherwise be controlled.
The working platform is too narrow for materials and must be widened with extra boards before any bricklaying starts on the upper lift of the scaffold.
The standards bear on loose bricks and a cracked slab, not base plates on firm sole boards, so the base could slip or settle.
The access ladder should stop level with the platform edge so that workers can step across the guardrail without a gap at the top.
why: Netting is a separate control that depends on the work and does not address the visible instability of the supports.
The deck is boarded at a suitable width, so this is not the significant fault in the scene.
A ladder should project well above the platform to give a handhold, so stopping it level would introduce a fault.
bank.ex: A scaffold's loads pass down through its standards, so each needs a base plate on a sound sole board or firm base, as loose bricks and cracked slabs can shift or crush.
bank.cm: Judging a scaffold safe from its platforms and rails without checking what the standards stand on.
bank.alt: A newly built scaffold against a house, with a worker on the platform, a ladder, and a person holding a clipboard on the lawn; the scaffold standards rest on the ground below.

bank.stem: A vibratory roller compacts hardcore for a car park 8 m from a terrace of old houses. Residents report rattling windows and one shows a new hairline plaster crack. The contractor says the roller is within its operator exposure rating. What is the best response?
o: Fit damping pads to the operator seat and reassess the operator's exposure, since reducing vibration at the machine reduces it at the houses too.
Give residents a notice of rolling times and keep to normal working hours, since vibration complaints are handled in the same way as noise, through hours alone.
Take no action unless a surveyor proves the roller caused the crack, because hairline plaster cracks in old houses usually come from age and settlement over many years.
Treat it as a separate off-site effect: monitor vibration at the nearest house, review roller settings and method, and record nearby property condition.
why: Seat damping protects the driver but has little effect on the ground-borne vibration transmitted to neighbouring properties.
Limiting hours may help but does not measure or reduce the vibration reaching the houses.
Waiting for proof of damage ignores the nuisance already reported, and ageing buildings are more sensitive to vibration.
bank.ex: Operator exposure limits do not protect neighbours, and vibration affecting nearby premises can be a statutory nuisance, so monitoring and changes to the method are needed.
bank.cm: Assuming that meeting the operator's exposure limits means neighbours are protected from the same vibration.

bank.stem: Scaffolders working beside a fenced 11 kV substation drop a hand tool that lands inside the locked compound near equipment. The foreman proposes climbing the fence to grab it because the unit is silent. What is the correct action?
o: Push a scaffold tube through the fence to drag the tool clear, because the tube never enters the equipment area and nobody has to climb in
Keep everyone out and report it to the operator via the notice contact, so an authorised person retrieves the tool once the area is safe
Send the site electrician in to fetch it, because a qualified electrician is competent to work safely around any high-voltage equipment on any premises
Climb in and retrieve it only while the equipment is silent, since the absence of any humming shows the apparatus is dead and the whole compound is safe
why: A long metal tube close to high-voltage apparatus can cause flashover or contact, and it still amounts to unauthorised work inside the operator's compound.
Competence on the site's own installation does not give authority to enter the operator's substation, which only the operator can grant.
Silence proves nothing about whether equipment is live, and entering without the operator's authority is the danger itself.
bank.ex: Only persons authorised by the operator may enter a substation, and silence does not show equipment is dead, so the operator must be told and must arrange safe recovery.
bank.cm: Assuming that quiet equipment behind a fence is safe to enter for a quick job.

bank.stem: A crew will install pipework in a 1.5 m deep concrete pump sump in a basement slab, reached by stepping over its open edge. The supervisor says the Work at Height Regulations only apply above 2 m, so extra care is enough. What is the correct approach?
o: Treat it as work at height with no minimum drop: assess the fall risk and provide edge protection or a secure cover and safe access first
Apply the regulations only to work done from above ground level, since a place below ground level falls outside the legal definition of height
Issue harnesses clipped to the existing pipework and skip edge protection, because personal fall protection satisfies the duty at any depth
Accept the supervisor's view, as falls of under two metres count as slips and trips, so normal housekeeping controls are all that is required
why: The definition expressly includes places at or below ground level, so a sump or pit is covered.
Collective measures such as edge protection or covers come before personal protection, and installed pipework is not a tested anchor.
There is no two-metre threshold, and the duty applies wherever a fall could cause personal injury.
bank.ex: The regulations cover any place, including at or below ground level, from which a person could fall a distance liable to cause injury, so a 1.5 m sump is covered and needs planned protection.
bank.cm: Assuming that falls only matter above a fixed height such as two metres.

bank.stem: A newly laid 150 mm water main is to be pressure tested with compressed air to save water. The gang plans to stand beside the pipe ends while the test runs. A senior engineer objects. What is the main reason for the objection?
o: Air tests take longer than water tests, so the gang would be exposed to the pipe for more of the day than necessary
Air cannot find leaks as well as water, so the main would need re-testing, and that is mainly a cost issue
Compressed air is a flammable gas, so the test needs a hot work permit and a fire watch for the duration of the test
Air stores far more energy than water, so a failure can throw parts violently; hydraulic testing is safer or exclusion zones are needed
why: The duration is not the main hazard; the stored energy is.
The objection concerns safety, not test accuracy.
Compressed air is not flammable and no hot work permit applies.
bank.ex: Compressed air is compressible and stores energy that is released suddenly in a failure, so water testing is preferred or people must be kept clear with restrained ends.
bank.cm: Treating a compressed air test as equal in safety to a water test.

bank.stem: A scaffolder falls from a mobile tower onto concrete and is unresponsive but breathing, with snoring sounds, and a first-aider suspects a neck injury. A colleague says nobody should touch his head until paramedics arrive. After 999 is called, what should the first-aider do?
o: Hold the head and neck in line and open the airway with a jaw thrust, using the recovery position only if the airway cannot be kept clear
Leave him exactly as found with the head untouched until the ambulance crew arrive, because any movement could worsen a possible injury to the spine
Tilt the head fully back and lift the chin firmly to clear the tongue, since this is the quickest way to open the airway of any unresponsive casualty
Roll him onto his side straight away with the help of a bystander, because the recovery position is required for every unresponsive breathing casualty
why: Snoring signals a partly blocked airway, and an obstructed airway is more immediately life-threatening than a suspected spinal injury.
Tilting the neck back is avoided with a suspected spinal injury, where a jaw thrust is the preferred technique.
Rolling is reserved for when the airway cannot be kept open by other means, as it risks moving the spine unnecessarily.
bank.ex: Keeping the airway open takes priority, and a jaw thrust does so with least neck movement; the recovery position is a last resort when the airway cannot be maintained.
bank.cm: Freezing in the belief that a possible spinal injury means nothing can be done about a blocked airway.

bank.stem: Look at the scene at the crushing area. The loader driver says he is fully trained and the crusher has its own emergency stop. What is the most serious problem?
o: The stockpile behind the crusher is too tall, because large heaps are the main cause of fatal injuries around mobile crushing plant
The loading shovel is working too close to the crusher, because machines this size need a clear zone of at least 12 metres between them
A labourer clears spillage beside the moving belt and drum while the plant runs, with no guard and out of the loader driver's view
Dust at the discharge point is the main hazard, because it will cause serious lung disease within a day if no respirator is worn
why: The stockpile is a secondary concern compared with a person working at unguarded moving machinery.
The loader's distance is not the key hazard, and no such fixed separation figure applies.
Dust is a real health risk but it is managed by suppression and does not match the immediate danger of the moving parts.
bank.ex: Clearing material next to running, unguarded conveyor parts risks entanglement, and standing where the loader driver cannot see him adds a risk of being struck.
bank.cm: Letting someone clean or clear material near running plant on the strength of an emergency stop being nearby.
bank.alt: A tracked crusher and conveyor run on a recycling site while a worker with a shovel works beside the conveyor and a wheel loader operates nearby.

bank.stem: Roofers cutting lead flashing clean their hands with alcohol gel and eat lunch beside the lead stack, as the welfare cabin is a short walk away. One says lead is only a problem when it is heated. What is the best response?
o: Wear gloves while eating and wash at home after the shift, because dust left on the skin during the working day cannot be swallowed by mistake
Move the lunch spot only on cutting days, since cold sheet and loose offcuts leave nothing on the hands that could be harmful if swallowed
Accept the gel as a substitute for washing, since it clears contamination from skin quickly provided lunch is eaten upwind of the work area
Wash hands and face with soap and water in the welfare cabin before eating, drinking or smoking, and keep food away from the work area
why: Gloves carry the dust to food and mouth, and delaying washing until home extends the time the lead stays on the skin.
Handling the sheet and offcuts transfers lead dust to the hands whether or not it is being cut, so the hygiene rule applies throughout the work.
Gel is designed to kill germs and does not remove metal dust, and being upwind does not stop dust on hands reaching the mouth.
bank.ex: Swallowing lead dust from hands, food and cigarettes is a main route into the body, so washing with soap and water and eating away from the work area breaks that route.
bank.cm: Believing a quick wipe or gel is enough, when only proper washing before eating, drinking or smoking removes lead dust from skin.

bank.stem: Two workers clear silt from a warm, humid 1.2 m culvert in planned three-hour entries. The supervisor lets them carry water bottles to sip at the work face and eat lunch inside to save time. What is the best approach?
o: Plan shorter entries with rest, drinks and food in a clean area outside, since heat builds up inside and silt on hands can be swallowed
Have them drink well before entering and after leaving only, because sipping inside would raise toilet needs and distract from the task
Keep three-hour entries and allow both inside, because time saved by not leaving means less total exposure and fewer awkward re-entries
Allow bottles but ban food inside, because water helps cooling at the work face and the contamination risk comes only from eating a meal
why: Fluid loss during hot work is real, and the answer is planned breaks outside rather than none during a three-hour entry.
Long entries in humid heat risk heat stress, and avoiding breaks does not reduce the harm of staying in the space.
Contaminated hands handling a bottle spout carry silt to the mouth just as they would with food.
bank.ex: Time in a hot, humid confined space may need limiting, and fluids and food should be taken in a clean place so that contaminated hands do not carry material to the mouth.
bank.cm: Judging that a drink at the workface is a kindness when it is actually a route for contamination.

bank.stem: A temporary roof of corrugated sheeting spans a tall scaffold over a re-roofing job. Overnight 15 cm of wet snow settles on it and the sheets are sagging. The supervisor wants two harnessed labourers to walk on the sheets and shovel it off. What is the correct approach?
o: Let the sun clear it and restrict work to areas under sheets that sag visibly, since unsagged areas are plainly carrying the load
Carry on working beneath it, since the weekly scaffold inspection was done only three days ago and so is still in date for use
Send the harnessed labourers up at once, because removing the load quickly is the safest way to relieve the roof and harnesses control the fall risk
Keep people off and from beneath it, have the temporary works designer assess it, clear the snow by an approved method, and inspect before reuse
why: Unseen overload and damage can exist in unsagged areas, so the whole structure needs assessment.
Exceptional weather requires an inspection in its own right, whatever stage the routine cycle has reached.
Sagging sheeting is fragile and may collapse under their weight, so a harness does not make walking on it acceptable.
bank.ex: Snow is an exceptional event that can overload the structure, so it needs assessment, a safe removal method that avoids walking on the sheeting, and inspection before work resumes.
bank.cm: Assuming a routine inspection date covers a structure after heavy snow, wind or other weather has loaded it.

bank.stem: At 06:15 in winter darkness, a haulier's own employee is told to unload plasterboard in an unlit site bay littered with offcuts. The site manager says the haulier alone must protect its driver, because site duties cover only the site's own workforce. Which statement is correct?
o: The site's duty is met by giving the driver a hi-vis vest and a verbal warning about the bay, since a visitor is taken to accept the conditions he finds there
The site's duty begins only once the driver has signed the site rules, so with no signature yet the manager has taken on no responsibility for him at all
Both owe duties: the site must run its work so the driver is not put at risk, including a lit, clear bay, alongside the haulier's own duty to him
Only the haulier is responsible, because it employs the driver and the site's legal duties stretch solely to people on its own payroll or on its direct contracts
why: A warning does not remove a hazard that the site can reasonably control, and visitors do not accept risk by arriving.
The duty arises from the site's activities exposing him to risk, not from any paperwork he has or has not signed.
Duties to people affected by the undertaking do not depend on who employs them, so the site cannot hand the whole duty to the haulier.
bank.ex: The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act requires an employer to conduct its undertaking so that people not in its employment are not exposed to risk, and this sits alongside the haulier's separate duty to its own employee.
bank.cm: Assuming that a visiting driver's safety belongs entirely to his own employer because he is not on the site's payroll.

bank.stem: A cladding subcontractor hands the principal contractor's manager its RAMS at 07:00, the planned start time. Knowing the firm is experienced, the manager proposes letting the crew begin prep work while he reads the documents at lunch. Which approach is correct?
o: Allow the prep work if the foreman signs to accept personal liability for anything the RAMS later turn out to have missed on this particular cladding job
Hold the hazardous work until the RAMS are checked against the construction phase plan and site conditions; the subcontractor still owns its method
Let the work start and approve the RAMS afterwards, which then transfers responsibility for the method from the subcontractor to the principal contractor
Let the crew start because the review is only a paperwork check, and the subcontractor's own duty to work safely will cover any gap left in the method it chose
why: A signature cannot transfer or remove the principal contractor's coordination duty, and it does nothing to prevent the hazard.
Approval does not transfer responsibility for the method, and approving after the work has started defeats the purpose of review.
Reviewing before work begins is part of coordination, and a subcontractor's own duty does not replace the principal contractor's.
bank.ex: The principal contractor must plan, manage, monitor and coordinate the construction phase, which means reviewing a subcontractor's method before it starts, while the subcontractor stays responsible for its own work.
bank.cm: Treating the principal contractor's review of subcontractor RAMS as a formality that can follow the start of work.

bank.stem: A trench on a former fuel depot fills with groundwater showing a rainbow sheen and a diesel smell. The contractor plans to pump it through a silt bag to a nearby stream under the Environment Agency's temporary dewatering position for clean water. What is the best course?
o: Stop pumping, contain the water, and arrange testing and treatment or disposal under a bespoke permit or water company consent, as the allowance excludes contamination
Dilute it by running clean mains water into the trench while pumping, so the sheen disappears before the water reaches the stream and nothing shows
Continue through the silt bag and add a second settlement tank in series, as settling removes the hydrocarbons and leaves the discharge compliant with the rules
Pump it to the nearest foul sewer manhole, since sewage works treat contaminants anyway and no consent is needed for temporary flows
why: Dilution does not remove the contamination and the discharge would still be unpermitted pollution of the stream.
Silt bags and settlement remove solids, not dissolved or emulsified hydrocarbons, and the discharge still lacks a permit.
Discharge to a sewer needs the sewerage company's consent, and fuel contamination can damage the sewer and its treatment.
bank.ex: The temporary dewatering position covers uncontaminated water only, so contaminated groundwater must be contained and discharged or removed with the proper permit or consent.
bank.cm: Assuming that any water pumped out of a trench can go to a stream or drain once it has passed through a silt bag.

bank.stem: Roofers leave a stripped roof under loosely tied sheeting overnight. A storm tears it off and rain ruins stock in the neighbouring shop. The HSE takes no action, and the contractor's manager says that without enforcement there is no liability. Which statement is correct?
o: The claim succeeds automatically without proof of fault, because damage caused by building work attracts strict liability for the contractor
The owner can sue in negligence for foreseeable loss whatever the HSE does, though breaching the Act's duties itself gives no civil claim
No claim is possible, because the duties of a contractor under the Act protect only employees and workers on site, not neighbouring businesses
The shop owner can claim only if the HSE prosecutes, because proof of a breach of the Act is what gives a neighbour the right to compensation
why: Negligence still requires a breach of the duty of care that caused foreseeable loss, so fault must be shown.
The Act also protects non-employees affected by the work, and the common-law duty of care extends to neighbours.
Section 47 removes any civil right of action for breach of the Act's general duties, and civil claims do not need a prosecution.
bank.ex: Civil liability rests on the common-law duty of care, and section 47 of the Act says its duties do not confer a right of action, so the claim does not depend on HSE enforcement.
bank.cm: Believing that no enforcement action means no liability, or that civil claims depend on the HSE.

bank.stem: A slinger-signaller with Type 1 diabetes, who skipped breakfast, becomes sweaty, shaky and muddled by mid-morning. A colleague says he must be drunk and should be left to sleep it off. What is the right action?
o: Keep him signalling but pair him with a second signaller, because he is conscious and his colleague can cover any errors he makes
Give no sugar until a breath test rules out alcohol, since sweet drinks could mask the real cause of his confusion
Take him off the lifting task, give a fast-acting sugary drink if he is conscious, and keep him supervised until he recovers
Let him rest in the cabin for an hour with nothing to eat or drink, because the confusion will pass once he is calm
why: A person with impaired judgement must not carry out safety-critical lifting duties, even with a second person alongside.
Delaying treatment while testing for alcohol risks worsening low blood sugar, and the symptoms point to a hypo first.
Rest alone does not raise blood sugar, so his condition can deteriorate towards unconsciousness.
bank.ex: Confusion, sweating and shaking in a person with diabetes suggests low blood sugar, which needs quick sugar and removal from safety-critical work until fully recovered.
bank.cm: Assuming that confusion and unsteadiness at work must come from alcohol rather than a treatable medical condition.

bank.stem: A fitter must change a wheel on an articulated dumper. He jacks the front axle clear of the ground and works beneath it on level ground with the engine off. He says the jack and the stopped engine make it safe. Which statement is most accurate?
o: A jack can slip or fail, so the axle needs rated stands or blocks, and the articulation lock must be fitted to stop folding
A jack plus the stopped engine is enough on level ground, so nothing more is needed under a raised axle while he works there
The articulation lock matters only when travelling on slopes, so fitting it for maintenance on level ground is unnecessary extra work
Chocks on the other wheels replace stands, because a chocked machine cannot move whatever happens to the jack at the raised end of it
why: A jack alone is not a safe support to work beneath, and level ground does not prevent it failing or slipping.
The lock is also a maintenance safeguard, preventing the frame from pivoting while someone works near the joint or beneath.
Chocks stop rolling but do nothing if the jack fails and the raised axle drops onto the person below.
bank.ex: Raised plant must be supported by suitably rated stands or blocks rather than a jack alone, and the articulation lock prevents the machine pivoting while someone is working under it.
bank.cm: Trusting a jack and a stopped engine to hold a raised machine while working beneath it.

bank.stem: After an injury caused by a worker who ignored a safe system of work, the employer argues it has no liability because it gave the worker full training and the breach was entirely the individual's fault. No supervision checks were ever carried out. Which view is most accurate?
o: The employer is not liable, because the negligence of an individual worker who knowingly ignored a trained safe system breaks the chain of responsibility
Liability rests with the supervisor personally, because employers pass their safety duties to supervisors when they appoint them to the role, even where none were checked
Training alone does not discharge the duty without supervision and monitoring to check the safe system is followed, so the employer can still be held responsible
The employer is liable only if the training was delivered within twelve months of the incident, as older training is treated as out of date in law and so does not count
why: An employee's fault may be relevant, but it does not erase the employer's duty to supervise and enforce.
Employers cannot delegate away their statutory duties by appointing a supervisor.
No fixed twelve-month rule decides liability; adequacy of training, supervision and enforcement does.
bank.ex: The employer's duty is to ensure safety so far as is reasonably practicable, which includes supervising and checking that arrangements are followed, so one worker's non-compliance does not automatically remove the employer's responsibility.
bank.cm: Assuming that once training is recorded, any later breach by the worker is the worker's problem alone.

bank.stem: To save money, a supervisor places a hazard warning sign above a physical barrier in his control options, reasoning that signs are cheaper and should be tried first. Which statement best corrects this?
o: Cost is the first factor in the hierarchy, so the cheapest reasonable control is applied first and barriers are only considered if signs fail to work
Signs and barriers sit at the same level of the hierarchy, so either may be chosen at will according to which is easier to install on site
A physical barrier is a stronger control than a sign, because the hierarchy ranks controls by how well they reduce risk, not by cost
Signs rank above barriers, because a sign warns everyone approaching the area whereas a barrier only blocks a single route into it, and signs cost less
why: The hierarchy is based on effectiveness; cost only matters when judging what is reasonably practicable.
They are not equal; physical controls rank above signage and instruction.
Warning signs depend on people noticing and obeying them; barriers physically prevent access.
bank.ex: Physical measures such as barriers sit above information and signage in the hierarchy of control, so a sign cannot replace a barrier where one is reasonably practicable.
bank.cm: Letting the cost of a control decide its place in the hierarchy instead of its effectiveness.

bank.stem: Days after clearing a silted drainage ditch, a worker with a cut on his hand has fever, headache and aching muscles. He assumes flu and does not mention the ditch work to his GP. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Symptoms of leptospirosis take months to appear, so this is too soon to be work-related and mentioning the ditch work would only confuse the diagnosis
Leptospirosis is possible after contact with water contaminated by rat urine, so he should tell his doctor about the ditch work and the cut
Leptospirosis spreads mainly by drinking contaminated water, so a skin cut is irrelevant and the symptoms point to ordinary flu needing rest at home
Washing hands and covering cuts reduces the risk to a level where leptospirosis can be ruled out, so he can treat the illness as ordinary flu
why: Symptoms typically appear within days to a few weeks, and exposure history is key to diagnosis.
Infection commonly occurs through broken skin or the eyes and mouth, so a cut is a significant route.
Hygiene measures reduce the risk but cannot rule out infection, and the illness still needs medical attention.
bank.ex: Weil's disease can enter through cuts and has flu-like early symptoms, so telling the doctor about the exposure allows prompt testing and treatment.
bank.cm: Dismissing flu-like illness after work near water or sewage as just a cold or flu without telling a doctor about the exposure.

bank.stem: At the end of a pour, an operative washes out a concrete mixer on hardstanding that slopes to a surface-water drain. He says the washings are only cement and water, so heavy dilution makes them harmless. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Rinsing is allowed on hardstanding in dry weather since no rainwater is running, and any liquid left will soak away harmlessly into the ground
Cement washings are highly alkaline and harm aquatic life, and surface drains discharge to watercourses, so a lined washout area must be used
Washing out is acceptable if the water flows continuously, because large volumes of water dilute the cement enough that no real harm reaches the stream
The only risk is a blocked drain, which cement settling in the pipe could cause, so a grit trap on the drain would resolve the problem
why: Washings still enter the drain or ground, and dry weather does not remove the pollution offence.
Dilution at the point of washing does not neutralise alkalinity, and extra water simply moves the pollution on.
The main hazard is pollution of the watercourse, which a grit trap does not stop.
bank.ex: Wet concrete washings are strongly alkaline and can pollute watercourses through surface-water drains, which may be an offence, so they must be contained and disposed of properly.
bank.cm: Assuming that washings are harmless because cement is a common material and the volume of water seems large.

bank.stem: Three 205-litre oil drums stand on pallets in a site yard, 3 metres from a surface-water gully, with no tray. The spill kit is locked in the site office and one drum weeps from its bung. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Leave the drums, put absorbent granules around them, and wash any residue towards the drain with water, because dilution makes small oil losses harmless
Leave the drums in place on a drip tray, because the tray alone contains a leak and a spill kit is needed only after major fuel spillages
Move the drums away from drains onto a drip tray or bund able to hold a spill, and keep a stocked spill kit beside them with workers trained to use it
Cover the gully with a plastic sheet and keep the kit in the office, since staff can fetch it within minutes and the sheet stops oil reaching the drain
why: Washing oil into a surface-water drain is a pollution offence, because dilution does not make oil harmless to watercourses.
A tray does not remove the pollution risk of the drain location, and a kit should be at hand for any spill.
A loose sheet does not seal a gully, and a spill kit locked away is not available when it is needed.
bank.ex: Oil must be stored where a leak cannot reach drains, on secondary containment, with a spill kit and trained people immediately to hand, to prevent pollution of surface water.
bank.cm: Assuming a small oil leak near a drain can be diluted away and that the spill kit can be fetched after the leak starts.

bank.stem: A labourer feeding a block saw all week has an aching, tingling right wrist that eases at weekends. The supervisor suggests a wrist strap and carrying on. Which response reflects good practice?
o: Remove him permanently from site work, because upper limb symptoms always mean a person is unfit for any construction duties
Give the whole gang extra breaks but record nothing, since an accident book entry is meant for injuries from a single event
Treat it as a possible work-related upper limb disorder: record the report, vary the task, and consider occupational health advice
Fit the wrist strap and look again only if pain stops him working, since easing at weekends shows the cause is not work-related
why: Early symptoms are normally manageable by changing the task, so permanent removal is an unnecessary over-reaction.
Gradual-onset conditions should still be recorded and investigated, so that the cause of the symptoms can be found and controlled.
Easing during rest days is typical of work-related strain, and waiting for severe pain allows the damage to progress.
bank.ex: Symptoms that ease away from work point to a work-related cause, and recognising them early with task variation and breaks usually allows full recovery.
bank.cm: Assuming that only a sudden, one-off incident counts as a work injury worth reporting.

bank.stem: Look at the scene at the edge of this site. What is the most significant problem?
o: The machine's slew radius reaches the public footway where a pedestrian is passing through a gap, with no barrier, banksman or diversion in place
The excavator is working inside the site line, so the arrangement is acceptable if the operator sounds the horn and keeps the bucket low as people pass
The pedestrian is not wearing high-visibility clothing or a hard hat, so the failing is mainly the PPE of the member of the public
The excavator is parked too close to the boundary, so the main concern is blocked access for deliveries and emergency vehicles along the road
why: Relying on the operator's vigilance is a weak control, and a gap in the hoarding exposes the public to the machine's reach.
Members of the public are protected by segregation and control of the work, not by wearing PPE.
Access is a secondary matter compared with the immediate risk of the machine striking a passing pedestrian.
bank.ex: Plant working beside a public highway must be segregated so its swing and bucket cannot reach pedestrians, which needs intact barriers, exclusion zones and controlled access.
bank.cm: Assuming that a machine working inside the site line is safe for passers-by so long as the operator is careful.
bank.alt: An excavator works behind timber hoarding beside a public footway, with its arm reaching toward the street where a pedestrian is walking.

bank.stem: At 22:00 a site manager sends an engineer alone to a closed, unlit plant compound to check a leaking valve. His only instruction is to text when he has finished. Which approach properly meets the employer's duty to manage this lone, out-of-hours task?
o: Rely on his mobile phone, since being able to call out in an emergency means the risks of working alone have already been dealt with
Cancel the task, because lone working out of hours is unlawful and a second person must always attend whatever the risk assessment concludes about it
Accept the finishing text as the control if he is experienced, because experienced staff do not need any contact or monitoring while the task is under way
Assess the task for this person and place, then agree set check-in times with a named contact and the action to take if one is missed
why: A phone is no help if he is injured or unconscious, has no signal, or cannot reach it, so it cannot be the only control.
Lone working is not prohibited in general and is often safe once the risks have been assessed and controlled.
A single text at the end gives no contact while the work is under way, and experience does not stop an accident, illness or assault.
bank.ex: Lone working is not unlawful, but the risk assessment must cover the person, the place and emergencies, and the employer must set regular contact and a defined response when contact fails.
bank.cm: Treating a phone in the pocket and a message at the end of the job as a full lone-working arrangement.

bank.stem: A worker's hand is crushed in an unguarded pinch point on a conveyor, and he is taken to hospital. The supervisor wants to clear the area, restart the line to hit the day's output and brief the team verbally. How should the site respond?
o: Have the fitter repair the guard immediately and record operator error as the cause, since the aim of an investigation is to identify who was at fault
Isolate the machine, keep the scene as it was, record photos and witness accounts, then investigate the underlying causes as well as the final act
Leave the conveyor running and untouched until an inspector arrives, because isolating the machine would disturb evidence and could cause further harm
Restart once the area is swept, because the injured worker has left site and the investigation can rely on his own account when he eventually returns to work
why: Investigations aim to find root causes to prevent a repeat, and repairing before recording destroys the evidence of what failed.
A dangerous machine must be isolated straight away, since protecting others takes priority and isolation can be done while recording the scene.
Clearing the scene destroys evidence, and one person's later recollection is not a reliable basis for finding causes.
bank.ex: The area must be made safe, but evidence should be preserved and the investigation should look for root causes such as the missing guard and the system that allowed it, not only the immediate event.
bank.cm: Believing an investigation exists to find someone to blame, so restoring production and tidying the scene comes first.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The foreman says the job is only a day's work and the crew are experienced roofers. What is the most significant problem?
o: The access ladder extends too far above the roof edge, which makes the ladder unstable and is the most significant issue in the picture
The membrane roll is too heavy for two workers to carry, so the manual handling risk outweighs any risk from the roof structure
Fragile rooflights are uncovered in the work area and the open roof edge has no guardrails, so a fall through or off is possible
The sheeting has weathered to a dull grey, which could be slippery when wet, and that is the main hazard shown on this roof
why: A ladder should extend above the landing point and it is shown tied, so it is not the main hazard.
Manual handling is a lesser risk than falling through a fragile surface or off an unprotected edge, which could be fatal.
Slipperiness is a concern in wet weather but it is not the main hazard here, where the scene shows a dry surface and far more serious fall risks.
bank.ex: Rooflights can break under a person's weight and are a leading cause of fatal falls, so they need to be covered or guarded, and the roof edge needs edge protection.
bank.cm: Assuming experienced roofers or a short job make fragile roof surfaces and open edges acceptable without covers or edge protection.
bank.alt: Two roofers carry a roll of material across a metal sheet roof that has several rooflight panels; a ladder leans against the edge of the building.

bank.stem: A bricklayer slumps, unresponsive and not breathing normally. A trained first aider reaches him within seconds, and the site defibrillator is in the office, two minutes' walk away. What is the best immediate action?
o: Place him in the recovery position and monitor his breathing until the ambulance arrives, because compressions risk injuring someone who may still be breathing
Send one person to call 999 and fetch the defibrillator while the first aider starts chest compressions, then follow the device's spoken prompts on arrival
Carry him to the site office on a flat board so treatment happens beside the defibrillator, and call 999 once the first aider has begun treatment there
Start compressions but leave the defibrillator until paramedics arrive, because shocks given by untrained bystanders can harm the casualty
why: The recovery position is for casualties who are breathing normally, and he is not, so he needs CPR.
Moving him delays compressions and the emergency call, and he should only be moved if the area is unsafe.
Public-access defibrillators give spoken instructions and will not shock unless it is advised, so early use improves survival.
bank.ex: Cardiac arrest needs compressions straight away and an early shock, so tasks are shared: an ambulance is called, the defibrillator is fetched and CPR continues without delay.
bank.cm: Waiting for the ambulance or for a more qualified person before starting CPR and fetching the defibrillator.

bank.stem: At 07:00 a dumper driver arrives smelling strongly of alcohol after a late night, insisting he feels fine. Short of drivers, the supervisor lets him start, since he is not slurring and will only drive on site. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Move him to banksman duty for the morning, because directing traffic needs no coordination or judgement and is a safer task to give him
Let him drive, since the road drink-drive limit applies only on public roads and an operator who seems alert and steady is not a real risk on private land
Keep him off driving and other safety-critical work, as alcohol still impairs judgement, and handle it under the site alcohol and drugs policy with support
Send him home in his own car and record the day as ordinary absence, avoiding a formal conversation until he is sober and calm
why: Banksman work is safety-critical and relies on alertness and judgement, so impairment is just as dangerous there.
Health and safety law requires employers and workers not to endanger others on site, whatever the road driving limit says.
Letting him drive while possibly over the limit endangers the public, and treating it as plain absence ignores the policy and any support he needs.
bank.ex: Residual alcohol can impair reaction and judgement even when someone feels well, so the supervisor must protect others by removing him from safety-critical duties and following the policy supportively.
bank.cm: Judging fitness for safety-critical work by whether someone looks and feels all right rather than by the risk of impairment.

bank.stem: A paving operative uses a breaker with a vibration magnitude of 7 m/s2 for two hours of trigger time a day. The manager notes that the exposure limit value is 5 m/s2 A(8) and says the job must stop. Which statement is most accurate?
o: About 3.5 m/s2 A(8), over the action value but below the limit, so controls, training and health surveillance are needed without banning the job
The exposure is 7 m/s2 because magnitude is what counts, and since this is over the limit value the operator must be taken off the tool immediately
The figure is about 1.75 m/s2 because two hours out of eight is a quarter, so it falls under the action value and no duties apply to the operator
The exposure is under the limit of 5, so duties begin only if symptoms are reported and no preventive action is needed until then
why: Exposure is worked out over an eight-hour reference period, so the tool's magnitude alone does not give the daily figure.
Exposure does not scale in a straight line with time, since it follows the square root of the time ratio.
Duties such as controls and health surveillance start at the action value, not at the limit or after symptoms.
bank.ex: Daily exposure scales with the square root of time, so 7 m/s2 for two hours is about 3.5 m/s2 A(8), above the action value of 2.5 but under the limit of 5.
bank.cm: Treating the limit value as the point where action starts instead of the action value.

bank.stem: A telehandler loads pallets through an extendable gate on a scaffold. Workers lift the gate handles while standing at the platform edge beside the gap. The mesh panel is held with one plastic cable tie. Which arrangement is correct?
o: Open the gate from 2 m back using a rope over a rail, secure the mesh as the supplier specifies, and check it at each 7-day inspection
Keep lifting the handles at the edge but clip a harness to the ledger, and add a second tie to the mesh panel whenever it loosens
Leave the single plastic tie in place, since the weekly scaffold inspection will pick up any slipping mesh before a person is harmed
Take the gate off during deliveries and hang a chain across the opening, as the telehandler operator will warn all workers to keep back
why: Working at the edge beside a gap more than a metre high remains unsafe, and a ledger is not a designed anchor point.
One plastic tie is inadequate to hold the mesh, and relying on the inspection allows an unsafe gate to be used for days.
A chain provides no equivalent of rails, mesh and toe board, and relying on the operator's warning is not edge protection.
bank.ex: HSE's safety bulletin on loading bay gates advises operating them from the rear of the platform, at least 2 m from the open edge, and properly securing and inspecting the mesh so it gives edge protection equal to rails.
bank.cm: Treating the loading gate as a temporary nuisance during deliveries instead of as edge protection that must work whether open or closed.
