bank.stem: A groundworks crew is given a new diesel generator to run lights and tools in a 2 m trench. The supervisor must choose the supply and position. Which arrangement is correct?
o: A 230 V output with RCD protection on every socket, placed beside the trench so that leads reach the working face with fewer joints
A 110 V centre-tapped earthed output sited well clear of the trench, needing no checks because new sets are tested by the manufacturer
A 110 V centre-tapped earthed output, set on timber mats at the trench edge with its exhaust blowing across the opening to keep leads short
A 110 V centre-tapped earthed output, sited well clear of the trench edge with exhaust directed away from it, and checked by the user before first use
why: 230 V is unsuitable for portable tools on a wet groundworks site, and a unit beside the trench edge is also wrongly positioned.
Manufacturer testing does not remove the need for checks on the set and its leads before first use on site.
Placing a generator at the edge of an excavation risks collapse and lets exhaust fumes collect in the trench.
bank.ex: Centre-tap earthing limits voltage to earth to 55 V, engines and generators should not stand near excavation edges where fumes collect, and new equipment still needs a pre-use check.
bank.cm: Assuming that because equipment is new and the voltage is reduced, its siting and set-up need no further thought.

bank.stem: A designer specifies 25 kg concrete lintels for a first-floor opening, although a 12 kg lightweight alternative of similar cost meets the load requirements. She adds a drawing note saying 'handle with care' and moves on. What should she have done?
o: Chosen the lighter lintel to reduce the handling risk at source, then passed on information about any remaining risk to the principal designer
Kept the heavy lintel and listed its weight in the specification, as residual risk information is reserved for major hazards like asbestos or collapse
Kept the 25 kg lintel, since her note shifts responsibility to the contractor who will be carrying out the lifting on site
Left the choice of lintel to the principal contractor on site, because designers have no duties over how work is carried out during construction
why: Designers must share information on significant residual risks of any kind, and here a safer option was available anyway.
A note does not transfer the designer's duty to reduce foreseeable risks through the design itself.
Designers must consider foreseeable construction risks when they make design decisions and cannot hand that choice to the contractor.
bank.ex: Designers must first eliminate or reduce foreseeable risks through their design choices, and only then provide information about the risks that remain so others can plan for them.
bank.cm: Believing a warning note on a drawing discharges the designer's duty when a safer design choice was available.

bank.stem: Groundwater seeps into a 2 m supported trench. A groundworker places a petrol-engined pump on the trench floor to clear it and carries on laying pipe beside it. What is the best assessment?
o: Exhaust can fill the trench with carbon monoxide, so site the pump at the surface or use electric, and re-inspect the support after the ingress
The pump is acceptable because trenches are open to the air, and any fumes will rise out of the top and disperse quickly in normal weather
Move the pump to the surface but skip further checks, because the support was inspected at the start of the shift this morning and passed
The pump is acceptable if run with the choke half open, since a rich mixture produces fewer fumes and lowers the poisoning risk in the trench
why: Exhaust gas can collect in a trench and linger in still air, which is how carbon monoxide poisoning happens.
Water ingress is a change in conditions, and a morning inspection does not cover its effect on the sides or support.
A rich mixture produces more carbon monoxide, and fuel settings are no substitute for removing the source from the trench.
bank.ex: Petrol exhaust gas can collect in a trench and cause fatal carbon monoxide poisoning, and water ingress can weaken the sides, so the support needs inspecting again.
bank.cm: Treating an open-topped trench as well ventilated even when an engine is running in it.

bank.stem: To reach a high soffit, a contractor wants two operatives to ride in a site-made steel cage fitted to the forks of a telehandler. The driver is experienced and says the machine is well within its capacity. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The lift is acceptable if the operatives wear full harnesses attached to the cage, which then prevents any fall from height
The lift is acceptable because the combined weight of the cage and operatives is below the rated capacity, and the driver is experienced
The lift is acceptable for short tasks of under an hour, since the extra risk to the operatives grows with the time spent in the cage
The machine is built for loads, so lifting people is for exceptional circumstances, and a purpose-designed platform or MEWP is safer
why: Harnesses do not make an unsuitable arrangement safe, and a harness cannot replace equipment designed for lifting people.
Capacity is only one factor, and a site-made cage on a machine not designed for lifting people does not meet the extra safety requirements.
Risk is not controlled by the length of time, because the cage could detach or the machine tip the moment it leaves the ground.
bank.ex: Equipment not designed to lift people should only be used in exceptional circumstances, so a MEWP or a purpose- designed platform with suitable planning and examination is the proper choice here.
bank.cm: Judging a person-lift on the telehandler's load rating alone, without asking whether the equipment was made to carry people.

bank.stem: A yard cuts steel reinforcement bars with an abrasive cut-off saw, giving about 100 dB(A) at the operator's ear. The manager asks which sequence of controls follows the hierarchy for noise. Which is correct?
o: Fit a screen and defenders together first, then rotate workers, and treat switching to a shear or pre-cut bars as a final option because it needs a purchase
Issue ear defenders straight away as the quickest control, then enclose the saw, then reduce the time spent cutting, and consider a quieter method last of all
Rotate operators first to limit each person's daily dose, then fit defenders, and enclose the saw or change the cutting method only if readings stay high
Order bars pre-cut off site; if not possible use a quieter shear; then enclose or screen the saw; then limit exposure time, with ear defenders as the last resort
why: Eliminating or substituting the noise source comes first, and purchase effort does not reorder the hierarchy.
This inverts the hierarchy by putting personal protection first and elimination or substitution last.
Administrative measures and PPE rank below removing or reducing noise at source.
bank.ex: Noise should be removed at source first, then substituted or engineered down, then managed by working arrangements, with hearing protection used only for the risk that remains.
bank.cm: Reaching for ear defenders first because they are quick and cheap, instead of working down from eliminating the noise.

bank.stem: Four labourers build a temporary flood barrier by lifting 25 kg wet sandbags from a lorry to waist height and stacking them on a slippery slope for four hours. One says 25 kg is the safe limit. Which approach best applies the manual handling hierarchy?
o: Provide back support belts and require lifting with bent knees, because the belts allow heavier repeated loads to be handled safely over a long period
Let each worker set his own pace and rest breaks, since assessment of the task applies only to single lifts that exceed the guideline weights
Mechanise or avoid the handling where possible, then cut load and repetition with smaller bags, a handling chain with rotation, and firm, dry footing
Treat 25 kg as a legal limit for men and rely on fitness checks and lifting technique training to cover the repetitive stacking on the slope
why: Back belts are not a recognised control and do not make repeated heavy lifting safe.
Repetitive handling and the environment must be assessed even when individual lifts are below guideline weights.
Guideline weights are not legal limits and repetition, twisting and slippery footing change the risk.
bank.ex: Manual handling controls start with avoiding or mechanising the task, then reduce the load, repetition and poor conditions identified through the task, individual, load and environment factors.
bank.cm: Treating a guideline weight as a safe limit and ignoring repetition, posture and ground conditions.

bank.stem: A 25-litre drum of acid-based brick cleaner splits when dropped on a paved wash area. The liquid runs towards a surface- water drain that discharges to a brook. Nobody has yet seen it enter the drain. What is the best response?
o: Absorb it with the kit, put the used absorbent in the general waste skip, and report only if the brook looks discoloured
Dilute it with plenty of water from the hose so the acid is weak enough to be washed safely down the drain
Stop the leak, cover the drain and dam the spill, absorb it, and phone the regulator's hotline if it may reach the brook
Neutralise it with a bag of cement powder, then sweep the residue into the drain once it has stopped fizzing
why: Used absorbent is hazardous waste, and waiting for visible damage delays a report that should follow the risk.
Dilution still delivers the chemical to the brook and increases the volume of polluted liquid to deal with.
Improvised neutralising is uncontrolled and adds alkaline pollution, and sweeping the residue into a drain still pollutes the brook.
bank.ex: Cutting off the source and protecting the drain stops the chemical reaching water, and a risk to a watercourse should be reported to the environment regulator straight away.
bank.cm: Waiting until pollution is visible in a watercourse before containing a spill or contacting the regulator.

bank.stem: A 1.4 m deep service trench is to run 0.5 m from the strip footing of a 1930s house whose base is about 0.6 m down. The supervisor says the trench box he has hired holds the sides, so nothing else is needed. Which action is best before digging?
o: Dig by hand in short lengths beside the footing and backfill each length immediately, as hand digging is gentle enough to avoid any ground movement
Get a competent engineer to assess whether the footing needs temporary support, then set a method and a way of watching for movement
Rely on the footing being 0.6 m deep, since foundations of that depth sit below the level where digging nearby could affect them
Keep the box tight against the trench sides, because a snug shield also prevents any movement of the soil beneath the neighbouring footing
why: Hand digging reduces vibration but does not stop the soil beside the footing losing support or the footing being undermined.
The trench is deeper than the footing, so the soil supporting it may be disturbed, and depth alone does not remove the risk.
A shield holds the trench walls and workers safe but does not guarantee the ground carrying the footing will stay stable.
bank.ex: Excavations must not undermine nearby foundations, and a trench box supports the trench sides without necessarily protecting the footing, so structural advice and monitoring are needed.
bank.cm: Assuming that supporting the sides of a trench also protects the foundations of any building close beside it.

bank.stem: A 13-tonne excavator working into a winter evening slews beside a temporary Heras fence, with 0.5 m between its tail swing and the fence. Its work lights shine on the trench. Walkers use the public footway behind the fence. Which action best deals with the risk?
o: Ask the operator to check the mirrors before each slew and to work slowly, since the trench lights are enough to show the fence line
Rely on the machine's flashing beacon and audible alarm to warn walkers, as the fence already prevents access to the swinging counterweight
Set the fence beyond the full tail-swing radius or limit the slew, and light the whole area so operator and walkers can see the boundary
Fit a second Heras panel against the first to thicken the barrier, so that a bumped fence can no longer be pushed into the footway
why: Operator vigilance is a weak control, and lighting aimed at the trench does not show the fence line or the walkers beyond it.
Beacons and alarms are only warnings, and a fence 0.5 m from the counterweight does not give enough clearance for a body or a hand through the mesh.
A thicker barrier does not increase clearance from the counterweight and may increase the crush point between the fence and the machine.
bank.ex: The tail swing must be kept clear of people and fixed barriers by a safe margin, and the lighting should cover the barrier and approach as well as the digging face.
bank.cm: Thinking a warning light and a barrier placed tight against the machine are enough to protect the public from tail swing.

bank.stem: A principal contractor runs a site with two buildings and four contractors. The fire sounder is audible only in the main block, and no evacuation drill has been held since the subcontractors arrived. Which arrangement best meets the CDM duty on emergency procedures?
o: Emergency arrangements cover evacuating any part of the site, suit its layout and headcount, are made known to all concerned, and are tested at suitable intervals
Each contractor writes its own evacuation plan for its own gang and chooses its own assembly point, because the sounder in the main block alerts everyone who needs it
The procedure is read out at each new starter's induction, which makes everyone familiar with it and removes the need for any later testing of the arrangements on site
One evacuation plan is pinned in the main cabin and signed by every contractors' supervisor, with any practice drill left until the next formal audit takes place
why: Separate uncoordinated plans leave people in the far building without a warning or a common assembly point.
Familiarity and testing are separate requirements, and a one-off reading does not show the arrangements actually work.
A displayed plan does not make workers familiar with it, and the arrangements must be tested at suitable intervals.
bank.ex: CDM 2015 requires suitable emergency arrangements, including evacuation, that reflect the site's size, layout and numbers, with those covered made familiar with them and the arrangements tested.
bank.cm: Assuming a written plan and an alarm in one cabin cover a multi-contractor site without anyone checking it works across the whole layout.

bank.stem: Labourers hand-sort timber from a soft strip, with protruding nails and broken glass in the waste. The supervisor issues standard cut-resistant fabric gloves and says that deals with it. What is the best improvement?
o: Keep the gloves because their cut rating also covers nail punctures, and ask everyone to confirm their tetanus vaccination is current
Remove nails and bag glass at source using pickers, then add puncture-resistant gloves and penetration-resistant footwear
Have one labourer sort at a time on rotation, so that only one person is exposed to the sharps at any moment
Change to thick leather gloves and ask workers to sort slowly, as extra care gives the same protection as removing the sharps
why: Cut and puncture resistance are tested separately, and a vaccination does not prevent injury.
Rotating people reduces numbers exposed but leaves each sorter with the same cut and puncture hazard.
Care and gloves alone leave the hazard in place, and leather can be punctured by nails.
bank.ex: Reducing the sharps at source comes first, and PPE for what remains must be rated for puncture as well as cut, which are separate performance ratings.
bank.cm: Assuming a glove marked as cut-resistant is also resistant to punctures from nails.

bank.stem: A faulty socket circuit in a busy plant room is to be repaired. The manager says that shutting it off would halt production for an afternoon, and that the competent electrician can work live if he wears insulating gloves. What do the Electricity at Work Regulations say?
o: Live work needs dead working to be unreasonable, live working reasonable and suitable precautions taken, so lost production alone is not enough
Live work is allowed on circuits below 400 volts, since the regulation applies only to high-voltage conductors that can arc over at distance
Live work is allowed if the manager signs a written instruction accepting the risk, as this makes the decision a managerial one to take
Live work is allowed where the electrician is competent and wears insulating gloves, because suitable precautions alone satisfy the regulation in full
why: The regulation applies to any live conductor where danger may arise, including ordinary mains voltage which can kill.
A signature does not meet the legal conditions, and the duty for safe working remains with the person doing the work as well.
Precautions are only the third condition, and the other two must also be met before any live work can start.
bank.ex: Regulation 14 requires all three conditions to be met, and inconvenience or cost of isolating does not alone make it unreasonable to work dead.
bank.cm: Treating live working as acceptable whenever isolation is inconvenient and the electrician is skilled.

bank.stem: A bricklayer's scaffold bay carries a notice marked "Loading Class 2". The foreman wants three pallets of bricks placed on the working platform and says the class number only shows how many people may stand on it. How should the class be understood?
o: It gives the distributed and point loads the platform was designed for, so workers and materials together must stay within it, or a higher class is needed
It states the weight of people only, because materials are carried by the ties and standards rather than by the boards of the platform
It states the scaffolder's competence grade, so a Class 2 notice shows skilled erectors built it and heavy stacking is then permitted
It states how many boarded lifts the scaffold may have, so three pallets are acceptable if only one lift is occupied at any one time
why: Materials load the boards directly, and the class covers workers, tools and materials together.
Loading class is a design capacity, not a measure of the erectors' skill, and does not authorise heavy stacking.
The class describes load capacity per platform and has nothing to do with how many lifts are in use.
bank.ex: Loading classes set the design load per square metre and point load for a working platform, so a task needing heavier stacking requires a platform designed and handed over for that duty.
bank.cm: Reading a scaffold notice as a pass for the structure instead of as the limit on what the platform carries.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative has all the PPE a petrol disc cutter needs. What is the most significant problem, and what should be done?
o: His ear defenders cannot cope with a petrol cutter, so he should add foam earplugs under them and then restart the cut
The water feed makes eye protection unnecessary, so the dust mask alone is enough and the cut can continue as it is
His visor is raised, leaving eyes and face open to fragments, so he should stop and lower it before resuming
His gloves are a risk near a spinning disc, so he should remove them and hold the slab with bare hands instead
why: The ear defenders are worn correctly, and the real gap is the unprotected face and eyes.
Spray does not stop fragments or chips flying from the disc, so face protection is still required.
Close- fitting gloves are acceptable here, and removing them would increase hand injuries without addressing the face.
bank.ex: A disc cutter throws fragments and spray at the face, so eye and face protection must be in place and worn correctly, not parked on the helmet.
bank.cm: Thinking that wearing a visor on the helmet counts as eye protection even when it is not lowered over the face.
bank.alt: A worker kneels to cut concrete paving slabs with a petrol disc cutter fed with water; he wears a helmet with a face visor, ear defenders, a dust mask and gloves.

bank.stem: A mobile crane lifts precast steps from the ground to a first- floor slab. The slinger signals while the load is at ground level, and a second person at the slab edge will receive it. The operator will respond to whoever signals. What is the best plan?
o: Leave the operator to judge the landing alone from the cab, because the person who controls the crane is the best placed to put the load down safely
Name one signaller at a time, hand over with a clear stop and confirm, keep the landing zone clear, and have the operator stop on an unclear signal
Have the slinger keep signalling after the load rises out of sight, since the slinger knows the load best and can judge the landing from below the slab
Let both signal together so the operator has two views, because duplicated signals give the operator a double check on each movement of the load
why: The operator may not see the landing, which is why a signaller is used and the plan must name one.
A signaller who cannot see the load or landing cannot direct it safely, so control must pass to someone who can.
Competing signals confuse the operator, who needs a single clear source of instruction.
bank.ex: Only one signaller should direct the operator at any time, handovers must be unambiguous, and the operator should stop on any signal that is unclear or lost.
bank.cm: Assuming several people can signal a crane at once, rather than naming one signaller who hands over clearly.

bank.stem: An electrician must fit six light fittings along a corridor ceiling from fully guarded podium steps. To save time, his mate suggests he push on the ceiling to roll the podium to each fitting with the brakes off. Which approach is correct?
o: Rolling is acceptable on a smooth floor if the mate steadies the frame and the electrician holds the guardrail throughout every move
Leave the brakes on and lean out to reach the next fitting, because the guardrails round the platform will stop him falling
Keep the brakes on and gate closed while working, and step down to move the podium and re-brake it at each position
Rolling is acceptable for short moves under two metres if he crouches in the centre and travels at walking pace
why: Moving the podium with a person aboard is unsafe because it can tip or the castors can catch and throw him.
Leaning beyond the guardrails shifts the centre of gravity and risks overturning, so the unit must be repositioned instead.
Short distance and crouching do not remove the risk of tipping, and the rule is to move it empty.
bank.ex: Podium steps are stable only when braked and used within their guarded platform, so they must be moved when unoccupied.
bank.cm: Thinking guardrails make a mobile platform safe to move or lean from while someone is standing on it.

bank.stem: While clearing bracken for a ground investigation, a surveyor finds a tick attached to his calf. A colleague suggests burning it off with a lighter. What is the best response?
o: Squeeze the body and pull it off quickly, then ignore the bite unless it stays red, hot and itchy for more than a few days afterwards
Burn it or smear it with petroleum jelly to make it drop off, then keep an eye on the bite for about a week and no longer
Leave it until it falls off after feeding, because pulling it out risks leaving the mouthparts behind and causing a worse infection
Remove it with fine tweezers or a tick tool close to the skin, clean the bite and watch for a rash or flu-like illness for three months
why: Squeezing the body can push infected contents into the skin, and the Lyme rash is usually neither hot nor itchy.
Heat and smothering are not recommended, and watching for only a week misses symptoms that can appear up to three months later.
The longer a tick stays attached the greater the infection risk, so correct early removal is recommended rather than waiting.
bank.ex: Prompt careful removal reduces the chance of infection, and Lyme disease can show as a spreading rash or flu- like symptoms weeks or even months after a bite, so early medical advice matters.
bank.cm: Thinking that a tick bite is only a concern if the bite site itself becomes sore or itchy.

bank.stem: An inspector serves an Improvement Notice on a Monday, giving 28 days to repair a faulty guard. On day 24 the contractor says he will now appeal, and that the notice will pause while the appeal is heard. Which statement is correct?
o: An appeal can be lodged at any point but never suspends an Improvement Notice, so the guard must be repaired by the original deadline either way
The appeal period is 21 days from service, so he is outside it, the notice is not suspended and the 28-day deadline stands
Appeals go to the magistrates' court within 28 days of service, and the notice stays suspended until the court has reached a final decision on it
The appeal period runs for the whole 28 days of the notice, so he can still appeal today and the notice will pause once the appeal has been lodged
why: A valid and timely appeal does suspend an Improvement Notice until it is heard or withdrawn, unlike a Prohibition Notice.
Appeals against notices go to the employment tribunal, and the time limit is 21 days rather than 28.
The appeal window is 21 days from service and is shorter than the compliance period, so day 24 is too late.
bank.ex: An appeal against an Improvement Notice must be lodged with the employment tribunal within 21 days of service, and only a valid appeal suspends the notice, so the compliance date stands.
bank.cm: Assuming the appeal window is the same length as the time given to put the problem right.

bank.stem: A risk assessment rates a rare but severe hazard, a pallet fork load falling from height, as 'low' because it has never happened on this firm's sites. The manager signs it off on that basis. Which comment is most accurate?
o: The rating is sound because severity matters only when an accident has already taken place on the site in question
The rating should reflect both likelihood and severity, so a potentially fatal hazard needs controls even where it is rare
The rating should be raised only if the pallet is heavier than a tonne, since weight alone decides the level of risk
The rating is sound because risk depends on past events only, and an event that has never occurred cannot be a significant risk
why: Severity must be considered in advance, not after harm has occurred.
Many factors, not one weight, decide the risk.
Absence of past accidents does not remove the possibility of a serious one.
bank.ex: Risk combines how likely harm is with how severe it could be, and a lack of past incidents does not make a potentially fatal outcome low risk.
bank.cm: Rating a severe hazard as low simply because nothing has gone wrong so far.

bank.stem: A 'Danger: overhead crane operations' sign is cable-tied to the entrance gate, 80 m from the lifting area. It is faded and half hidden behind a poster. The manager says it covers the hazard, so no new sign is needed. What is the right response?
o: Add a second gate sign and rely on induction to cover the lifting area, because more signs inside the site would clutter it and distract the crane crew
Replace it with a clean, legible sign where people approach the lifting area, and keep it maintained as a supplement to barriers and a signaller
Keep the gate sign but enlarge it, since a sign read on entry will be remembered by everyone when they later pass near the lifting area on their rounds
Leave the faded sign until the next monthly inspection, as a displayed warning sign gives legal cover provided it was in place when lifting began
why: Induction does not replace a legible sign where the risk exists, and the problem here is placement and condition, not volume.
Size does not fix its position, and a warning must be seen at the point of risk, not recalled from 80 m away.
Signs have to be maintained so they remain legible, and a faded, half-hidden sign cannot warn anyone.
bank.ex: Safety signs must be clear and legible and provided and maintained where a significant risk remains, so they need to be seen in time at the hazard and supplement other controls.
bank.cm: Assuming a sign has done its job once it is fixed to the site gate, wherever the hazard is and however faded the sign becomes.

bank.stem: A fencer sprays a solvent-based timber preservative in a garage workshop, creating both vapour and fine mist. He wears a half-mask with brown gas filters only, and a colleague says white filters are better. Which advice is correct?
o: Stay with the brown gas filters alone, because white only denotes dust and the carbon in a brown filter also traps liquid mist as well as vapour in the air
Use combination filters such as A2P3, where brown handles organic vapour and white stops the mist particles, with a suitable face fit
Choose grey B filters, because grey is the standard colour for chemical vapours and is the correct choice for any solvent- based liquid
Swap to white P3 filters alone, because P3 is the highest class and its pleated medium will also absorb the solvent vapours in the air
why: A gas filter does not capture airborne droplets, so the mist needs the white particle filter in addition to the brown vapour filter.
Grey type B is for certain inorganic gases and vapours, whereas organic solvent vapour needs brown type A.
A particle filter does nothing against vapours, and so he would breathe the solvent unprotected through a filter that looks high-grade.
bank.ex: Type A (brown) filters deal with organic vapours of higher boiling point and P (white) filters deal with particles and mist, so spray work with both hazards needs both functions.
bank.cm: Choosing a respirator filter by its class number or familiarity without matching its type and colour to both the vapour and particle hazards.

bank.stem: On a fit-out, the alarm sounds. After two minutes the panel operator silences it because nobody has seen smoke or flames, and workers who gathered at the assembly point start drifting back inside. What is the correct response?
o: Workers may return to ground-floor areas after ten minutes, since a fire that has not grown by then is very unlikely to threaten the lower floors of the building
Workers may return once the bell stops, because a silenced alarm with no visible smoke indicates a false alarm and carrying on saves a good deal of lost time
Everyone stays at the assembly point until the person in charge has checked the cause and gives a clear all-clear, with the fire service called if none is found
Each firm's supervisor decides for his own gang, because contractors know their own areas best and can judge whether it is safe to go back
why: A fixed waiting time is not a safety check, and smoke and fire can spread to any level without being seen.
Silencing a sounder says nothing about the cause, and a fire can be developing out of sight in a void or store.
Re-entry needs one coordinated decision by the person in charge, not separate judgements made by several firms without checking the cause.
bank.ex: An alarm must be treated as a real fire until the cause is confirmed, so re-entry waits for an authorised all-clear, and silencing the sounder does not remove the possible danger.
bank.cm: Treating a silenced fire alarm as proof that there is no fire.

bank.stem: A site manager says the Health and Safety at Work Act is the only real law, that regulations such as the Work at Height Regulations are just HSE opinion, and that HSE guidance leaflets are binding on everyone. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Regulations and guidance carry the same legal force as the Act itself, so any departure from the wording of an HSE leaflet is a criminal offence in its own right
Regulations bind only employers with five or more staff, and guidance becomes law once the employer has been handed a copy of the relevant leaflet by an HSE inspector
Only the Act creates offences, regulations are enforced through civil claims alone, and guidance must be followed to the letter on every single job to avoid prosecution
Regulations are made under the Act and breaching them is an offence, whereas HSE guidance is optional and a different method that meets the law is allowed
why: Guidance is not compulsory, so departing from it is not itself an offence if the law is still met.
Regulations apply regardless of headcount, and handing over guidance does not turn it into law.
Contravening health and safety regulations is itself a criminal offence, and guidance can be replaced by an equivalent method.
bank.ex: Regulations have full legal force under section 33 of the Act, whereas HSE guidance is advice that normally demonstrates compliance but may be replaced by an alternative that still meets the legal duty.
bank.cm: Assuming that only the Act counts as law, or that every HSE leaflet is a legal command.

bank.stem: On a sunny day a labourer brushes coal-tar creosote onto post ends in a T-shirt and fabric gloves. By evening his forearms are red and sore. A colleague says it is ordinary sunburn that moisturiser will fix. Which response is correct?
o: Creosote is harmful only if swallowed or inhaled, so the redness is plain sunburn needing after-sun cream and a sun hat for the next shift ahead
Creosote on skin can heighten sunlight sensitivity and cause burns, so he should wash it off, report it and use sleeves and chemical-resistant gloves
The only risk is vapour, so a dust mask and working in the shade would remove the hazard, with no need to change the way he handles it
Thicker fabric gloves would keep the product off his skin, and the redness is a normal reaction to sun that does not need to be reported
why: Skin is a significant route of exposure for creosote and sunlight can worsen the damage.
A dust mask does not stop vapour or skin contact, so neither route is controlled by shade and a paper mask.
Fabric absorbs creosote and holds it against the skin, and the injury should still be reported and investigated.
bank.ex: Skin contact with creosote can increase sensitivity to light and cause burns and irritation, so exposure must be controlled at the skin and the incident reported for review.
bank.cm: Putting skin reactions down to sunburn or weather instead of asking what substance was on the skin.

bank.stem: A fitter must use a braced mobile tower on a gentle concrete ramp between two warehouse bays. The crew apply all four castor brakes and say stabilisers are unnecessary because the wheels are locked. What is the main flaw?
o: A ramp is acceptable if the tower is half-height and cross- braced, since the height-to-base ratio is the only measure of stability on any surface
Stabilisers should be left off on a ramp because they lift the castors clear and leave the brakes carrying less of the tower's weight
Locked castors do not stop tipping on a slope; check the maker's gradient limits, use adjustable legs on base plates and fit the specified stabilisers
Locked castors prevent movement in every direction, so on a ramp the only extra check needed is that the platform boards are secured to the frame
why: Stability also depends on the slope, the ground and the manufacturer's instructions, not height alone.
Stabilisers are fitted as the manufacturer's schedule requires and help to prevent the tower overturning.
Brakes cannot prevent overturning, which is the main danger on a slope.
bank.ex: Brakes only stop rolling, whereas stability on a slope depends on the manufacturer's gradient limits, levelling and stabilisers, and base plates are safer than castors on a slope.
bank.cm: Believing that locking the castor brakes makes a mobile tower safe on any surface.

bank.stem: A mechanic puts engine-oil-soaked rags and used oil filters in a lidded drum marked "oily waste". The manager books the registered skip firm to collect it, with no consignment note because the quantity is small. What is the correct position?
o: The rags can go in general waste once wrung out, because only free-flowing liquid oil makes waste hazardous, not material soaked in it
Oily rags and filters are hazardous waste, so a consignment note is completed and kept in the register for three years at the premises
The note can be skipped because the drum is lidded and labelled, since proper storage already shows that the duty of care has been met
A waste transfer note is enough because the carrier is registered, as consignment notes apply only to hazardous waste that is exported abroad
why: Oil-soaked material remains contaminated and hazardous even without free liquid.
Storage and labelling do not replace the required paperwork when the waste is collected.
Consignment notes apply to hazardous waste moved within the country, not just exports.
bank.ex: Hazardous waste leaving site needs a consignment note, and the producer must keep the register of notes for three years at the premises that produced or stored the waste.
bank.cm: Thinking a registered carrier or a small quantity removes the need for hazardous waste paperwork.

bank.stem: On a facade lift, 38 mm boards project about 350 mm beyond the last transom, and across one bay the boards sag underfoot because the transoms are far apart. The scaffolder says the boards are tied, so they are safe. What is the best response?
o: Paint the overhang as a warning and limit the bay to one person at a time, since such light use will not overstress the boards
Accept the overhang as tying prevents any tipping, and lay a second layer of boards over the sagging bay to stiffen it up
Cut the overhang to no more than four times board thickness and support the boards on transoms at each end and between
Fit a toe board along the overhang and keep people out of the sagging bay until the next scheduled inspection of the lift is done
why: A warning and fewer users leave the defect in place, and a board can still tip or break under a single person.
Tying does not make a long overhang safe, and doubling boards across a poorly supported span only adds load.
A toe board does not support the board end, and leaving a known defect in use is not an acceptable control.
bank.ex: HSE guidance says boards must be properly supported and not overhang excessively, with four times the board thickness as the example, and a sagging span shows inadequate intermediate support.
bank.cm: Judging a platform safe because it feels firm or is tied, without checking that every board is properly supported along its length.

bank.stem: A hired floating-earth generator powers a mixer and a cutting saw, both Class I tools, on a paved yard. The foreman wants to fit a link between the generator's neutral and earth terminals so it will behave like the mains. What is the best course?
o: Drive an earth rod beside the generator and bond it to both tool bodies, which gives any fault current a clear path back to the source of supply
Leave the generator's connections as supplied, follow the hire firm's instructions, and run one Class I tool at a time or use Class II tools
Fit the link, since linking neutral to earth is how every supply is earthed, and the saw and mixer will then be safe to run together on it
Leave the generator as supplied but run both tools together, because the circuit RCD makes sure that any fault is cut off at once and safely
why: Linking tool bodies to a rod does not create a return path to the source on this type of supply and may add hazards.
Altering the internal connections can defeat the protection the generator was designed to give and is not for the hirer to do.
An RCD helps but does not make it acceptable to run two Class I items at once on a floating-earth set.
bank.ex: A floating-earth generator relies on its designed arrangement, so hirers must not change its connections, and limiting the load to one Class I item or to Class II tools keeps a fault from putting dangerous voltages on other equipment.
bank.cm: Thinking every temporary supply must be earthed like the mains, when a floating-earth generator relies on its designed arrangement left unaltered.

bank.stem: A day crew rated removing a plant-room boiler as medium risk, then leave at 18:00 with the pipework half cut and drained. The night crew, three instead of six, are told the job is assessed, so carry on. Which approach best manages the risk at changeover?
o: Keep the medium rating, because the task and method are unchanged and the day supervisor has already approved the assessment for the night crew to use
Pass on the day crew's method statement alone, because it describes every step and the incoming crew can work out what is already done from it
Lower the rating, because fewer people are exposed overnight with the building empty and so the likelihood of anyone being harmed is reduced
Re-rate the task against its partly finished state and smaller crew, with a face-to-face handover of what is isolated, drained or cut
why: The state of the work and the crew size have changed, so the original rating no longer fits.
A written method describes the plan, not the actual condition of a half-finished job.
Fewer people does not offset unknown isolation status, fatigue and thinner supervision, which raise the likelihood.
bank.ex: A risk assessment must be reviewed when circumstances change, and a half-completed task with a different crew is not the situation the day rating covered.
bank.cm: Assuming a risk rating stays valid across a shift change because the task has the same name.

bank.stem: Joiners fixing fibre-cement cladding boards cut about eighty a day with a circular saw on trestles in a ground-floor room with the windows shut. Other trades are working in adjacent rooms. Which change controls the dust best?
o: Carry on cutting indoors but issue FFP3 masks to the saw operators, since a good mask fully protects the one person who is doing the cutting
Change to a fine-toothed wood blade, because it produces larger chips that fall quickly and so leaves less harmful airborne dust behind
Open the windows and run a fan to push the dust outside, which dilutes the airborne dust below the level that matters to health
Cut at a dedicated outdoor station, using shears or a saw with H or M class on-tool extraction, keep others clear, and treat RPE as the back-up
why: Relying on RPE alone leaves the dust in the building and exposes other trades.
Blade choice does not remove fine respirable dust, and the hazardous fraction stays airborne.
Dilution ventilation does not capture dust at source and can carry it into neighbouring rooms.
bank.ex: Cement-based boards can release harmful respirable dust, which is best controlled at source and away from other people, with RPE only as a back-up.
bank.cm: Handing masks to the cutter and treating that as the dust control, while the dust still spreads to everyone nearby.

bank.stem: A scaffold stair tower serves six lifts. Plasterers carry 20 kg tubs of adhesive up it, one hand on the rail, and prop each landing gate open with a tub to get past. The supervisor says stairs are safer than ladders. Which response is best?
o: Replace the gates with a single strip of tape across each landing, which is quicker to move for loads and still warns people of the edge
Keep the gates shut and move heavy or bulky loads by hoist or another mechanical route, so a hand is always free to hold the handrail
Accept the stairs as the main control, since the treads and handrails are designed for carrying and extra measures for materials add little protection
Allow open gates while one person is on the stair at a time, because the chance of a fall through a landing opening depends on how crowded it is
why: Tape warns but cannot stop a person falling, so it is not edge protection.
Stairs do not make carrying 20 kg tubs safe, because a loaded worker cannot hold the rail or see the treads.
One person can fall through an open landing just as easily, and the gate exists to prevent exactly that.
bank.ex: A gate is the edge protection at a landing and must be closed, and stairs only reduce risk if users keep a hand free rather than carrying awkward loads.
bank.cm: Assuming a stair tower is so safe that carrying loads and defeating the gates is acceptable.

bank.stem: A 13-tonne excavator lowers drain pipes into a trench. The operator cannot see the trench bottom, so a groundworker gives informal waves and thumbs-up, while another labourer sometimes shouts. Which arrangement is best?
o: Allow any worker to signal, since the operator can judge which signals are sensible from experience and then keep moving at a slow pace
Let the groundworker signal from the trench because he sees the pipe best, and have the operator carry on slowly if the signal is lost
Rely on shouted instructions over the engine noise, with gestures as a backup because they leave the signaller's hands free
Appoint one trained signaller using agreed standard signals in clear view, and have the operator stop if a signal is unclear or lost
why: Competing signals from different people cause confusion, and judging signals by experience is no substitute for a clear system.
Operators must stop when the signaller cannot be seen or understood, because carrying on blind is how people are hit.
Shouted words are easily lost under engine noise, so they are unreliable as the main method.
bank.ex: A single known signaller using standard signals removes confusion, and a rule to stop on any doubt stops the machine moving blind.
bank.cm: Assuming that informal gestures between two people who know each other are as safe as an agreed signal system.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the carpenter is wearing every item of PPE listed in the drilling task assessment. What is the most significant problem?
o: His eye protection is inadequate for bench drilling, so a full-face visor must replace the safety glasses even though the glasses have side shields
The gloves and loose cuffs near the rotating bit can be caught and drag his hand in, so they should be taken off or secured despite being PPE
A dust mask is missing, so respiratory protection is the main gap because drilling any timber creates dust above the workplace exposure limit
The chuck guard is in place but should be removed so he can see the cutting point, since the clamped workpiece and gloves protect his hands
why: Side-shielded safety glasses are suitable for drilling timber, and a visor would not address the entanglement risk.
A few drilled holes produce little dust, and respiratory protection would not remove the more serious risk of entanglement.
Guards must stay in place, and gloves do not protect hands from rotating parts, which is the very hazard they add.
bank.ex: Gloves and loose sleeves near a rotating spindle can wind onto the bit and drag the hand in, so the PPE itself creates an entanglement hazard that outweighs any protection from handling.
bank.cm: Assuming that more PPE is always safer, when gloves and loose cuffs near rotating machinery can themselves pull the hand in.
bank.alt: In a workshop, a carpenter drills a piece of timber on a pillar drill wearing long leather gauntlet gloves, safety glasses and ear defenders.

bank.stem: A specialist firm will radiograph pipe welds in a plant room on Friday evening. The site manager says the radiographer will look after everything, so other trades need not be told. Which approach is correct?
o: Let other trades pass through while the work continues, as radiation harms only those who stand directly in front of the equipment while an exposure is under way
Give the contractor advance written notice and agree access control, so trades are told of the controlled area and kept out until the source is confirmed secured
Let other trades carry on behind the plant room wall, since any wall absorbs the radiation and access control is needed only inside the room where the work happens
Tell only the night security guard, since the radiographer's lead apron also protects any other worker who happens to wander into the area during a short exposure
why: Scattered radiation can affect people outside the direct beam, so the controlled area has to be kept clear.
Shielding and distance must be assessed by the contractor, and a wall cannot simply be assumed to make the area outside safe.
A lead apron worn by someone else gives other workers no protection, and access must be physically controlled.
bank.ex: Radiography contractors need advance notice and liaison on restricting access to their controlled area, so everyone else on site is excluded while the source is exposed.
bank.cm: Leaving a specialist contractor to manage their own hazard without telling the other trades who share the site.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The foreman says the painter is fully protected because he wears a respirator, goggles, coveralls and gloves. What is the most significant problem, and what should be done?
o: His gloves are the wrong type, and thick chemical- resistant gauntlets would stop paint penetrating at spray pressure, so he could then clean the tip safely while it is live
His coveralls are inadequate, since liquid-tight Type 3 suits are needed for paint contact with skin, and that is the main route of harm from airless spraying
His respirator is inadequate, because airless spraying of any coating requires an air-fed hood, and that is the main hazard to put right before any other change
He is wiping the tip of a gun still under pressure, and gloves cannot stop paint injecting through skin, so release the pressure and lock the trigger first
why: No glove withstands high-pressure injection, so changing glove type does not make wiping a live tip safe.
The serious danger is injection at the nozzle, which a different suit would not prevent.
Respiratory protection depends on the coating's assessment, and it is not the most urgent danger shown in the picture.
bank.ex: Airless paint leaves the nozzle at a pressure that can inject through skin and glove alike, so the only safe controls are depressurising, locking the trigger and fitting a tip guard.
bank.cm: Believing that wearing gloves makes it safe to touch the tip of a pressurised spray gun.
bank.alt: A painter in white coveralls, respirator, goggles and gloves holds an airless spray gun and wipes its tip with a cloth; the spray pump stands beside him.

bank.stem: A steel fixer works 7 m up a portal-frame column, held by a waist belt and an adjustable positioning lanyard looped round the column so both hands are free to bolt. Nothing else is fitted. The supervisor says a taut lanyard means he cannot fall. Which statement is most accurate?
o: A second positioning lanyard looped round the same column counts as the required back-up, since it would give him identical protection should the first lanyard slip
The belt and lanyard are enough alone, because a taut lanyard stops any fall and a back-up is needed only for rope work carried out above ten metres high
A work positioning system may be used only with a suitable back-up that prevents or arrests a fall, such as a separate fall-arrest line to a harness
Replacing the belt with a full-body harness allows the lanyard to serve as the only system, since a harness spreads load and removes the need for a back-up
why: A second line of the same kind on the same anchorage does not arrest a fall if the positioning method fails.
A back-up is required whatever the height, and the ten-metre threshold is invented.
A harness improves body support but the positioning system still needs its own separate back-up.
bank.ex: Schedule 5 of the Work at Height Regulations allows work positioning only with a suitable back-up, because a positioning line can slacken or fail and the user may fall.
bank.cm: Assuming that a tight positioning line, by itself, makes a separate fall-arrest back-up unnecessary.

bank.stem: In a site cabin corridor, a fire door is wedged open 'for airflow' and stored materials partly block the route to the final exit, described as 'temporary'. Which combination of failings does this show?
o: The wedged door defeats the compartmentation that slows smoke and fire, and the obstruction compromises the means of escape, which must stay clear
Neither is a failing provided a suitable extinguisher is positioned close to the door and the cabin has a working smoke detector fitted
Only the obstruction matters, because fire doors mainly provide security and sound control rather than holding back fire and smoke
Only the wedge matters, because short-term obstructions are acceptable while a competent person is nearby and ready to move them at once
why: Extinguishers and detectors do not replace compartmentation or clear escape routes.
Fire doors are specifically designed to hold back fire and smoke.
Escape routes must be clear at all times; staffing a blockage is not an exemption.
bank.ex: Fire doors only work when closed, and escape routes must be kept unobstructed whenever the building is occupied, so both are separate failures.
bank.cm: Treating a fire door or escape route as a convenience that can be compromised temporarily.

bank.stem: A worker uses three different vibrating tools through one shift. Each tool's use was assessed separately and judged under the action value, but nobody totalled the day's exposure. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The total only needs calculating once a worker reports symptoms such as tingling or numbness, when health surveillance is triggered
Daily exposure must be calculated across all vibrating tools used in the day, as each can be under the action value alone while the total exceeds it
Only the tool with the highest vibration level matters for the daily total, as the others contribute little to overall exposure
Each tool is rightly assessed on its own, because vibration from different tools does not combine in the body, so a combined total is meaningless for a shift
why: Assessment is preventive and should be done before symptoms develop.
All tools and their durations contribute to the daily exposure.
Exposure is added across the day from all sources.
bank.ex: Hand-arm vibration exposure accumulates through the whole shift, so assessing tools in isolation can hide an overall exposure above the action or limit value.
bank.cm: Assessing each tool in isolation instead of totalling exposure across the whole day.

bank.stem: A groundworker kneels in wet concrete wearing cotton-lined gloves. Cement soaks through his trousers at the knees, but he feels no discomfort and plans to wash at the end of the shift. What is the correct view?
o: Only people with sensitive skin develop dermatitis from cement, so he can carry on unless a rash appears and then report it to the first aider
Wet cement is alkaline and can burn without immediate pain, so he should remove soaked clothing, wash promptly, and use waterproof gloves and kneepads
Absence of pain shows the cement is not harming him, so washing at the end of the shift is enough provided that barrier cream was applied beforehand
The cotton-lined gloves give adequate protection because they absorb the moisture, and the soaked trousers can be left to dry out on his body
why: Cement can cause irritant dermatitis or burns in anyone, and allergic dermatitis can develop after repeated exposure.
Cement burns are often painless at first, and barrier cream is not a substitute for waterproof protective clothing.
Absorbent gloves and trousers hold alkaline wet cement against the skin, which increases the risk of burns.
bank.ex: Wet cement can cause chemical burns and dermatitis before any pain is felt, so contaminated clothing must come off, skin must be washed at once, and waterproof protection must be used.
bank.cm: Waiting for pain or a rash before dealing with cement on the skin, when burns and dermatitis can develop without any early warning.

bank.stem: A contractor covers a stairwell opening in a new floor with a loose sheet of thin plywood cut slightly larger than the hole, with nothing to mark it. Which statement describes what is needed?
o: The cover may be lifted by whoever needs access, provided that they replace it afterwards and mention the removal to their own supervisor
Any sheet larger than the opening is acceptable because its own weight and overlap hold it in place, and marking only matters for visitors to the site
The cover must be strong enough for foreseeable loads, fixed against movement and clearly marked, or the opening needs guardrails and toe boards
A strip of hazard tape around the opening is sufficient, as the tape warns people away and removes the need to secure the covering itself
why: Covers should only be removed by authorised people under control, with protection in place while open.
A loose sheet can slide, flex or be moved, and marking is needed for all workers to avoid removing it.
Tape is a warning only and gives no physical protection if the cover fails or is walked on.
bank.ex: A temporary cover is only effective if it cannot be displaced or overloaded and people can tell it covers an opening; otherwise edge protection is needed.
bank.cm: Assuming that a loose board over an opening is safe because it looks as if it covers the gap.

bank.stem: A bundle of scaffold tubes slips from a hoist and lands in an unbarriered walkway; nobody is hit. The assessor records 'Hazard: tubes. Risk: be careful. Control: toolbox talk' and files it. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The falling load is the hazard and the chance of being struck is the risk; the near miss requires a review with firmer controls such as exclusion zones
The tubes are the risk and being struck is the hazard; the toolbox talk is adequate because nobody was hurt, so the assessment stands until an actual injury occurs
The assessment is sound because hazard, risk and control are all written down; a review is needed only when the work method changes, and a near miss is not a change
The hazard is the hoist, the risk is its breakdown and the control is to retrain the operator; the assessment can wait for its next scheduled annual review
why: The terms are swapped, and the absence of injury is not grounds to leave a failed control in place.
A review is also needed when there is reason to doubt the assessment is still valid, and "be careful" is not a real control measure.
This misidentifies the hazard and delays a review that the near miss makes necessary now.
bank.ex: A hazard is the potential to cause harm and risk is the likelihood and severity of that harm, and a near miss shows existing controls have failed, so the assessment must be reviewed and the controls strengthened.
bank.cm: Treating a near miss with no injury as a non-event and relying on a reminder to be careful instead of reviewing the assessment and its controls.

bank.stem: Look at the decanting bay, where the worker has just splashed corrosive admixture near his eyes. The green sign marks the emergency eyewash. What is the most significant problem with the provision?
o: There is no significant problem, since the green sign confirms provision exists and his safety glasses make eyewash only a secondary precaution
A wall-mounted bottle can never be used for corrosive splashes, so only a plumbed shower in the same room counts as acceptable provision
The sign is the wrong colour, as emergency equipment must be marked in red so that workers notice it before other safe-condition signs
The station cannot be reached quickly and its bottle looks opened and part-used, so immediate flushing with clean fluid could not happen
why: A sign alone does not give protection, and eyewash is needed because splashes can still reach the eyes.
The fault shown is access and condition, and the statement overstates what the picture demonstrates about the type of unit.
Green is the correct colour for safe-condition signs such as first aid and emergency eyewash, so the colour is not the fault.
bank.ex: Emergency eyewash must be immediately accessible and kept ready for use, so an obstructed route and a compromised bottle defeat its purpose despite the correct sign.
bank.cm: Assuming that a correct safety sign means the emergency equipment behind it is accessible and fit for use.
bank.alt: A worker rubs his eye beside a chemical store; a green emergency eyewash sign and an eyewash bottle are on the wall behind a drum and a trolley.

bank.stem: A floor-layer mixing a two-part epoxy screed gets itchy red patches on his forearms and hands that clear during holidays. The foreman suggests barrier cream and cleaning his hands with thinners. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Switch to thinner solvent for removing resin from his hands, because it dissolves the product quickly and leaves less residue on the skin than washing
Report it as possible work-related dermatitis, cut skin contact with better controls and suitable gloves, and wash with mild soap not solvent
Carry on with barrier cream applied before each mix, because it forms a reliable layer on the skin that works in place of gloves and other controls
Wait until the rash is severe before seeing anyone, because dermatitis only counts as work-related once it has caused a period of time off work
why: Solvents damage the skin barrier and can carry resin through it, making dermatitis and sensitisation worse.
Barrier creams are not dependable protection against resins and are not a substitute for avoiding skin contact.
Early reporting prevents lasting sensitisation, and a rash need not cause absence to be work-related.
bank.ex: Epoxy resins can sensitise the skin, so suspected dermatitis needs reporting and a review of controls, while solvents strip protective oils and drive the product deeper into the skin.
bank.cm: Treating a recurring rash as a minor nuisance to manage with creams rather than an early warning of sensitisation to a hazardous product.

bank.stem: A joiner tells her employer in writing that she is pregnant. Her role involves carrying heavy boards, using vibrating tools and working with solvent adhesives. The general risk assessment covers none of this. What must the employer do?
o: Extend the assessment to cover her risks, alter her conditions or hours if that avoids them, and if not offer suitable alternative work or suspend her on pay
Place her on statutory sick pay for the rest of the pregnancy, because suspension on full pay is available only after the baby has been born
Wait until the third trimester before acting, as the specific duty to change her work starts then unless she asks for different duties earlier
Issue gloves and a respirator for the adhesive work and keep her on current duties until a doctor or midwife has certified her as unfit to work
why: Suspension on full pay can apply during pregnancy, and sick pay is not the lawful route for avoiding a workplace risk.
The duty is triggered by the risk and her notification, not by a particular stage of pregnancy.
PPE is a last resort, and the employer must act on the assessed risks rather than wait for a medical certificate.
bank.ex: The assessment must cover risks to new or expectant mothers, and if altering conditions or hours cannot avoid the risk the employer must act further, including suspension on pay under the Employment Rights Act.
bank.cm: Treating a pregnancy as a medical matter for the worker's doctor rather than a workplace risk the employer must assess and control.

bank.stem: While stripping slates from a barn roof, a roofer finds droppings and one small bat in the eaves. His foreman says it is a common species and the bat has now flown off, so work can continue. What is the correct action?
o: Collect any bats found and release them in a nearby tree before continuing, because moving the animals removes any risk of committing an offence
Continue but strip the eaves only after dusk, when the bats are out feeding, since work done while they are away cannot disturb them
Carry on, since only rare species receive legal protection and a common bat that has left the roost gives no reason to stop the work
Stop work on the eaves, leave the area undisturbed and consult a licensed bat ecologist, because roosts are protected even when empty
why: Handling or moving bats without a licence is itself an offence and does not make destroying the roost lawful.
Timing does not matter because destroying or damaging the roost is the offence and the bats will return to it.
All UK bat species and their roosts are protected, not just rare ones.
bank.ex: Bats and their breeding sites and resting places are legally protected, so damaging a roost is an offence even if it is empty, and work must pause for specialist advice and any licence.
bank.cm: Assuming that a roost with no bats visible at that moment has no legal protection.

bank.stem: An excavator is refuelled from a mobile bowser parked on bare ground close to a surface-water drain. A little diesel splashes on the ground, and the operator rakes soil over it, saying no one will see it. What is the best response?
o: Wash the splash away with water from a hose, so the diluted diesel soaks away and leaves no visible trace on the ground
Raking soil over the spill is acceptable for a small splash, because the soil absorbs the diesel and bacteria in the ground break it down
Refuel away from drains using a drip tray, clean up with a spill kit at once, and dispose of contaminated material as waste
Refuel next to the drain so any splashes are caught, since a gully trap can hold the fuel before it leaves the site through the pipework
why: Washing spreads the fuel towards drains and watercourses and does not remove it, so a hose is the wrong response.
Burying fuel spreads contamination, and it can still reach the drain and groundwater, so it must be cleaned up and disposed of properly.
A drain does not trap fuel, which would travel into the sewer or a watercourse and cause pollution.
bank.ex: Fuel should be handled away from drains with drips contained, spills cleaned immediately with absorbent material, and contaminated absorbents dealt with as waste rather than hidden in the ground.
bank.cm: Treating small fuel spills as trivial and hiding them instead of containing and cleaning them up straight away.

bank.stem: The boom of a telehandler touches an overhead power line and the machine stops. The operator is unhurt and nothing is on fire. Which action is correct?
o: Stay in the cab, warn everyone to keep well clear, and wait until the line owner confirms the line is dead before moving
Have a banksman push the boom clear with a dry timber pole, since wood is a poor conductor and the line then goes dead
Reverse the machine away to break contact and then inspect it, since a tripped line is no longer live and cannot re-energise
Climb down at once and walk away normally, because the tyres insulate the machine and the line will already have tripped
why: Touching the machine or its load, even with timber, is dangerous and nobody should approach until the line is confirmed dead.
Lines can re-energise automatically after tripping, so the operator must not assume the line is dead without confirmation from the owner.
Stepping down onto energised ground can pass current through the body, and tyres do not reliably insulate a machine.
bank.ex: A line that is touched must be treated as live, and the cab is the safest place until the owner has isolated it and said it is safe.
bank.cm: Assuming that a line which has tripped or a rubber-tyred machine means the contact is no longer dangerous.

bank.stem: During a mobile crane lift of steel beams, the slinger and the site manager both wave signals, and the operator follows whichever he sees first. Operatives walk under the load's route to reach a cabin. What is the main correction?
o: Keep both people signalling and have the operator slow the load, since slower movement gives walkers time to get clear of the route
Keep the slinger as signaller but allow operatives across when the load is held still and the slinger waves them through the route
Use one trained, competent signaller the operator recognises, and keep the load path and slew area clear of anyone uninvolved
Let the manager take over all signalling because seniority gives clarity, and shout a warning to anyone who crosses beneath the load route
why: Two signallers still give conflicting signals, and a slow load is still dangerous to anyone beneath it.
Nobody should pass beneath a suspended load, even when it is held, because it can still slip or fail.
Seniority is not competence, and a shouted warning is no substitute for keeping people out of the danger area.
bank.ex: Conflicting signals confuse the operator, so a single competent signaller must control the lift, and people not involved must be kept out of the area a load could fall or swing into.
bank.cm: Thinking anyone who is visible and experienced may give crane signals, and that a stationary suspended load is safe to walk under.

bank.stem: A three-day re-tile of a terraced house roof is planned. The foreman proposes roof ladders hooked over the ridge and no scaffold, saying his tilers are experienced and the pitch is under 45 degrees. What is the correct view?
o: Ladders are acceptable for the full duration if each is securely hooked and tied, because experienced tilers can safely work from them over several days
Pitches below 45 degrees count as low risk, so a harness clipped to the roof ladder rung is a reasonable substitute for edge protection
Scaffold is needed only at the street side, since the rear is a private garden where a fall will not endanger members of the public
Roof ladders suit only very short jobs; three days needs scaffold with edge protection at the eaves, at both front and rear of the house
why: Roof ladders are only for short tasks, and securing them does not make them a safe platform for days of work.
There is no pitch below which edge protection is unnecessary, and a ladder rung is not a reliable anchor point.
Edge protection is needed at the eaves on both sides, as workers falling in the garden are equally at risk.
bank.ex: HSE guidance restricts roof ladders to jobs lasting minutes and requires edge protection at the eaves of any roof, on terraced houses at front and rear.
bank.cm: Treating roof ladders as a cheap substitute for scaffold on any roof job a competent crew says is quick.

bank.stem: Operatives opening a ceiling void under an approved method statement find several unlabelled cables that were not on the drawings or in the risk assessment. The supervisor says the paperwork is signed off, so the work should carry on as written. What is the correct response?
o: Tag the cables as live and work around them, which is enough as long as the changes are mentioned at the end of the day
Carry on with extra care, as skilled operatives can judge the cables themselves and recording a finding would only slow the job down
Stop, make the area safe, carry out a fresh assessment of the new hazard, and update the paperwork and brief the crew before resuming
Carry on as written, since a signed-off method statement covers the task and anything unexpected is dealt with at the next review
why: The assessment and briefing must come before work resumes, not after.
Skill is no substitute for assessing and controlling a new hazard.
Approval does not cover hazards that the assessment never considered.
bank.ex: Unexpected hazards need an immediate dynamic reassessment, and where they change the method the written documents must be revised.
bank.cm: Treating a signed-off assessment as covering hazards nobody knew about when it was written.

bank.stem: A labourer is told to use a hired trench compactor he has never been trained on, as the usual operator is off sick. The supervisor says it works like the old one. Which statement about duties is most accurate?
o: He may start once he has read the hire company's handbook, because an employee's only duty is to follow the manufacturer's written instructions
Training is required only for self-propelled plant, so he can use the compactor as directed and raise any concern after the shift
The employer must give training on this machine, and the labourer should tell the supervisor he is untrained instead of just starting it
Following the supervisor's instruction passes all responsibility to the supervisor, so he meets his own duty by using the machine as carefully as he can
why: A handbook does not replace the employer's duty to train, and employee duties are wider than following manufacturer's instructions.
Training duties apply to any work equipment that carries a risk, and concerns must be raised before use, not afterwards.
Employees keep their own duty to use equipment as trained and to take reasonable care, whatever the instruction given.
bank.ex: Employers must provide adequate information and training, and employees must follow the training they have had and raise concerns, so an untrained worker should not operate unfamiliar plant.
bank.cm: Assuming that a supervisor's instruction or a similar-looking machine removes the need for specific training before use.

bank.stem: Two groundworkers eat lunch in a closed van with a petrol-fuelled cab heater running. Afterwards both have a headache and feel drowsy and nauseous. One says it is just a hangover, and the other says they would smell any harmful gas. What should happen?
o: Let them rest in the van with the heater on so they warm up, and only seek help if either one collapses or loses consciousness
Give them water and send them back to work, because headaches after a break are most often caused by dehydration and not by gas
Open the van door briefly, keep the heater on low, and watch how they feel for the rest of lunch, since any harmful gas would have a smell that they would notice
Get them into fresh air, stop using the heater and seek medical advice, as carbon monoxide has no smell and mimics flu or tiredness
why: Waiting for collapse delays treatment, and staying with the source increases the exposure.
Assuming a harmless cause ignores the evidence of a fuel-burning appliance in an enclosed space and leaves the hazard in place.
Carbon monoxide cannot be smelt, so the lack of an odour gives no reassurance, and the heater remains a continuing source.
bank.ex: Carbon monoxide is odourless and its early symptoms are easily mistaken for other illness, so removing people from the source and obtaining medical advice is essential.
bank.cm: Trusting your nose to warn you about dangerous fumes, or putting headaches and drowsiness down to tiredness when a fuel-burning heater is running.

bank.stem: A banksman works beside a block-cutting saw at about 92 dB(A) among reversing dumpers. He keeps lifting his ear defenders off whenever a vehicle moves, to hear the alarms. What is the best way to resolve this?
o: Fit louder alarms on all the dumpers so they cut through the defenders, as the noise regulations cover only the equipment that the banksman himself personally uses
Choose protectors giving roughly 70 to 85 dB at the ear, have him wear them throughout, and add visual warnings and segregation so alarms are not the only cue
Issue the lowest-rated plugs available so the alarms stay clear, since once any hearing protection has been handed out the employer's duty to protect is met
Let him lift them off when a vehicle comes within about ten metres, because such short removals add very little to his exposure and the alarm is the main vehicle warning
why: Louder alarms add to everyone's noise exposure, and the regulations require noise to be controlled for all workers affected.
Protection that leaves his ear exposure above 85 dB does not control the noise risk, whatever has been issued.
Even brief removal cuts the protection achieved over a shift, and an audible alarm should never be the only control on vehicle movements.
bank.ex: Protection must be worn continuously to work, and selecting an attenuation that avoids both under- and over- protection, with other vehicle controls, keeps him safe from noise and traffic.
bank.cm: Taking hearing protection off for moments to hear a warning, as though a short removal costs little protection.

bank.stem: Look at the lift. The slinger says the chains and pallet are well inside the crane's rated capacity. What is the most significant problem?
o: Bricks on a banded wooden pallet cannot be crane-lifted and must be moved in a lifting cage or skip designed for loose building materials
The hook has no working safety catch, so the sling master link could slip off the hook if the load shifts or the chains go slack
The slinger is standing too close to the lorry while the chains are tensioned and must move back to at least the full height of the jib
A worker is holding a tag line, which keeps his hands close to the load and should be replaced by steadying the pallet with a long pole
why: Banded, properly packaged pallets can be lifted on suitable slings, so this is not the key defect.
The slinger is clear of the load path, and no rule requires standing back by the jib's full height.
Tag lines are a standard way to control a load from a safe distance and are not the hazard here.
bank.ex: Lifting hooks must have a functioning safety catch or equivalent so the load cannot become detached, whatever the rated capacity.
bank.cm: Judging a lift safe because the load is under the rated capacity, without checking the lifting accessories and hook condition.
bank.alt: A crane lifts a pallet of bricks on chains while a slinger guides it with a tag line; an inset shows a close-up of the crane hook.

bank.stem: While stripping plaster in a ground-floor flat, a joiner smells gas strongly. Two colleagues are working upstairs and the lights are off. He is about to switch them on to look for the cause. What is the correct action?
o: Turn the lights on to find the source, then tighten any visible joints before the smell spreads, because the fault is probably small
Avoid switches and flames, open doors and windows on the way out, evacuate everyone and report the leak from outside
Switch off the power at the consumer unit to remove ignition sources, then continue working in the other rooms while the gas disperses
Wait for the site plumber to arrive and check it, as the workers are better placed to judge whether the leak is serious enough
why: Operating a switch may ignite the gas, and untrained repairs inside a gas-filled space add to the danger.
Operating the consumer unit can itself spark, and staying inside leaves workers exposed to an explosion.
Nobody should stay in the building to investigate, and a plumber is not the emergency service for a suspected leak.
bank.ex: Any switch can spark and ignite a gas build-up, so ignition sources are avoided, ventilation is helped, people are evacuated and the leak is reported from a safe place.
bank.cm: Assuming that switching off electrics or investigating the source yourself is safer than getting out first.

bank.stem: A principal contractor shortlists a demolition subcontractor holding a valid SSIP-recognised certificate. The job is dismantling a tall chimney beside an occupied school, and the firm has so far done only low-rise strip-outs. What should the principal contractor do before appointing it?
o: Appoint it on the certificate alone, because HSE accepts accreditation as full proof of capability for any project the firm takes on
Reject any firm without a previous chimney of this exact height, since only identical past projects can prove organisational capability
Appoint it now and assess its competence through the method statement once work is under way and the chimney scaffold is up
