bank.cm: Reading a run of injury-free days as proof that the safety management system is working.

bank.stem: Workers heading to the cabins after dark must pass a 1.8 m deep, supported excavation across the walkway, marked by a single strand of tape on stakes and one cone. The foreman says the sides are shored, so nobody can be buried. What is the best assessment?
o: Shoring makes the excavation compliant, because a properly supported excavation cannot injure anybody who accidentally steps or falls into it from the walkway
A banksman is needed during working hours, since an excavation left overnight is not covered by the excavation rules until work starts again
Support covers collapse only; people must also be stopped from falling in, so it needs a solid barrier, lighting and a protected route
Tape and a cone are enough because the excavation is under 2 m deep, the depth at which fall protection becomes a legal requirement for pedestrians
why: A person can still be injured by falling into a supported excavation, and support does not prevent that.
Duties continue while the excavation is open, and the risk to people walking past is greater when it is dark and unattended.
No such depth threshold exists, and the duty to prevent falls into an excavation applies at any depth where a person could be injured.
bank.ex: CDM 2015 regulation 22 requires steps to stop people falling into an excavation as well as protection against collapse, which tape and a cone do not give, especially in the dark.
bank.cm: Thinking that supporting the sides of an excavation is all that is required to make it safe.

bank.stem: A 1960s office block with no surviving drawings is to be stripped out and then demolished. The foreman proposes to start at once by removing partitions and edge columns on the top floor, and to have material tested as it turns up. How should the work be planned?
o: Remove the edge columns and heavy walls first to open up access, because a structure will always stay stable while its floors remain intact above
Start stripping now but stop and test whenever suspect material turns up, as a full survey is only needed before the final demolition stage begins
Rely on the original design intent for blocks of that age, as an unrecorded building from the 1960s will have followed standard practice throughout
Get asbestos and structural surveys first, then set a sequence that keeps the frame stable, removing non-critical parts before the stiff ones
why: Taking out structural members early can cause an uncontrolled collapse, since the stability of a frame depends on its remaining members.
Testing as suspect material appears risks disturbing asbestos before anyone knows where it is, and the survey must come before any work starts.
Old buildings are often altered or built differently from the standard, so assumptions cannot replace a survey of the actual structure.
bank.ex: Surveys must come before work starts, and the sequence must prevent uncontrolled collapse by keeping stabilising elements until last.
bank.cm: Starting strip-out on the assumption that surprises can be dealt with as they appear.

bank.stem: Before loft insulation goes in, two labourers must clear years of pigeon droppings from a roof void. The foreman suggests sweeping the dry material into sacks and using a plain nuisance- dust mask. What is the best approach to the biological hazard?
o: Dampen the droppings, scoop them into sealed bags, and wear disposable coveralls and an FFP3 respirator, washing before eating
Do the work in the cooler evening and keep the hatch open, because ventilation alone dilutes any airborne spores to a safe level
Brush the dry droppings briskly into sacks to shorten exposure time, and wear a nuisance-dust mask for the short job
Leave the droppings in place and treat the void only with a disinfectant spray, as the spray kills any organisms present
why: General ventilation does not control a dust and spore release in a confined void, so source controls and respirators are still needed.
Dry sweeping throws fine infectious dust into the air, and a nuisance- dust mask is not suitable respiratory protection for a biological agent.
Spraying alone does not remove the material, and disturbing it later still releases dust and organisms.
bank.ex: Dried droppings can carry organisms that cause lung infections such as histoplasmosis, so dust must be suppressed and suitable respiratory protection, clothing and hygiene used under COSHH.
bank.cm: Thinking old dry droppings are harmless dust that a basic mask and a quick sweep can deal with.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. A supervisor walks up to this cutting task while it is in progress. What should the supervisor do first?
o: Accept the glasses on his forehead, since he can drop them down in a moment if sparks begin to fly towards his face
Stop the cutting, have eye protection worn over the eyes, and move the bystander clear of the sparks before restarting
Replace his ear defenders with earplugs, because the hearing protection is the item most likely to let him down during grinding
Let him finish the cut to avoid leaving a half-cut bar clamped in the vice, then remind him about his glasses at the next toolbox talk
why: Sparks and fragments start the instant the disc touches the steel, so the protection must already be in place and not be put on after the exposure has begun.
His ear defenders are not the failing item, and swapping them does not address the uncovered eyes or the bystander.
Allowing work to continue knowingly exposes unprotected eyes to sparks, and a later talk does nothing to remove that immediate danger.
bank.ex: The operative's eye protection is not covering his eyes and a colleague is in the path of the sparks, so the work must stop until both exposures are controlled.
bank.cm: Counting PPE as worn because it is on the person, when it is not positioned to protect the part of the body at risk.
bank.alt: A worker cuts steel bar held in a vice with an angle grinder, throwing sparks, while a colleague stands nearby measuring with a tape.

bank.stem: Steel erectors must fix roof sheeting to a portal frame 9 m up, where edge protection cannot be fitted before the sheets go on. The contractor weighs harnesses clipped to a wire along the purlins against safety nets rigged below. Which choice follows the hierarchy for fall protection?
o: Rig nets along the building perimeter only, leaving erectors in the middle of the roof to rely on harnesses and a short lanyard.
Rig safety nets under the work area using competent riggers, because collective protection works for everyone without relying on each person to clip on.
Choose harnesses because a person who lands in a net can still be injured, so only a lanyard that stops the fall at once is really safe.
Use harnesses on a wire along the purlins, because a trained team on site can recover a fallen worker quickly and nets are then not needed at all.
why: Perimeter nets do not catch someone falling through the roof area, and the centre workers would still depend on personal systems.
Nets are designed to catch falls at limited height, and a sudden stop on a lanyard can itself cause injury or suspension trauma.
Personal systems depend on every worker clipping on correctly and need prompt rescue, so they rank below collective protection.
bank.ex: Where a fall cannot be prevented, collective measures that limit the consequences of a fall are preferred over personal systems that depend on individual use.
bank.cm: Choosing harnesses because they are cheaper and easier to fit, rather than ranking collective measures first.

bank.stem: A gun-wash thinner for cleaning spray equipment carries a flame pictogram and hazard statements H225 and H336. The operative plans a dust mask because he has no dust task, and will clean the equipment beside the site heater. What should the supervisor say?
o: The flame symbol covers storage only, so use it near the heater if the container is closed between uses and fit a dust mask to deal with the vapour
The ignition risk is controlled once the heater is turned down to its lowest setting, so no further ventilation or respiratory protection is needed for the cleaning task
H336 is a low-level warning for comfort only, so the operative can carry on if he feels well and keeps the thinner away from skin contact
It is a highly flammable liquid whose vapour can cause drowsiness, so remove ignition sources, ventilate well, and use the respiratory protection that the data sheet specifies
why: Vapour released during use is the ignition hazard, and a dust mask does not protect against solvent vapour.
A lowered heater is still an ignition source, and ventilation and suitable respiratory protection are still needed for the vapour.
H336 signals a narcotic effect on the nervous system, which can impair judgement and is a real health risk.
bank.ex: H225 means highly flammable liquid and vapour and H336 means it may cause drowsiness or dizziness, so both fire control and a vapour-appropriate control are needed.
bank.cm: Reading only the pictogram and missing that the hazard statements describe separate fire and health risks needing separate controls.

bank.stem: Two installers will fit solar panels on a south-facing slope of a two-storey house, eaves at 6 metres, over three days. The firm proposes harnesses clipped to ridge anchors with no scaffold, and carrying the panels up by hand. What is the best plan?
o: Accept the harnesses and ridge anchors, as trained installers clipped on throughout are equally protected, provided the anchors are inspected before each use
Fit the scaffold to the eaves but allow installers to carry panels along the slope by hand, because edge protection removes any real concern about wind
Erect a scaffold with edge protection at the eaves, move panels mechanically instead of carrying them, and stop lifting in wind that could catch them
Use only a single guardrail on gutter brackets, since a pitched roof below 45 degrees does not need full edge protection for installers working on it
why: Work at height rules require collective measures that protect everyone to be preferred over personal systems that depend on each person's behaviour.
Edge protection does not stop a gust catching a panel and pulling the carrier off balance, so handling and wind still need controlling.
There is no pitch below which edge protection is not needed, and a single gutter-fixed rail would not be strong enough or complete.
bank.ex: Collective protection such as scaffold edge protection comes before personal fall protection, and large panels can act as sails, so wind limits and mechanical handling are part of planning the work.
bank.cm: Choosing harnesses because they look quicker than scaffold, forgetting that collective protection should come first.

bank.stem: Roofers torch-on bitumen felt to a flat roof while joiners fit foam insulation boards on the deck below in the same bay. Each subcontractor's assessment rates its own work as low risk. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Let the roofers sign a hot work permit and keep an extinguisher on the roof, since the permit also covers the joiners working beneath them
Treat the overlap as a combined risk, with the principal contractor coordinating through the construction phase plan so the tasks are separated or sequenced
Raise the score on both assessments by one level and let the work continue, because a higher rating shows that the overlap has been properly considered
Accept both assessments, since each employer answers only for its own workers and the combined effect lies outside what either firm must consider here
why: A permit and extinguisher respond to a fire but do not separate hot work from flammable insulation and the people below it.
Changing a score is not a control measure, and nothing in the work method or sequence has altered.
Contractors must cooperate and coordinate because one trade's work creates risks for others, so the interaction cannot be ignored.
bank.ex: Two activities that are low risk alone can create a serious fire risk together, so the principal contractor must coordinate the trades and the assessments must reflect the interaction.
bank.cm: Assuming that if every subcontractor's own assessment looks acceptable, the combined activity on the same part of the building must be acceptable too.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. A painter needs to reach a high soffit. Which feature of the set-up most increases the chance of a serious fall?
o: The tower stands on a smooth concrete floor, which cannot hold castors in position even when every brake is firmly applied
A paint tray and bucket on the platform floor will slide off the edge unless every item is tied to the guardrail with rope
A second worker stands at the base looking up, so he is likely to be struck by falling tools from the platform above him
A stepladder is opened on the tower platform, so he works above the guardrails on an unsteady, extended footing
why: Braked castors on a level concrete floor are acceptable, and the floor is not the main problem shown.
Tools and containers can be managed with toe boards, so this is a lesser matter than standing above the guardrails.
The colleague at the base is a minor risk compared with the painter's own exposure to a fall from a ladder on a platform.
bank.ex: Adding a stepladder to a tower platform lifts him above the guardrail protection and adds instability, so the correct fix is to build the tower higher or use a suitable platform.
bank.cm: Believing a tower's guardrails still protect you when you stand on something to gain extra height.
bank.alt: In a tall atrium, a painter works on a high ceiling from a mobile tower while a colleague stands on the floor below.

bank.stem: A groundworker must dig a pit in a factory yard owned by the client. The electricity company's plan shows nothing there, but the client supplies its own old cable layout. He proposes machine- digging to the depth marked on that layout. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Treat both plans as a rough guide because private cables may be unrecorded, then trace routes with a trained locator user and confirm by hand-dug trial holes
Follow the client's layout to its marked depth, because the owner's own record is more reliable than a locator and needs no further checking before digging
Rely on the electricity company's plan showing nothing, because statutory undertakers must record every cable in the area including those owned privately by the client
Dig by machine to half the marked depth and then change to hand tools, because the drawn depth gives a safe margin above the buried cable
why: An old layout shows only an approximate position and depth, and it can be wrong or out of date, so it still has to be checked on the ground.
A utility plan covers that company's own apparatus and not necessarily the client's private cables, so a blank plan does not prove the ground is clear.
Cables are not always at the drawn depth or position, so mechanical digging before locating and trial holes can still strike a cable.
bank.ex: Plans only indicate location and number of services, and private cables may not appear on a utility plan, so locating by a competent person and confirming with hand-dug trial holes comes before mechanical digging.
bank.cm: Treating a drawing or a blank utility plan as proof about what lies underground, rather than as a rough guide to be checked.

bank.stem: A 40-person site buys a defibrillator. The manager now plans to cut the number of first aiders from two to none, because the device covers the heart risk, and to keep it locked in his office. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Provision is voluntary, so it can stay locked in the manager's office with no routine checks, because first aiders will fetch it whenever needed
The law requires one on sites above 25 workers, which meets the first-aid duty, so first-aider numbers may fall once the device is installed
Once bought it counts as medical equipment outside PUWER, so the supplier handles upkeep and no written instructions are needed for would-be users
The needs assessment sets first-aider numbers, and a provided defibrillator is work equipment, so it needs accessible siting, upkeep and written user instructions
why: Equipment meant for an emergency has to be readily accessible and in working order, which a locked office and an absence of checks cannot ensure.
Health and safety law does not require a defibrillator at any workforce size, and it does not replace the first- aid arrangements the needs assessment calls for.
HSE says PUWER applies to a defibrillator that is provided, so the employer must ensure maintenance and give users information and instructions.
bank.ex: HSE states that no law requires a defibrillator and that first aider numbers come from the needs assessment, while one that is provided falls under PUWER, including instructions and maintenance.
bank.cm: Believing that buying a defibrillator reduces the need for trained first aiders and other first-aid provision.

bank.stem: After a wet fortnight, a drainage labourer working in a flooded trench in leaking wellingtons reports cold, numb, swollen and painful feet by evening. The foreman says it is just tiredness and the crew can carry on. Which response is best?
o: Rub the feet briskly with a towel and apply a hot pad, because strong warming restores circulation and prevents lasting tissue damage in the toes
Treat it as possible trench foot: get him out of the wet, dry and gently warm his feet, and arrange medical advice and better boots and socks
Let him finish the shift in dry socks, since a symptom that eases by the next morning cannot be a lasting cold or wet injury to the feet
Advise thicker waterproof boots worn all day and treat it as solved, because keeping feet warm matters more than drying them regularly
why: Numb, chilled tissue is easily damaged by rubbing or fierce heat, so warming must be gentle and followed by medical advice.
Tissue and nerve damage can persist or worsen after the pain eases, and the wet conditions causing it would be unchanged.
Sealed boots hold sweat and water against the skin, so feet still need regular drying and clean dry socks.
bank.ex: Long exposure of the feet to cold and wet damages nerves and tissue, so he needs prompt dry conditions and medical advice, and the site must remove the cause by fixing footwear and drying arrangements.
bank.cm: Dismissing numb, swollen, painful feet after long wet shifts as ordinary tiredness that will pass.

bank.stem: A housing-site haul road for loaded dumpers is planned to cross a live gas main and a cable duct laid just below the surface. The plan says operators know where the services run, so no works are needed. What is the best control?
o: Locate the lines with a cable avoidance tool before each crossing and then allow free travel, since knowing their position prevents damage to them
Let dumpers cross anywhere along the line when empty, since lightly loaded wheels cannot damage a service buried just below the surface of the road
Spread a thin layer of loose spoil over the line and mark it with tape, since a little extra cover is enough to carry the passing vehicles
Limit crossing to one marked point, agree temporary protection such as plates or a raft with the service owners, and keep vehicles off elsewhere
why: Locating a service shows where it is but does nothing to protect it from the weight of passing vehicles.
An empty dumper is still heavy, shallow services are vulnerable, and crossings should be restricted to protected places.
Loose spoil gives no controlled load spreading and tape only marks the position without protecting the service.
bank.ex: Vehicle crossings over buried services should be kept to a minimum at marked places with temporary protection agreed with the owners, because shallow services are easily damaged by wheel loads.
bank.cm: Thinking that knowing where a buried service lies is the same as protecting it from vehicle loads.

bank.stem: A fit-out finishes with 40 unopened, undamaged plasterboard sheets and a heap of clean offcuts. The manager wants the cheapest disposal, with everything going into the general waste skip. Applying the waste hierarchy, what should happen?
o: Put everything in the general skip, since the hierarchy only requires that a registered carrier removes the waste and not that it is sorted first
Return or reuse the unopened sheets first, and send clean offcuts to a plasterboard recycler, kept dry and apart from other waste
Send the offcuts for energy recovery as the next best option after reuse, since burning board recovers more value than recycling it does
Tip the offcuts into the timber skip, since both are non- hazardous and the recycling contractor will sort them out later on
why: The hierarchy requires reasonable steps to prevent, reuse and recycle waste before it is disposed of.
Recycling ranks above energy recovery in the hierarchy, and plasterboard is not suitable for burning.
Gypsum contaminates timber recycling, and plasterboard must be kept apart from biodegradable waste.
bank.ex: The waste hierarchy puts prevention and reuse before recycling, and plasterboard must be segregated so it can be recycled and kept out of landfill with biodegradable waste.
bank.cm: Treating the cheapest skip as the compliant option because a licensed carrier collects it.

bank.stem: A new joiner has existing hearing loss shown in a pre- employment test. His average daily noise exposure at the machines is 82 dB(A), below the upper action value. The employer says hearing surveillance applies only above 85 dB(A). What is the correct position?
o: He should be included, since existing hearing loss puts him at risk even below the upper value, and early tests give a baseline
Surveillance can wait until he reports hearing difficulty, since testing is triggered by symptoms and not by exposure level or individual susceptibility
He must be moved off all noisy work immediately, as a person with hearing loss cannot lawfully be exposed to any noise at work
Surveillance is optional below 85 dB(A), but ear protectors must then be compulsory for him, which removes the exposure risk and any need for testing
why: Surveillance exists to detect damage early, before the worker notices symptoms.
There is no ban on such work; the duty is to control the risk and monitor his hearing.
Hearing protection does not remove the need for surveillance for a worker already at risk.
bank.ex: Hearing surveillance covers workers likely to be regularly exposed above the upper action value and those at risk for other reasons, such as existing hearing loss.
bank.cm: Treating the upper action value as the only trigger for hearing checks, ignoring workers who are more vulnerable.

bank.stem: At the end of a cold day a manager leaves a thermostatic electric fan heater running in the empty drying room. Cardboard boxes of fixings are stacked against its grille. He says the tip-over switch and thermal cut-out make this safe. What is the best response?
o: Plug it into a timer socket so it runs for a limited period, because shorter running time reduces the fire load and the cardboard can then stay put
Fit a wire guard over the grille and leave it running, because a guard stops the boxes touching the element so the stack can stay exactly where it is
Move the boxes back about 100 mm and leave it running overnight, since the cut-outs make unattended use acceptable once nothing is touching the grille
Switch it off when the room is unattended and keep combustibles well clear, because built-in cut-outs are a backup and do not justify stacking stock against it
why: A timer still leaves the heater running unattended next to combustibles during the period it is on.
A guard does not stop radiated heat or airflow blockage igniting cardboard stored right beside the heater.
A token gap is not adequate separation, and leaving a heater running unattended still relies on devices that can fail.
bank.ex: Safety devices can fail, and unattended heating with combustible materials touching it is a clear ignition and fire- spread risk that is controlled by separation and switching off.
bank.cm: Trusting a heater's built-in safety cut-outs instead of keeping combustibles away and switching it off when nobody is there.

bank.stem: Pipelayers lever 400 kg concrete pipe sections into a trench, all wearing S3 steel-toecap boots. One has his instep crushed when a pipe rolls onto his foot, though his toes are unhurt. What should the manager do next?
o: Issue boots with a higher-rated steel toecap, because the instep injury shows the toecaps in use were not strong enough for the load
Retrain the injured pipelayer in foot placement, as the boots met the standard and the fault lay with the way he positioned himself
Switch to higher-ankle boots with extra support, because a taller upper protects the instep against a rolling load better than low boots do
Review the task assessment and issue boots marked M for metatarsal protection as well as a toecap, and review the pipe- handling method too
why: A stronger toecap still leaves the instep uncovered, so the risk remains.
Blaming the worker ignores the foreseeable risk to the instep that the PPE selection did not cover.
Ankle height gives support, not crush protection over the top of the foot.
bank.ex: A toecap protects only the toes, so a crushing risk to the top of the foot calls for a metatarsal guard, and the handling method should still be improved.
bank.cm: Assuming that any safety boot with a toecap protects the whole foot from heavy rolling or dropped loads.

bank.stem: A plumbed emergency eyewash in a chemical store has not been run since installation six weeks ago. A test run gives rust- brown, cloudy water for several seconds before clearing. The foreman signs the tag, saying it clearly works. What is the best response?
o: Treat it as not ready: run it regularly as the maker directs to clear stagnant water, check flow and temperature, and keep records
Arrange an annual engineer service only, because frequent running wastes water and wears the valve, and a yearly check shows whether it works
Accept the tag, because water that clears shows the pipework is clean, so flushing is needed only after a unit has actually been used
Swap it for a sterile saline bottle and stop running the unit, since stagnant water is only a risk to drinking supplies and not to eyes
why: A yearly check leaves the water stagnating for months, so the unit could be unfit exactly when it is needed.
Clearing after several seconds proves contamination was present, and a casualty cannot wait for the water to run clean.
Contaminated water in the eyes is a serious hazard, and a single small bottle cannot give the sustained flushing of a plumbed unit.
bank.ex: Standing water breeds contamination and corrosion debris that would be flushed into a casualty's eyes, so plumbed units need regular activation, flow checks and records.
bank.cm: Signing off an eyewash because water comes out, without asking what condition the water is in.

bank.stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the operative's PPE is fine, since he has glasses, a dust mask and gloves. What is the most significant problem?
o: The bucket sits on the floor, and bending to mix creates a manual handling hazard that outweighs any hazard from the spinning paddle
His nitrile-coated gloves should be leather gauntlets for mixing, because thicker gloves are always the safer choice around powered tools
His FFP2 dust mask is inadequate for tile adhesive, which needs an air-fed hood, so respiratory protection is the most serious failing
Something hanging from his neck could be caught by the rotating paddle and pull him in, so it should be removed or be a breakaway type
why: Posture is a real concern, but a snagging risk can cause severe injury within a moment.
Thick or loose gloves near rotating parts add an entanglement risk, and the gloves shown are not the main failing.
An FFP2 or FFP3 mask is the usual protection against cement-based dust, and it does not match the immediate danger of entanglement.
bank.ex: Loose items near rotating tools can be snagged and drag the wearer into the machine, so neck cords should be removed or of a quick-release design.
bank.cm: Checking the PPE list and missing the loose item near the moving part.
bank.alt: A worker kneels to mix material in a bucket with a paddle mixer, wearing glasses, a dust mask and gloves.

bank.stem: Overnight, someone dumps about forty used car tyres inside the site gate. The manager wants the area tidy before a client visit, by tipping them into the general waste skip due for collection tomorrow. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Photograph and log the dumping, report it to the local authority, and have a registered waste carrier remove the tyres under a transfer note describing them
Accept a passing man with a van who offers to take them away for cash, provided he promises to dispose of them properly elsewhere
Stack them at the back of the site until completion, since one later removal costs less and dumped items are not the site's responsibility
Tip them into the skip as planned, since waste left on the site becomes site waste and a general skip carrier will accept any mixed load
why: An unregistered carrier with no transfer note leaves the site liable if the tyres are dumped elsewhere.
The occupier remains responsible for waste on the land, and a stack of tyres is a fire hazard.
The skip's waste description would not include tyres, so this misdescribes the load and breaks the duty of care.
bank.ex: Waste on the site must be described accurately, passed only to a registered carrier with a transfer note under the duty of care, and a general skip does not describe or cover tyres.
bank.cm: Assuming waste dumped by someone else stops being the site's problem, or can be hidden in the next skip.

bank.stem: On a concrete frame, a gang fixes slab reinforcement beside the lift core while another gang, on a platform on the core wall 3 m higher, strikes and passes formwork. Nothing separates the two gangs. What is the best control?
o: Issue the slab gang with impact-rated hard hats and let both gangs carry on as planned, because head protection is the standard control for overhead work
Fit a debris net at slab level beneath the core platform and let the formwork gang work as before, as the net will catch anything dropped
Stop objects falling with toe boards and secured materials on the platform, and bar people from the area below where a fall remains possible
Have a banksman shout when formwork is being moved overhead, as a verbal warning gives the slab gang time to step clear of the area
why: PPE is a last resort and does not replace preventing falls or keeping people clear.
A net at slab level would sit where the other gang works and cannot take the place of preventing falls or exclusion.
A shouted warning is unreliable and does not prevent objects falling or people being struck.
bank.ex: The Work at Height Regulations require steps to prevent objects falling first, then steps to prevent anyone being struck where that is not reasonably practicable.
bank.cm: Treating hard hats or warning shouts as the answer to work going on above people instead of preventing falls and separating the gangs.

bank.stem: A mobile crane lifts a plant unit into a courtyard where the operator cannot see the landing point. The signaller plans to direct the lift by mobile phone on speaker, saying everyone has signal. Which arrangement is best?
o: Use a dedicated crane radio, with one voice giving commands, test the link each shift, and have the operator stop if communication is lost
Keep the phone but add a second person shouting and waving to the operator as a backup, so two signalling methods run at the same time during the whole lift
Keep the open call but allow the operator to carry on with the last command until the call reconnects, so the load is not left hanging
Use a chain of two relayed hand signals instead and allow the operator to guess at the intended landing point if one signal is missed
why: Two people signalling gives conflicting instructions; commands should come from one person only.
Continuing blind after a lost link is the very risk, and the operator should stop.
Relayed signals are slow and unreliable, and guessing a movement is unacceptable in a lift.
bank.ex: HSE guidance on crane radio use says commands come from one person, the link is checked each shift, and the operator stops the operation if communication breaks down.
bank.cm: Treating a personal phone as equal to a dedicated, tested crane radio and carrying on moving when the link drops.

bank.stem: A manager plans the hazard walk-round for a three-week refurbishment. He will tour the empty rooms alone on Sunday with the drawings and a checklist, then brief the gang on Monday. Which change would most improve how well hazards are identified?
o: Walk the areas with operatives who will do the work and ask how each task will really be done, including cleaning and maintenance
Delay the walk-round until the gang has started, so hazards are recorded as they appear and the findings reflect real working conditions
Limit the walk to supervisors and the safety adviser for independence, then ask operatives to sign the findings during the Monday briefing
Rely on the checklist and past accident-book entries, because operatives' views are subjective and a consistent method gives more reliable results
why: Hazards must be identified and controlled before exposure begins, not discovered once people are already working.
Signing a finished list is not involvement, and it leaves out the first-hand knowledge that would improve the assessment.
Checklists and past accidents only reveal known or recorded hazards, and they ignore the practical knowledge of the workers.
bank.ex: The people doing the work know the shortcuts, awkward access and non-routine tasks, so involving them finds hazards that drawings and checklists miss.
bank.cm: Treating a hazard walk-round as a desk or checklist exercise for managers rather than a conversation with the people who do the work.

bank.stem: On a wet road-widening job, a labourer works beside reversing plant in a dark green waterproof jacket, with the hood up over his hard hat. His hi-vis vest is back in the van. He says the hood keeps him dry. Which approach best deals with the wet- weather clothing?
o: Supply waterproofs that are high-visibility, with a hood that fits under or around the helmet without limiting side vision or muffling alarms
Keep the dark jacket and hood, and add a banksman to warn him of moving plant, so awareness becomes the banksman's job
Replace the jacket with a hi-vis vest over a thick hooded sweatshirt, since a fluorescent colour is all that matters for safety near plant
Allow the dark jacket and hood, adding a reflective strip across the hood, since reflective material makes up for lost vision and hearing
why: A banksman cannot replace the worker's own ability to see and hear, and a dark garment still leaves him hard for drivers to spot.
A hooded sweatshirt does not keep out rain and the hood still limits side vision and hearing, so the problem remains.
A reflective strip may help drivers see him but does nothing to restore the vision and hearing he loses with the hood up.
bank.ex: Wet-weather clothing has to keep the wearer visible to drivers and still allow him to see and hear plant, so conspicuity and the hood design both matter.
bank.cm: Judging wet-weather clothing only on whether it keeps the wearer dry, ignoring its effect on being seen and on hearing plant.

bank.stem: A fitter wipes a hydraulic hose on a tracked excavator with his gloved hand and feels a sting. There is a tiny pinhole in his fingertip, with little pain and no bleeding. He wants to finish the shift. What should happen?
o: Clean and plaster the puncture, then watch it for a day, as a small painless wound with no bleeding is unlikely to be deep
Squeeze the finger to push the oil back out and wash it with soap, because removing the fluid quickly stops it spreading
He should go to hospital urgently and tell staff it may be a high-pressure injection, as deep damage can hide beneath a small mark
Record it in the accident book and see his GP if swelling appears, since hospital treatment is for wounds that bleed or hurt badly
why: The small, painless appearance is typical of an injection injury, and delay can lead to amputation.
Squeezing can drive the fluid further into the tissue, and washing does not remove what is already under the skin.
Waiting for swelling or pain wastes the critical early hours, and the severity of the injury does not match its look.
bank.ex: Fluid forced under the skin by a pinhole leak can destroy deep tissue while the surface looks trivial, so it needs urgent specialist treatment.
bank.cm: Judging an injury by how small and painless it looks rather than by what was under pressure.

bank.stem: A contractor will pressure-wash flaking old paint, possibly lead-based, and algae from a brick facade beside a road. The run- off would flow along the kerb to a surface-water drain, and the foreman suggests a gully sock to catch the solids. What is better?
o: Keep the gully sock and add a spill kit beside the drain, since a sock removes dissolved paint residues as well as solids
Add a biodegradable detergent to the wash water, because water treated with it is safe for the surface-water drain
Wash only on dry, warm days so the run-off evaporates, because the water will dry before it can reach the gully
Collect the run-off with bunds and a vacuum, settle or filter it, and dispose of it with the sewerage undertaker's consent or as waste
why: A sock catches only coarse solids and does nothing to dissolved or very fine pollutants such as lead compounds.
Detergent adds pollution, and it does not make water containing paint residues acceptable for a surface-water drain.
Run-off from pressure washing flows freely and is not removed by evaporation, so the paint residues still reach the drain.
bank.ex: Surface-water drains lead to watercourses, so contaminated wash water must be contained and disposed of through a route with consent rather than allowed into them.
bank.cm: Treating a gully sock or a spill kit as enough to let contaminated wash water run into a surface-water drain.

diag.stem: An electrician employed by a subcontractor arrives to start work on a new-build site. He assumes the induction is the main contractor's job alone and plans to skim the rules afterwards. Which statement is correct?
o: The principal contractor must provide the induction, but responsibility for the rules then rests with the site manager rather than with individual workers
The principal contractor must ensure a suitable induction is provided, and the electrician must still follow the site rules and report shortcomings
The electrician's own employer must run the induction, and the principal contractor only has to confirm that the electrician holds a valid CSCS card
Induction is good practice rather than a legal requirement, so the electrician may decline it if he has worked on similar sites before
why: Workers have their own legal duties to follow site rules and to take reasonable care.
The principal contractor must ensure a suitable site-specific induction, and a card does not replace it.
Site induction is a requirement under CDM, and previous experience elsewhere does not remove it.
diag.ex: The principal contractor must make sure a suitable induction is given, but each worker also has a legal duty to cooperate, follow the site rules and report dangers.
diag.cm: Thinking that once the principal contractor has run the induction, the worker has no further duties to follow the rules or speak up. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 1 --- Legal Responsibilities

diag.stem: A groundworks firm starts on a small site on Monday. The client says toilets and washing facilities will arrive on Wednesday, and meanwhile the crew can use a tap by the neighbouring yard, which is marked as not for drinking. What is the correct view?
o: The duty to provide welfare belongs to the client, so the firm can start work and leave the delay for the client to resolve
Two days without them is acceptable for a small crew, provided the crew is told to bring bottled water and use the yard toilets
Toilets, washing facilities and drinking water must be there from the start, so work should not begin until they are provided
The tap is fine for washing and for drinking in an emergency, as long as the crew boils the water before they use it
why: Contractors also have duties for the welfare of their own workers, and the client cannot remove them.
There is no grace period, and relying on a neighbour's facilities does not meet the duty to provide welfare.
A supply marked as not for drinking is unsuitable for drinking, and boiling does not make an unknown supply wholesome.
diag.ex: Welfare facilities, including a supply of wholesome drinking water, have to be in place when work starts, and a tap marked as not for drinking cannot meet that duty.
diag.cm: Treating welfare as something that can follow the start of work. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 5 --- Occupational Health and Welfare

diag.stem: Look at the scene. The supervisor says the worker is properly protected because he is wearing an FFP3 mask rated for fine dust. What is the main problem with this view?
o: The mask is rated too low for plaster dust, so a higher-grade disposable mask with a valve would give the seal and protection that he needs
A tight-fitting mask can only protect if it seals to bare skin, so a different type of RPE or a change of work method is needed
The only fault is that the window is closed, since fresh air through the room will carry the remaining dust away from his face and lungs
The mask needs only a quick check on the day, and tightening the straps will close the gaps and keep dust out of the breathing zone
why: A higher grade does not cure a leaking seal, because every tight-fitting mask depends on contact with skin.
Ventilation helps, but it does not replace RPE that actually fits the wearer.
Tighter straps cannot make a mask seal over hair, and a fit test is not a strap adjustment.
diag.ex: Tight-fitting facepieces rely on a seal against the skin, so the rating alone does not guarantee protection and alternative RPE or better dust control is needed.
diag.cm: Judging respiratory protection by the mask's rating without checking that it can seal against the wearer's face. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 6 --- PPE and Signage
diag.alt: A worker sands a wall with a long-handled sander connected to an extractor; he wears a hard hat, glasses, a disposable mask, a hi-vis vest and gloves.

diag.stem: Roofers must replace flashings on an old warehouse roof. The rooflights are green with moss and look just like the sheets around them, and the foreman says that anything which is not obviously glass can be walked on. What is the best plan?
o: Treat every rooflight and sheet as fragile whatever it looks like, and use edge protection, rooflight covers and staging for any walking
Walk only on the sheets that look sound and sit next to a purlin line, and mark the rooflights with spray paint so the crew can step around them
Rely on a harness clipped to a long lanyard anywhere across the roof, since a fall would then be arrested before the worker reached the floor
Test each rooflight by pressing a boot on it first, and only keep clear of those that flex or crack when they take weight
why: Appearance is not a reliable guide, and paint marks do not stop a person falling through.
Fall arrest at height across a fragile roof is a last resort that was not planned, and clearance is rarely enough.
A test of this kind can itself cause a failure and tells the worker nothing about how it will bear a fall.
diag.ex: Weathered rooflights and old sheets can fail without warning, so they should be treated as fragile and protected with covers, edge protection and load-spreading staging.
diag.cm: Judging whether a roof will carry weight by how it looks instead of treating the whole surface as fragile until proved otherwise. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 7 --- Working at Height

diag.stem: On a school refurbishment, all waste goes into one skip and is sorted by the waste firm later. The site manager decides to improve things. Which arrangement best supports both recycling and safe disposal?
o: Separate the waste where it arises into clearly signed skips for each type, brief the crews on what goes where, and keep hazardous waste apart
Provide signed skips only at the main gate, and ask the crews to carry their waste across site to them at the end of each working week
Label the skips by colour but give no briefing, since workers can identify the right container from the colours without needing to be told
Keep one mixed skip but add a large sign that lists forbidden items, since the waste firm will sort whatever arrives and carries the legal duty
why: Skips need to be close to where waste arises, or crews will dump it in the nearest place instead.
Labels work only if the crews know what they mean, so some briefing is needed.
Mixed loads cut recycling, and the producer of the waste still has duties for how it is handled.
diag.ex: Segregating at source into clearly labelled containers keeps materials clean enough to recycle and prevents hazardous items contaminating other loads.
diag.cm: Assuming a mixed skip is acceptable because someone further down the chain will sort the waste out. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 10 --- Environmental Protection

diag.stem: A slab pour was assessed for a concrete pump, but the pump breaks down and the gang proposes barrowing from a skip beside an unprotected edge. The supervisor says the assessment already covers placing concrete. What is the correct response?
o: Carry on with the barrows, then amend the assessment at the next monthly review, as the existing document already names concrete placing as a task
Pause the pour, review the assessment for the new method, amend controls such as routes and edge protection, and brief the gang first
Allow the most experienced operative to choose safe barrow routes by judgement on the day, and note any changes on the paperwork after the pour
Add a handwritten line to the original assessment saying barrows may be used, and have the supervisor initial it before the first load goes out
why: Waiting for a scheduled review lets the new hazards go uncontrolled, whereas a significant change requires review before work.
Leaving controls to individual judgement and writing them up afterwards does not give workers the planned controls before they start.
A single line adds no assessment of the new manual handling, edge or route hazards and tells the gang nothing about controls.
diag.ex: A significant change in the work means the assessment must be reviewed and changed before the new method starts, and workers told of the new controls.
diag.cm: Do not assume an assessment covering the task name stays valid when the way of doing it changes. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 2 --- Risk Assessment

diag.stem: Look at the scene. The bricklayer says the scaffold is tied, fully boarded and has a ladder, so it is ready for work. What is the most significant problem?
o: The scaffold boards cover the lift fully and leave no space for storing bricks and mortar tubs, so materials need a separate tray
The ladder rises through a hatch in the platform and should be moved to the outside of the scaffold at the end bay
The ties to the wall are visible and will need to be removed before he can lay the courses near the top of the wall
He has built himself a higher standing level on the boards, so the guardrails no longer protect him from falling over the edge
why: Full boarding is correct, and materials can be stored on the platform within its loading limits.
A ladder through a protected hatch is an accepted access arrangement and is not the main hazard here.
Ties must stay in place while the scaffold is in use and cannot be removed to suit the work.
diag.ex: Standing on stacked blocks and bricks raises his position above the guardrail, so the edge protection is no longer effective; the scaffold should be adjusted to the correct working height.
diag.cm: Checking that scaffold parts are present without checking how people actually stand and work on them. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 7 --- Working at Height
diag.alt: A bricklayer works on a scaffold lift with blocks and bricks stacked on the boards; other workers stand on the ground below.

diag.stem: A supervisor reads the safety data sheet for a solvent-based floor primer. Section 8 suggests organic-vapour respirators, so he orders them. A water-based primer, suitable for the substrate, is available at a slightly higher price. What is the best next step?
o: Keep the solvent product and add forced ventilation, because extra cost is a valid reason to skip substitution whenever a control already exists
Switch to the water-based product and drop the assessment, since a less hazardous product removes any need for a record of the risks
Follow the sheet exactly, because suppliers set the required controls and the employer has met its duty once the recommended respirators are issued
Use the data sheet as input to the COSHH assessment, and first consider swapping to the water-based product before relying on respirators
why: Substitution comes before other controls where reasonably practicable, and a small price difference does not make it impracticable.
Even a safer product needs checking through the assessment, and its own data sheet must be read.
The sheet is supplier information, and the employer must still assess the risk and consider substitution first.
diag.ex: COSHH requires employers to eliminate or substitute a hazardous substance where reasonably practicable before controls such as RPE, and the sheet only informs the assessment.
diag.cm: Treating the PPE section of a data sheet as the finished control plan instead of first asking whether the hazard can be removed. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 4 --- Hazardous Substances, Noise, Vibration and Manual Handling

diag.stem: A delivery lorry must reverse into a tight yard. The storeman acting as banksman keeps stepping away to sign delivery notes, then stands directly behind the lorry to stop it at the wall. What is the most appropriate correction?
o: Keep the storeman as banksman, but ask the driver to reverse more slowly and sound the horn, because speed is the main danger in a tight yard
Let the driver judge the wall using his mirrors and camera, and call the storeman only if he feels unsure, as the driver has final control of the lorry
Give the signaller no other duties while the lorry moves, agree signals first, and place them in a safe visible spot beside the path
Let the storeman keep both jobs but stand behind the lorry so the driver can see his hi-vis in the mirrors, as that gives the closest view of the wall
why: Slower speed and a horn do not fix a distracted signaller or an unsafe position, and they replace no proper control.
The driver cannot see everything behind the lorry, and relying on him to ask for help removes the supervision the site planned.
Standing in the reversing path puts the signaller where he can be crushed, and divided attention leaves the movement unsupervised.
diag.ex: A banksman needs full attention, agreed signals and a protected position in the driver's view, because standing in the swept path or being distracted defeats the control.
diag.cm: Do not assume that any person in hi-vis who stands behind a reversing vehicle counts as a proper banksman. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 9 --- Plant, Vehicles and Lifting

diag.stem: A 1.8 m supported trench has a ladder with its top level with the ground, and a spoil heap beside the access point. The excavator is parked next to the heap. Which set of changes best provides safe access and edge control?
o: Extend the secured ladder about 1 m above the landing, keep the landing clear, set spoil back from the edge and park the machine well away
Provide a longer ladder resting on the spoil heap, so the climb is shorter, and park the excavator behind it, to prevent anyone being struck by the bucket
Leave the ladder where it is, but trim the spoil heap flat at the access point so workers can step across it, and keep the excavator engine switched off
Remove the ladder and rely on the excavator bucket to lift workers out in an emergency, since a bucket can reach the trench floor faster than climbing
why: A ladder resting on loose spoil is on an unstable base, and parking the machine close to the edge still adds load to the sides.
Spoil left at the edge still loads the sides and can fall in, and a ladder that does not rise above the landing gives no handhold.
Lifting people in a bucket is not an approved means of access, and an everyday climb out needs a proper secured route.
diag.ex: A ladder should stand firmly and rise at least 1 m above the landing, with spoil and plant kept back so they add no load to the sides or into the access.
diag.cm: Do not treat a ladder that merely reaches ground level as proper access, or plant parked beside the edge as harmless. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 8 --- Excavations, Confined Spaces and Electrical

diag.stem: Look at the picture of a precast beam being placed. The crane operator says the beam is well within the load chart and the slings are in date. What is the most significant problem, and the best correction?
o: Only one signaller is present, so a second one should stand beneath the beam beside the first to confirm each movement as it is lowered
The lifted beam has no spreader beam fitted, so the lift should continue until the bricklayers have a spreader beam delivered to the working area
A person is working under the load, so stop, lower it and keep everyone clear until positioning is arranged from outside its path
The man's hard hat gives no protection from a beam, so he should wear a higher-grade helmet and stay in place while the beam is lowered
why: A second person in the same position doubles the number exposed to the load and fixes nothing.
Missing lifting accessories are not the main issue in the picture, and continuing the lift leaves the man under the load.
No helmet will protect against a precast beam falling, and PPE does not replace keeping people out of the danger zone.
diag.ex: No one should be beneath or within reach of a suspended load, because a slip or failure would crush them, so positioning must be planned from a safe place.
diag.cm: Do not think a load within the chart and good slings makes it safe for someone to stand under it. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 9 --- Plant, Vehicles and Lifting
diag.alt: A mobile crane lifts a precast concrete beam on chains near a block wall; a worker reaches up to the beam while another signals to the crane.

diag.stem: A trained worker opens a first-floor storeroom with one door and finds a waste bin burning by the far wall, flames at knee height. A water extinguisher hangs beside the door. Which response is correct?
o: Close the door on the fire, walk back to the cabin to find the supervisor, and leave the decision about the alarm to him once he has looked
Tackle it straight away while it is small, because speed matters most, and raise the alarm afterwards only if the extinguisher fails to put the fire out
Move past the bin to attack it from the far side, keeping a clear view of the whole fire, and shout for help only if flames reach the wall
Shout and operate the alarm so others leave, then tackle it only while it stays small and the door is behind him, withdrawing at once if it grows
why: Closing the door is sensible, but walking off to find someone instead of raising the alarm immediately wastes vital minutes for everyone else in the building.
Delaying the alarm leaves others unaware and gives no warning if the attempt fails, so raising the alarm must come before any fire-fighting.
Standing beyond the fire puts it between him and the only exit, which breaks the rule of always fighting a fire with an escape route behind you.
diag.ex: The alarm must be raised first so everyone can escape, and a trained person should only attempt a small fire while keeping a clear exit behind them.
diag.cm: Assuming that a small fire and a trained person mean you can deal with it first and sort out the alarm and your escape route later. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 3 --- Accidents and Fire

diag.stem: A 65 kg cast-iron roll-top bath must reach a first-floor bathroom up a narrow stair with a turn. A window opening is wide enough, and a telehandler with a suitable lifting attachment is on site. What is the correct approach?
o: Have four fit workers carry it up the stair, since their combined strength comfortably exceeds the weight of the bath and the carry is only short
Brief the team on good lifting posture and agree rest breaks, since training and job rotation are the main controls for heavy awkward loads
Avoid the stair carry by hoisting the bath through the window, then assess and reduce the short remaining handling with aids and trained people
Strap it to a stair-climbing sack truck and send two workers up, as a mechanical aid means the route and load need no further assessment
why: Adding people does not remove the awkward shape, narrow turn and poor grip, and it skips the duty to avoid the handling when a mechanical option exists.
Training and rotation are weak controls that cannot make a 65 kg awkward load safe, and they ignore the higher-order option of avoiding the carry.
A truck reduces some effort but is not the first step, and the stair turn, footing and load stability still have to be assessed.
diag.ex: The regulations require hazardous handling to be avoided where reasonably practicable, and only then assessed and reduced, so a mechanical lift through the window comes before any carrying plan.
diag.cm: Jumping straight to who is strong enough to lift the load instead of first asking whether it needs to be carried by hand at all. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 4 --- Hazardous Substances, Noise, Vibration and Manual Handling

diag.stem: Look at the scene. The labourer says the lead is heavy-duty and the tool is protected by an RCD, so it is fine to carry on. What is the most significant risk of electric shock?
o: A cable coupling sits in standing water at ground level, so water can reach live parts; raise it clear and use a waterproof type
The lead is much longer than the job needs, so it should be wound tightly onto a drum to cut voltage drop and stop anyone tripping on it
The lead is yellow, a colour meant for dry indoor work only, so it should be swapped for a blue 230 V lead to cope with the rain
The lead passes close to the scaffold tubes, which can conduct current into the structure, so it must be rerouted well away from all scaffolding
why: A cable wound tightly on a drum while in use can overheat, and length and tripping are not the shock hazard the picture shows.
Yellow identifies the reduced 110 V supply that is the preferred choice on site, and a 230 V lead would raise the shock risk in wet conditions.
Scaffold tubes carry no current from an undamaged lead, and the real concern is the water reaching the connection, not simple proximity to the scaffold.
diag.ex: Connections left in puddles can let water reach live conductors, so couplings must be kept off the ground and be of a suitably water-resistant rating, not relied on to be saved by an RCD.
diag.cm: Believing that an RCD or a heavy-duty lead makes it acceptable to leave electrical connections lying in water. CHAPTER TO REVISE: Chapter 8 --- Excavations, Confined Spaces and Electrical
diag.alt: A worker uses a power tool on a wet, puddled site; a yellow extension lead runs from a site distribution unit across the ground.

diag.stem: At shift start an operator finds a boom MEWP left by the night crew, who say it ran fine. The hire firm's thorough examination report is in date. The route to the work area crosses a bay with overhead pipework. What should he do?
o: Do a visual walk-round for leaks and damage, since function tests belong to the hire company, then plan the route while he drives the machine
Carry out his own pre-use check, including emergency stop and lowering function tests from both control positions, and survey the route and work area first
Rely on the night crew's word and the in-date examination report, and watch for the overhead pipework as he travels with the basket raised
Test only the controls he will use from the basket, because ground controls and emergency lowering are covered by the six-monthly examination
why: Visual checks alone miss failed controls and safety devices, and route planning must be done before the machine moves, not during travel.
Another crew's verbal assurance is no substitute for his own checks, and spotting obstructions only while travelling raised comes too late.
The ground controls and emergency lowering must be proved before use since they are what a rescuer depends on, and the examination interval cannot cover daily faults.
diag.ex: Each operator should check the machine and test its controls before use, as an in-date examination does not replace the daily check, and the route and working area must be surveyed for hazards.
diag.cm: Treating an in-date examination report or a colleague's say-so as proof that the machine is safe to use today.
